script.speaker: A
script.text: Good afternoon, Westbrook Adult College, Maria speaking. How can I help you?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hi there. I picked up a leaflet about your evening classes, and I wondered whether there are still places on the pottery course.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Let me have a look. We actually run two this term. There's a beginners' group and an intermediate one.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I've never touched clay in my life, so beginners, definitely.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That one still has four places left. Shall I take a few details? Could I have your name?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes, it's Callum Reyes. Reyes is spelt R, E, Y, E, S.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thank you, Callum. Now, the leaflet says the course begins on the second of September, but that's a mistake, I'm afraid. The studio is being repainted that week, so the first session is on the ninth of September.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The ninth. That's fine. And it's in the evening?

script.speaker: A
script.text: It is. Classes start at seven, and they used to finish at nine, but the tutor asked for extra time for clearing up, so you'll be out by nine fifteen.

script.speaker: B
script.text: OK. Where do I go when I arrive?

script.speaker: A
script.text: It's in the arts block, which is the building behind the car park. You want room fourteen, on the ground floor. Room twelve next door is the painting studio, and people often walk into that one by accident.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fourteen, got it. How much does it cost?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The full fee is one hundred and forty pounds for the ten weeks. Do you live in Westbrook itself?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I do, yes, on Canal Street.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then you qualify for the residents' rate, which is one hundred and twenty-five pounds. That includes all the clay and the firing.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Great. Do I need to buy any tools?

script.speaker: A
script.text: No, tools are provided. The only thing we ask you to bring is an old apron, because it does get messy. Can I ask what made you choose pottery?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Well, my job means I stare at a computer all day, and I really want to get away from screens and make something with my hands. A friend suggested a painting class, but that didn't appeal to me.

script.speaker: A
script.text: You'll enjoy it, then. The tutor, Helen, has been with us for ten years. She used to run sessions for children as well, though she's stopped those now, and she still shows her own work at the gallery in town.

script.speaker: B
script.text: She sounds good. What happens if I have to miss a week? I travel for work now and then.

script.speaker: A
script.text: We can't refund single sessions, and the Thursday group is full, so you couldn't swap. But there's an open studio every Saturday morning where you can catch up on whatever you missed.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's useful. Can I pay now?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Of course, I can take a card payment over the phone.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Oh, my card's in my jacket downstairs. Could I pay through your website instead?

script.speaker: A
script.text: You can, but we only hold the place for forty-eight hours.

script.speaker: B
script.text: No problem. I'll do it tonight when I get home.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good morning, everybody, and thank you for giving up your time to help at the Harbour Museum. My name's Graham, and I look after the volunteer team. I'll keep this short, because the best way to learn is to get out onto the floor.

script.speaker: C
script.text: First, a little background. People often think the museum has always been here on the quay, but it only moved into this building six years ago. Before that, the collection was squeezed into two rooms above the town library. This building was originally a warehouse for storing grain, and you can still see the old lifting equipment in the roof.

script.speaker: C
script.text: You might wonder why we need volunteers at all. It isn't really about saving money. Our visitor surveys showed that what people remember most is talking to somebody who knows the place, and paid staff simply don't have time for long conversations. So that's where you come in.

script.speaker: C
script.text: You'll each do one shift a week, and a shift lasts three and a half hours. We did try full days when the scheme began, but people found them exhausting. During your first month, you'll always be paired with an experienced volunteer. After that, you'll usually work on your own.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, uniform. There isn't one, apart from the blue badge I'm about to hand out. Wear whatever is comfortable, but please choose sensible shoes, because the floors are stone and you'll be standing for a long time.

script.speaker: C
script.text: If a visitor asks something you can't answer, please don't guess. Write the question in the red notebook at the information desk, and one of the curators will reply to the visitor by email. Visitors really appreciate that.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let me explain what you'll do in each part of the building. In the entrance hall, your job is simply to give out the audio guides. Tickets are checked by the staff at the desk, so you needn't worry about those.

script.speaker: C
script.text: In the maritime gallery, the model ships are very fragile, and I'm afraid people can't resist putting their hands on them. Your main task there is to stop that happening, as politely as you can.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The discovery room is aimed at families. Children can try on sailors' clothes and tie knots, and you'll be supervising those activities and keeping things tidy.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The temporary exhibition changes every three months, so we don't expect you to be an expert on it. We just need you to keep a count of the people going in, using the small clicker by the door, because our funding depends on those figures.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, the garden. In summer, visitors wander out there and can't find their way back to the café or the exit, so volunteers in the garden mostly give directions. Right, let's collect your badges.

title: Urban heat presentation and the history of timekeeping

parts.context: You will hear two geography students, Aisha and Tom, planning a presentation about urban heat islands.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.prompt: What surprised Tom in his reading about urban heat islands?

options.A: how much heat is produced by traffic
options.C: how little difference air conditioning makes

questions.prompt: What was the tutor's criticism of their previous presentation?

options.B: The slides were difficult to follow.
options.C: It tried to include too much.

questions.prompt: Aisha prefers Leicester as a case study because

options.A: it will be more familiar to the audience.
options.B: more data has been collected there.
options.C: no other group has studied a British city.

questions.prompt: The temperature map of Leicester was produced using
The students decide to recommend reflective roofs mainly because they

options.A: are quick to have an effect.
options.B: also provide shade in the street.

groups.instruction: What do the students decide about each part of the presentation? Choose FIVE answers from the list and write the correct letter, A-G, next to questions 6-10.

options.D: They will ask another student to do it.
options.E: They will ask the tutor for it.

questions.prompt: introduction
graphic of the temperature map
solutions section
questions for the end
handout

parts.context: You will hear part of a lecture about the history of measuring time.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Right, Tom, we've got two weeks until the presentation. Shall we decide how to divide it up?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Sure. I've been reading about why cities are hotter than the countryside, and honestly I assumed it was all down to traffic and air conditioning pumping out heat.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's what most people think. But the reading list makes it clear that the biggest factor is the materials. Concrete and tarmac soak up heat all day and release it at night.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes, that surprised me. So we should lead with that, not with car exhausts.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Agreed. Now, Doctor Patel said our last presentation was well researched. Her criticism was that we tried to cover too much and ran out of time.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I thought she didn't like the slides.

script.speaker: A
script.text: No, she said the slides were clear. It was the timing. So this time we need to be selective.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fine. What about a case study? I was going to suggest Phoenix, since there's so much data on it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Everyone does Phoenix. I'd rather use the study of Leicester, because it's a medium-sized city and it's closer to what our audience knows.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Is there enough information on Leicester?

script.speaker: A
script.text: There's a full temperature map, made by volunteers who fixed sensors to their bicycles.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Oh, I like that. OK, Leicester it is. And for the solutions section, the obvious one is planting trees.

script.speaker: A
script.text: It is, but the article by Santos argues that trees take twenty years to make a real difference. Painting roofs white works almost immediately and costs far less.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Although a white roof doesn't give you shade on the street.

script.speaker: A
script.text: True, and we should say so. But I think the speed is what makes it worth recommending.

script.speaker: B
script.text: All right, I'm persuaded. We'll recommend reflective roofs and mention trees as the long-term measure.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Now, who does what? I'll write the introduction, because I've already drafted most of it.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Then I'll take the causes, since I've done that reading. What about the map of Leicester? Somebody needs to turn the data into a graphic.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Neither of us is much good at that. My flatmate studies design. I'll ask her to do it, and we'll credit her on the slide.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good idea. And the solutions section?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Let's write that together on Friday, because that's the part we disagree on most.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fair enough. The questions at the end worry me. Doctor Patel always asks something difficult.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Last year's group told me she gives you the questions in advance if you ask.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Really? Then let's request them from her. I'll send the email today.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Great. And the handout?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Do we need one? It's a lot of printing.

script.speaker: A
script.text: We don't have to print. The department wants everything on the course website now, so we'll just upload it there the night before.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Perfect. Then I think we've got a plan.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Today I want to look at how people have measured time, and at how each new method changed the way societies were organised.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The earliest devices were shadow clocks, used in Egypt about three and a half thousand years ago. They divided daylight into twelve parts, but the length of each part changed with the season, so a summer hour was longer than a winter one. Nobody found this strange. And of course a shadow clock had one obvious weakness, which is that it could not be used at night.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The solution was the water clock, in which water dripped at a steady rate from one container into another. These were used in courts of law in ancient Athens to limit how long each speaker could talk. Their drawback was temperature, because in cold weather the water flowed more slowly and the clock lost time.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Mechanical clocks appeared in Europe around the end of the thirteenth century. Interestingly, the first ones had no face and no hands. They simply rang a bell, and the people who needed them most were monks, who had to pray at fixed times of day and night. Early clocks were driven by a falling weight, which meant they had to be placed high up in a tower.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The great leap in accuracy came in sixteen fifty-six, when the Dutch scientist Huygens built a clock controlled by a pendulum. Before that, a good clock might lose fifteen minutes a day. Afterwards, the error fell to about fifteen seconds, and for the first time it made sense to add a minute hand.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Pendulum clocks were useless at sea, however, because of the movement of the ship. This mattered a great deal, since a navigator needed the exact time in order to work out his longitude. The problem was solved by John Harrison, who was trained not as a scientist but as a carpenter. His fourth timekeeper looked like a large pocket watch, and on a voyage to Jamaica it lost only five seconds.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Until the nineteenth century, every town still kept its own local time, set by the sun. Bristol was about ten minutes behind London, and it didn't matter until the arrival of the railways. Timetables were impossible with dozens of local times, so the railway companies imposed a single standard, and the news of the correct time was sent along the lines by telegraph.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, in the twentieth century, the pendulum gave way to the vibrations of a quartz crystal, and then to the atomic clock. And it's worth remembering that the satellite navigation in your phone depends entirely on atomic clocks agreeing with one another.

explanations.1: He had assumed traffic and air conditioning were the cause; the biggest factor is concrete and tarmac.
explanations.2: She said it was well researched and the slides were clear, but they ran out of time.
explanations.3: It is medium-sized and closer to what the audience knows; Phoenix has more data.
explanations.4: Volunteers fixed sensors to their bicycles.
explanations.5: Trees take twenty years; white roofs work almost immediately.
explanations.6: Aisha has already drafted most of it.
explanations.7: Aisha will ask her flatmate, who studies design.
explanations.8: They will write it together on Friday.
explanations.9: They will request the questions from Doctor Patel.
explanations.10: It will be uploaded to the course website rather than printed.

options.C: It was too expensive for most people.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Hello, Dawson Lettings, Peter speaking.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hi, I'm calling about the one-bedroom flat you've advertised on Marlow Road. Is it still available?

script.speaker: A
script.text: It is, yes. Are you looking for yourself?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes, just me. I'm starting a job at the hospital next month.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Lovely. Let me give you the details, and then we can arrange a viewing. The flat's on the second floor. There isn't a lift, I should say, but the stairs are wide.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's fine. The advert said the rent was eight hundred and fifty pounds a month. Does that include bills?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The eight fifty covers water, but nothing else. You'd pay for electricity and the internet yourself. Heating is electric, so there's no gas bill.

script.speaker: B
script.text: OK. And the deposit?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The deposit is one thousand two hundred pounds. It used to be two months' rent, but the owner reduced it last year.

script.speaker: B
script.text: One thousand two hundred. Right. Is the flat furnished?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Partly. There's a bed, a sofa and a wardrobe. What it doesn't have is a washing machine, although there's space for one in the kitchen. The last tenant took hers when she left.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I've got my own, so that's no problem. What about parking? I'll be driving to work.

script.speaker: A
script.text: There's no private parking, but you can apply to the council for a permit to park on the street. It costs about sixty pounds a year.

script.speaker: B
script.text: A permit. OK. And how long is the contract?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The owner wants a minimum of twelve months. After that it continues month by month.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I was hoping for six, to be honest, but I suppose twelve is all right. Are pets allowed? I have a cat.

script.speaker: A
script.text: A cat should be fine. The owner refused a tenant with a large dog once, but she's told us that cats are acceptable, provided you pay for a professional clean at the end.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's reasonable. When could I see it?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I've got Wednesday at five, or Friday morning at half past ten.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'm working on Friday. Wednesday at five, please.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. I'll meet you outside. Look for the green door, between the bakery and the pharmacy. The number has fallen off, so people walk straight past it.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Green door, by the bakery. Got it. What do I need to bring if I decide to take it?

script.speaker: A
script.text: A photo ID, and a letter from your employer confirming your salary. We don't need bank statements.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The hospital can give me a letter. And who do I ask for on Wednesday?

script.speaker: A
script.text: It'll be me, Peter Vance. That's V, A, N, C, E.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Thanks, Peter. One last thing. When could I move in?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The flat is being decorated at the moment, so the earliest date would be the third of June.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The third of June would suit me perfectly.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, if you've walked through the city centre this week, you'll have noticed rows of bright orange bicycles. They belong to Northfield Wheels, the hire scheme that started on Monday, and I've been finding out how it works.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The idea isn't new, of course. A similar scheme was tried here eight years ago, and it closed within eighteen months. The bikes were fine. The trouble was that there were only five places to collect and return them, so they were never where people needed them. This time, there are forty docking stations, and none is more than four hundred metres from the next.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Who's paying for it? Well, many people assume it comes out of council tax, but in fact the council has only provided the land. The bikes themselves were paid for by a regional transport grant, and the running costs should be covered by the hire charges.

script.speaker: C
script.text: So, how do you use it? You need to register first, and the simplest way is with the phone app, although you can also do it at the tourist office in Market Square. Then you unlock a bike by scanning the code on the handlebars.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The first thirty minutes of every journey are free. After that, you pay one pound for each extra half hour. If you think you'll use the bikes regularly, an annual pass is thirty-five pounds, and that gives you a free hour each time rather than half an hour.

script.speaker: C
script.text: I tried one yesterday. The bike is heavier than my own, but it's comfortable, and it has three gears, which is enough for our hills. There's a basket at the front, big enough for a small bag of shopping, and the lights come on automatically. What you don't get is a helmet, so you'll have to bring your own.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A few rules. You must be at least sixteen to hire a bike. The bikes can be used between five in the morning and midnight, and you have to return them to a docking station, not leave them in the street. Leave one outside a station and you'll be charged a fee of twenty pounds.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, there have been complaints already. Several listeners have told us that the station outside the railway station was empty by eight in the morning. The company says a van will move bikes around the city during the day, and that they'll add a second station there before the summer.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And one more date for your diary. On the last Sunday of this month, the scheme is running free guided rides for nervous cyclists, starting from the park gates. Places are limited, so book through the app.

explanations.11: The bikes were fine, but there were only five places to collect and return them.
explanations.12: The council only provided the land; hire charges cover the running costs.
explanations.13: The simplest way is with the phone app.
explanations.14: A free hour each time rather than half an hour.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Come in, Marco. So, I've read your proposal on bilingual children. Tell me how you arrived at the topic.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Well, I'd planned to write about how adults learn a second language. Then last summer I worked at a holiday club where half the children spoke Polish at home, and I got curious about how they moved between the two languages.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So it grew out of experience, not out of the lectures. That's often the best way. Now, your research question is whether bilingual children are better at switching between tasks. What made you focus on that?

script.speaker: B
script.text: A lot of articles claim there's a bilingual advantage in attention. But when I looked closely, the recent, larger studies often fail to find it. I'd like to know which side is right.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. That disagreement is exactly what makes it worth doing. How many children are you hoping to test?

script.speaker: B
script.text: My proposal said a hundred, but I'm beginning to think that's unrealistic. Each session takes forty minutes.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'd aim for sixty. Thirty bilingual and thirty monolingual would be enough for the statistics, and you could finish in a term.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Sixty sounds manageable. I'll use two primary schools where I already have contacts.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Fine. Now, I have a concern about how you're matching the groups. You say the children will be the same age. Is that enough?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I thought so. Should I match them on school results as well?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Not results. Family income. Several of the early studies compared bilingual children from wealthy families with monolingual children from poorer ones, and the so-called advantage may simply have been the effect of income.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I see. I could ask the parents about their jobs on the consent form.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That would work. And the task itself, the card-sorting game. Why that one, and not a computer test?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The computer tests give more precise timings. But the children I worked with got bored in front of a screen, and with cards I can keep them interested.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's a sensible reason, as long as you record the sessions. Now, let's talk about the order of things. What comes first?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Ethics approval from the department. Nothing can happen until I've got that.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Right. It takes about three weeks, so apply now. And while you're waiting?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll run a pilot with a few children from my neighbour's family, to check that the instructions are clear.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. After the pilot, you'll need written consent from the parents. Don't leave that late, because the forms come back slowly.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Then the testing itself, in the spring term. And then the analysis.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Before you analyse anything, give me your raw data to check. Students often find mistakes in the coding at that stage. Then book a session with the statistics adviser, and only after that start writing.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Understood. Should I send you a chapter each month?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Just the literature review by the end of January. We'll plan the rest from there.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good morning. This week we turn to bioluminescence, which simply means light produced by living things. On land it's rare. You may know fireflies and a few kinds of fungus. But in the deep ocean it's the normal state of affairs, and it's estimated that three quarters of the animals living there can make light.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let's start with how it works. The light comes from a chemical reaction. A molecule called luciferin combines with oxygen, and energy is released in the form of light. What's remarkable is the efficiency. An ordinary light bulb wastes most of its energy as heat, whereas this reaction produces almost none, which is why it's sometimes called cold light.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The colour is worth noting too. In the sea, nearly all of it is blue, and there's a good reason. Blue light travels furthest through water, while red light is absorbed within a few metres.

script.speaker: C
script.text: So what is the light for? Biologists have identified several functions. The first is defence. Some squid, when attacked, release a cloud of glowing liquid, which confuses the predator while the squid escapes into the dark.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A second defensive use is harder to spot. Many fish have rows of lights along the belly. Seen from below, the fish would normally appear as a dark shape against the faint light from the surface. By glowing, it hides its own shadow. So here, light is being used as camouflage.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Light is also used for hunting. The best known example is the anglerfish, which has a glowing lure hanging in front of its mouth. Interestingly, the fish doesn't make the light itself. The lure is full of bacteria, and these do the work in exchange for food and shelter.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The third function is communication. Fireflies are the classic case. Each species has its own pattern of flashes, and males and females use it to find a mate. There's even one species that imitates the signal of another, in order to attract males and eat them.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, why should the rest of us care? Well, the genes responsible have become one of the most useful tools in medicine. Researchers attach them to cancer cells, so that a tumour literally glows and its growth can be followed without surgery. The same reaction is used in the food industry, where it shows within minutes whether a surface is contaminated, a test that used to take two days.

script.speaker: C
script.text: There are more playful ideas as well. One company in France is experimenting with bacteria to light shop windows at night, which would need no electricity at all. Whether that can ever be bright enough is another matter, and that's where we'll pick up next week.

explanations.1: He worked at a holiday club where half the children spoke Polish at home.
explanations.2: Many articles claim an advantage, but recent larger studies often fail to find it.
explanations.3: Thirty bilingual and thirty monolingual, sixty in all; a hundred is unrealistic.
explanations.4: The advantage in early studies may simply have been the effect of income.
explanations.5: Children got bored in front of a screen; computer tests give more precise timings.

script.speaker: C

script.speaker: C

options.A: The equipment was not available in March.
options.B: Their tutor was away in March.
options.C: The water level was dangerous in March.

questions.prompt: Which equipment caused a problem during the survey?
The students counted insects because insects

options.B: show the quality of the water over a long period.

options.A: The river was most polluted outside the town.
options.B: The river was cleaner than in earlier surveys.
options.C: The readings varied very little between sites.

options.B: moving the cattle to another field
options.C: putting up a fence along the bank

groups.instruction: What did the students find at each of the following sites? Choose FIVE answers from the list and write the correct letter, A-G, next to questions 6-10.

options.E: water moving too fast to sample properly
options.G: clear water with a wide range of insects

questions.prompt: Site 1, above the farm
Site 2, below the farm
Site 3, beside the old factory
Site 4, under the town bridge
Site 5, at the weir

parts.context: You will hear part of a lecture about the psychology of waiting in queues.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So, Karim, the river report is due on Monday. Have you been through the results?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I have. First of all, I'm glad we went in April in the end. I wanted to go in March, remember.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I do. And the equipment had been booked for March. But the river was so high that nobody could have stood in it safely.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Exactly. Now, we ought to mention the problems with the equipment as a limitation.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes. I'd assumed the oxygen meter would let us down, because it's so old, but it behaved perfectly. It was the nets. Two of them had holes, and we lost half of one sample.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Right. And in the method section, I think we should explain why we counted insects instead of relying on chemical tests.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Because a chemical test only tells you about the moment you take the sample. The insects living on the river bed reflect what conditions have been like over several months.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good, that's clear. They're harder to identify, though. It took us hours.

script.speaker: A
script.text: It did. Now, what struck you most about the results overall?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Honestly, I expected the stretch through the town to be the dirtiest. All those roads and drains. But the worst readings were out in the countryside.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That surprised me too. So let's go through the sites one at a time. Site one, above the farm.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The water was completely clear there, and we found nine kinds of insect, including mayflies, which can only live in clean water. It's our best site by far.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then site two, just below the farm.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's where the nitrate reading was the highest of anywhere, three times the level at site one. I thought the number of insects would fall as well, but it hardly changed.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Not yet, perhaps. Site three, beside the old factory.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I was sure we'd find chemicals there. The readings were normal. What we did notice was that the water was a strange orange colour.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Doctor Hale says that's iron from the old mine workings, and it's harmless.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Then site four, under the town bridge. A shopping trolley, plastic bags, dozens of bottles. I took photographs.

script.speaker: A
script.text: A man fishing there told us the river was full of fish, but we never saw one.

script.speaker: B
script.text: No. And site five, at the weir. The current was so strong that we could hardly hold the net still, so we only managed one sample instead of three.

script.speaker: A
script.text: We'll have to say the results from that site are less reliable. Now, recommendations.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'd like to suggest planting trees along the bank below the farm.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Trees would take years. The cattle walk straight into the water there. If the farmer put up a fence, the bank would recover within a season.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's more realistic. A fence, then. Shall I draft that section?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Please. I'll do the tables.

script.speaker: C
script.text: This afternoon I'd like to talk about something we all do and nearly all dislike, which is waiting in a queue. It turns out that how long a wait feels has surprisingly little to do with how long it actually is.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let's begin with a basic finding. When researchers time people in a queue and then ask them how long they waited, the estimates are consistently too high. On average, people believe they have waited about a third longer than they really have.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The first principle is that time passes more slowly when we have nothing to do. A famous example comes from an office building in New York, where tenants complained about slow lifts. Speeding up the lifts would have been expensive. Instead, the manager had mirrors fitted beside the lift doors. People now had something to look at, namely themselves, and the complaints almost stopped.

script.speaker: C
script.text: An airport in Texas found a similar solution. Passengers were complaining about the wait for their bags. So the airport moved the arrival gates further away. Passengers now had to walk for six minutes before reaching the hall, the bags were already there when they arrived, and everyone was satisfied, although the total time had not changed at all.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The second principle is that uncertainty makes a wait feel longer. That's why theme parks put up signs showing the waiting time. And notice that the time shown is deliberately too long. If the sign says forty minutes and you reach the front in thirty, you feel that you've gained something.

script.speaker: C
script.text: In the same way, people tolerate a delay much better when they are given an explanation. A pilot who tells passengers why the plane isn't moving gets far fewer complaints than one who says nothing.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Third, fairness. Nothing makes people angrier than seeing someone who arrived later being served first. This is why banks and airports have moved to one winding line feeding several desks. Interestingly, people accept exceptions when they understand the reason. In a hospital emergency department, nobody objects when a patient whose need is urgent goes straight in.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Fourth, and this comes from research on memory, we don't judge an experience by its average. What matters most is the end. A queue that crawls and then suddenly speeds up is remembered far more kindly than one that starts quickly and then stops.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Businesses apply all this. Supermarkets put magazines beside the tills, partly to sell them, of course, but also to keep us occupied. And telephone helplines now tell callers their position in the queue, because knowing you are third is far easier to bear than silence.

explanations.1: The equipment had been booked for March, but the river was too high to stand in safely.
explanations.2: The old oxygen meter behaved perfectly; two nets had holes.
explanations.3: A chemical test only describes one moment; insects reflect conditions over several months.
explanations.4: They expected the town stretch to be dirtiest, but the worst readings were in the countryside.
explanations.5: Trees would take years; a fence would let the bank recover within a season.
explanations.6: Clear water and nine kinds of insect, including mayflies.
explanations.7: The highest nitrate reading; the number of insects hardly changed.
explanations.8: Normal readings, but the water was orange because of iron.
explanations.9: A trolley, bags and bottles; no fish were seen.
explanations.10: The current was too strong to hold the net still.

script.text: She asked for a new logo, to be honest. But I think that's the wrong place to start. What she needs first is to find out who her customers actually are now.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I agree. A survey, then. We could leave paper forms on the tables.

script.speaker: B
script.text: People never fill those in. I'd rather stand in the cafe for a few days and talk to customers face to face. We'd get fewer answers, but better ones.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That takes time, though. We've only got three weeks.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Two afternoons each would do it. Thirty short conversations would be enough for a project like this.

script.speaker: A
script.text: All right. And what about social media? Her page hasn't been updated since March.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I looked at it. The photos are good, but every post is an advertisement. Special offer, special offer. Nobody shares that.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So what should she post?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Stories. She buys her beans from one family farm in Peru. She should talk about that, about the people.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I like that. Now, the loyalty card. She stamps a paper card and gives the tenth coffee free.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And half the cards get lost. An app would solve that, but she can't afford one.

script.speaker: A
script.text: There's a cheaper way. Some cafes simply keep the card behind the counter, in a box, in alphabetical order. The customer never has to carry it.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's clever. And it means the staff learn people's names.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Exactly. Now, for the report, Professor Lund wants us to measure whether our ideas work.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We can't measure profit in three weeks.

script.speaker: A
script.text: No, but we can count how many customers come back within a week. The till records every card payment.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Repeat visits. Good. And the presentation? I hate talking to slides.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Why don't we film the owner explaining her problem in her own words, and build the talk around that?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Much better. I'll ask her on Thursday.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good afternoon. Today's subject is sleep, and in particular the remarkable variety of ways in which animals do it. Every animal that has been studied carefully turns out to sleep in some form, which suggests that sleep does something essential. Yet the way it's done differs enormously.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Take the amount. A large bat may sleep for nineteen hours a day, while a giraffe manages on less than two. The best predictor is not the size of the brain, as was once thought, but diet. Animals that eat plants must spend most of the day feeding, and so they have little time left for sleep, whereas meat eaters, such as lions, can afford long rests after a meal.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Then there's the question of safety. A sleeping animal is an easy target. Horses deal with this by sleeping on their feet, thanks to a locking mechanism in the legs. They do need to lie down for the deepest stage of sleep, but only for a few minutes at a time.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Dolphins face a different difficulty. They have to come to the surface to breathe, and they do that consciously. If a dolphin slept as we do, it would drown. Its solution is to rest one half of the brain at a time. The other half stays alert, and one eye remains open.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Some birds do the same thing. Ducks sleeping in a row are a nice example. Those at the ends of the row keep the outward eye open, watching for predators, while those in the middle sleep with both eyes closed.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Birds that migrate raise an even stranger problem. The frigatebird may stay in the air over the ocean for two months without landing. Recordings of its brain show that it does sleep while flying, but for only about forty minutes a day, in bursts of a few seconds. On land, the same bird sleeps for twelve hours.

script.speaker: C
script.text: What about much simpler animals? Fruit flies have been shown to sleep, and if they are kept awake, they sleep longer afterwards, exactly as we do. Even jellyfish, which have no brain at all, become less active at night.

script.speaker: C
script.text: So why do we sleep? One influential idea is that sleep allows the brain to clear away waste produced during the day. Another is that it's needed to fix memories. Young animals, which are learning fastest, sleep the most.

script.speaker: C
script.text: I'll finish with a warning about method. Almost everything we know comes from animals in zoos and laboratories. When sloths were finally studied in the wild, they slept for under ten hours, not sixteen. Captive animals, with nothing to fear and nothing to find, may simply be bored.

explanations.1: Regulars stayed loyal; the art department moved to another campus.
explanations.2: She asked for a logo, but he thinks she first needs to find out who her customers are.
explanations.3: Dan says people never fill in paper forms; he would rather talk face to face.
explanations.4: The photos are good, but every post is a special offer.
explanations.5: The card stays in a box behind the counter, so customers never carry it.

script.text: Good afternoon, Coastline Car Hire. This is Marcus.

script.text: No, I'm happy with a manual. What about insurance?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Basic insurance is included. But with the basic cover, if the car is damaged, you pay the first eight hundred pounds yourself. For six pounds a day you can reduce that to zero.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Eight hundred is a lot. I'll take the extra cover. Is there a limit on how far I can drive?

script.speaker: A
script.text: No, mileage is unlimited. And the car comes with a full tank. Just return it full, or we charge for the fuel.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Understood. My husband might drive as well. Does that cost more?

script.speaker: A
script.text: A second driver is five pounds a day, and he'd need to show his licence too.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hmm. It's not really worth it for four days. I'll do all the driving myself.

script.speaker: A
script.text: OK. Do you need a child seat?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes, one, please. My daughter is three.

script.speaker: A
script.text: No problem, there's no charge for that. Can I take your name?

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: A
script.text: Two hundred pounds. It's returned within five days, provided the car comes back undamaged.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Lovely. And if my flight is delayed?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Call this number, and we'll hold the car until six, when the office closes.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good morning, and welcome to the new Ashby Central Library. I'm Joanne, the head librarian, and before you explore, I'd like to tell you what has changed and help you find your way around.

script.speaker: C
script.text: As you know, the library has been closed for fourteen months. We'd planned for ten, but when the builders lifted the old floor, they discovered part of a Roman road underneath, and work had to stop while the archaeologists recorded it. You can now see a section of that road under a glass panel in the entrance hall.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The first thing regular visitors will notice is that there are fewer books on the shelves. Please don't be alarmed. We haven't thrown anything away. The less popular titles are in a store in the basement, and if you request one at the desk, a member of staff will bring it up within fifteen minutes.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Opening hours have changed as well. We used to close at five. From today we're open until eight on weekdays, though on Saturdays we still close at five, and we remain closed on Sundays.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Borrowing is simpler too. You no longer need to queue at the desk. Scan your card and your books at one of the machines by the door. And we've scrapped fines for late returns. Our research showed that fines didn't bring books back any faster. They just stopped people coming in.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, let me describe the ground floor. You're standing in the entrance hall, with the main doors behind you. Immediately on your left is the cafe, which is run by a local bakery. On your right, where the old newspaper room used to be, is the children's library, with its own small garden.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Straight ahead of you, in the centre of the building, is the information desk. Behind the desk, at the very back of the building, you'll find the quiet study room. Please note that phones and conversation aren't allowed in there.

script.speaker: C
script.text: To the left of the information desk, beyond the cafe, is the computer suite. There are forty machines, and you can book one for up to two hours.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, to the right of the desk, next to the stairs, is our local history collection, with maps and photographs of the city going back two hundred years.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Upstairs you'll find fiction and the meeting rooms, but I'll let you discover those yourselves. Enjoy your visit.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Come in, both of you. So, the primary school project. How did the site visit go?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Really well. We spent a whole day there, and the head teacher gave us a tour.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The building is from the nineteen sixties. I was expecting it to be in poor condition, but structurally it's sound. What struck us was how dark it is. The corridors have no windows at all.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And what did the teachers tell you they wanted?

script.speaker: B
script.text: We thought they'd ask for bigger classrooms. In fact, nearly all of them said the classrooms were fine. What they complained about was the noise. The hall is right in the middle, and when one class is doing music, nobody else can concentrate.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Interesting. Did you speak to the children?

script.speaker: C
script.text: We did better than that. We gave them paper and asked them to draw their favourite place in the school.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And hardly anyone drew a classroom, or even the playground. Most of them drew the library corner, which is really just a few cushions under the stairs.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So children want small, enclosed spaces. That's a useful finding. Now, what's your main idea for the design?

script.speaker: C
script.text: I wanted to knock down the hall and rebuild it at the edge of the site.

script.speaker: B
script.text: But the budget wouldn't allow that. So we've agreed to keep the hall where it is and wrap a new corridor around it, with glass in the roof. That brings light in, and the corridor acts as a barrier against the noise.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. That solves two problems with one move. What about materials?

script.speaker: B
script.text: We'd like to use timber for the new parts. It's warmer than concrete, and children can see how it's put together.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Timber needs maintaining, remember. Schools have very little money for that.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We've thought about that. We'd leave it unpainted, so it simply turns grey over time and never needs repainting.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Fine. Now, your drawings. I looked at the plans you sent, and they're accurate, but they're difficult for a client to read. A head teacher doesn't think in plans.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Should we make a model?

script.speaker: A
script.text: A model takes a week you haven't got. What I'd do is draw three or four views at a child's eye level. Show what a seven-year-old would actually see.

script.speaker: C
script.text: I can do those. I enjoy that kind of drawing.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And Nadia, I'd like you to work out the costs properly. At the moment your figures are guesses.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll ask the quantity surveying students to check them. They owe me a favour.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Excellent. One more thing. When you present, don't begin with the building. Begin with the children's drawings. That's your evidence.

script.speaker: C
script.text: That's a great idea. We'll put them on the first slide.

script.speaker: D
script.text: It's hard for us to imagine now, when salt costs almost nothing, but for most of human history it was one of the most valuable substances on earth. In today's lecture I want to explain why, and to show how salt shaped trade, taxation and even language.

script.speaker: D
script.text: The reason is simple. Before refrigeration, salt was the main way of preserving food. Meat and fish packed in salt could be kept through the winter or carried on a long voyage. A community without salt could not store food, and a community that could not store food could not survive a bad harvest.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Salt was produced in two ways. Near the coast, sea water was run into shallow ponds and left to evaporate in the sun. Inland, it had to be mined. The mine at Hallstatt in Austria was being worked seven thousand years ago, and the miners' leather bags and wooden tools have survived, preserved by the salt itself.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Because everyone needed it, salt was easy to tax. In China, a tax on salt was introduced more than two thousand years ago, and at times it provided half of the government's income. In France, a hated salt tax was one of the grievances that led to the revolution.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Salt also built roads. In Italy, a very early road, the Via Salaria, was laid out to carry salt from the coast to Rome. And it's often said that Roman soldiers were paid in salt. The evidence for that is actually weak. What we can say is that the word salary comes from the Latin word for salt, probably because soldiers received an allowance to buy it.

script.speaker: D
script.text: In West Africa, the salt trade crossed the Sahara. Slabs of salt were cut from the desert floor and carried south by camel, and according to Arab travellers, in some markets salt was exchanged for an equal weight of gold.

script.speaker: D
script.text: So what ended salt's importance? Not refrigeration at first, but canning, which was developed in the early nineteenth century to feed armies. Then, with modern drilling, vast underground deposits were discovered, and the price collapsed.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Today, less than a tenth of the salt produced is eaten. Most goes to the chemical industry, and in cold countries a huge quantity is spread on roads in winter to melt ice.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Ironically, the modern problem is that we eat too much. Doctors link a high intake of salt with raised blood pressure, and most of what we consume is hidden in processed food, especially bread, not added at the table.

explanations.1: It is structurally sound, but the corridors have no windows at all.
explanations.2: Nearly all said the classrooms were fine; music in the central hall disturbs everyone.
explanations.3: Most drew the library corner, a few cushions under the stairs.
explanations.4: Moving the hall is beyond the budget; a glass-roofed corridor brings in light and blocks noise.
explanations.5: Unpainted timber turns grey and never needs repainting.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Hello, Diane speaking.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Oh, hello. Is that the Elmstead Photography Club? I found this number on a poster in the camera shop.

script.speaker: A
script.text: It is, yes. I'm the club secretary. Are you thinking of joining us?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I am. I've just retired, and my daughter gave me a camera for my birthday. I've no idea how to use it properly.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then you're exactly the sort of person we like. About half our members are beginners. Shall I tell you how it works?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Please.

script.speaker: A
script.text: We meet every Thursday evening, from half past seven until about half past nine. We used to meet in the church hall, but it got too small for us, so since January we've been in the community centre on Bridge Street.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Bridge Street. I know it. Is there parking?

script.speaker: A
script.text: There's a car park at the back, and it's free after six.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good. And what happens at the meetings?

script.speaker: A
script.text: It varies. On the first Thursday of the month, we have a guest speaker. Next month it's a wildlife photographer. On the second Thursday, there's a practical workshop. The other weeks, members bring their own pictures, and we discuss them.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That sounds a bit frightening, having my pictures discussed.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Everyone says that. Nobody is unkind, I promise. And you needn't show anything until you feel ready.

script.speaker: B
script.text: All right. How much does it cost?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The annual subscription is forty-five pounds. For retired people, it's reduced to thirty.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Thirty pounds. That's very reasonable. Can I come along once before I decide?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Of course. Your first two visits are free. After that, we'd ask you to join.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fair enough. Do I need any special equipment? My camera's quite basic.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Just the camera, and its instruction book if you still have it. People do ask whether they need a tripod, and the answer is not yet. We have a few that members can borrow.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I do have the instruction book, though I can't make sense of it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Bring it along, and someone will go through it with you. We also run outings. The next one is to Farley Castle, on the twelfth of October.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Is that by coach?

script.speaker: A
script.text: We share cars, to keep the cost down. You'd just pay for your own entrance ticket.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Lovely. Who should I ask for when I arrive?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Ask for Colin. He looks after new members. He'll be wearing a red badge. And could I take your name, so I can tell him to expect you?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes, it's Arthur Pym. That's P, Y, M.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thank you, Arthur. We'll see you on Thursday.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Port Lowen. My name's Ben, and I'll be your guide for the next hour and a half. We'll walk right round the harbour, and I'll explain a little of its history as we go.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let me begin with the name. Many visitors think Lowen was the family who owned the land. Actually, it comes from an old local word meaning happy, though whether the fishermen who worked here were happy is another question.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The harbour you can see was built in seventeen ninety, and not for fishing, as you might expect. It was built to export copper from the mines in the hills behind us. Fishing only became important a century later, when the copper ran out.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, a word about safety. The harbour wall is perfectly safe to walk on, but the stone steps down to the water are covered in seaweed and extremely slippery. Please don't use them, however good the photograph might be.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let me tell you what we'll see. Our first stop is the customs house, the tall white building on the corner. It's the oldest building in the port, and today it houses a small museum, which you're welcome to visit after the tour.

script.speaker: C
script.text: From there, we'll walk along to the fish market. I'm afraid you won't see any fish being sold. The market closed twenty years ago, and the building is now used by a group of artists as their studios. Several of them will be at work this morning.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Next to the market is the ice house. Before electricity, ice was brought here by ship from Norway and stored underground. It's the one place on the tour where you'll be glad of a jacket, because even in August it's cold in there.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Then we come to the lifeboat station. The crew are all volunteers, and if we're lucky, they'll be carrying out their weekly training exercise. They launch the boat at eleven, and it's quite a sight.

script.speaker: C
script.text: At the far end of the harbour wall stands the lighthouse. It's no longer in use, and I'm sorry to say that you can't go up, because the staircase is being repaired. But it's the best spot for a view back over the town.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We finish at the Old Sail Loft, where sails were once made and mended. It's now a restaurant, and they've kindly offered everyone on the tour a ten per cent discount on lunch. Just show them your ticket.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Right, if everyone's ready, let's set off.

explanations.13: It was built to export copper; fishing became important a century later.

parts.context: You will hear part of a lecture about attempts to restore damaged coral reefs.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Sam, shall we go through the design for our experiment? Doctor Reyes wants the plan by Friday.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good idea. So the basic question is whether listening to music helps people remember a list of words.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes. And I've been reading the background. There was a famous study in the nineties claiming that classical music makes you cleverer.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The one about Mozart. Everybody's heard of that.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Right, but when other researchers repeated it, the effect mostly disappeared. What they found is that any music you enjoy puts you in a better mood, and it's the mood that improves performance for a short time.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So it's not really about the music at all. Interesting. Then our experiment should compare different conditions.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I thought three groups. One learns the words in silence, one with instrumental music, and one with songs that have lyrics.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'd predict the songs will be worst. If you're trying to learn words and someone's singing other words at you, they'll interfere.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's my guess too. Now, the participants. I was going to ask people in our seminar group.

script.speaker: B
script.text: They all know what we're testing. I'd rather use first-year students from another department, who have no idea what the study is about.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Fair point. Engineering students, maybe. How many do we need?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Doctor Reyes said at least fifteen in each group, so forty-five.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And the word list. I'd assumed we'd write our own.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We could, but then nobody can compare our results with anyone else's. There's a standard list that's been used for decades. Let's use that.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Fine. How long do we give them to learn it?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Two minutes is usual. Then they do an unrelated task, some simple arithmetic, to stop them repeating the words in their heads. Then they write down what they remember.

script.speaker: A
script.text: One thing worries me. Suppose the people in the music groups just happen to have better memories.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's why we give everyone a short memory test at the start, before any music. Then we can check that the three groups are equal.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. And volume? If it's too loud, it becomes a different experiment.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We'll play it through headphones at a fixed level, the same for everyone.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What about the ethics form? We're not doing anything harmful.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We still need it. And we have to tell people at the end what the study was really about.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Of course. I'll draft the form tonight. Can you book the lab?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll do it now. Room four has the best headphones.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to roughly a quarter of all marine species. Over the last thirty years, about half of the world's coral has been lost. Today I'm going to describe some of the methods being used to bring reefs back, and to be honest with you about their limits.

script.speaker: C
script.text: First, a reminder of what coral is. It looks like rock or a plant, but it is in fact an animal, or rather a colony of thousands of tiny animals. Inside their tissue live microscopic algae, and it's these that give coral both its colour and most of its food. When the water becomes too warm, the coral expels the algae and turns white. This is known as bleaching, and if it lasts more than a few weeks, the coral starves.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The oldest method of restoration is often called coral gardening. Divers break small pieces from a healthy colony and hang them on underwater frames that look rather like trees. After a year or so, the pieces are large enough to be attached to the damaged reef, traditionally with cement, although nowadays a simple clip is often used.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A discovery made by accident has speeded this up. A researcher in Florida broke a piece of coral while cleaning a tank and noticed that the fragments grew far faster than the original. Cutting coral into very small pieces, it turns out, makes it grow up to forty times more quickly.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A second approach uses sound. A dead reef is silent, and young fish avoid it. In one experiment in Australia, scientists placed speakers on damaged reef and played recordings of a healthy one. The number of fish settling there doubled, and fish matter, because they eat the seaweed that would otherwise smother young coral.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A third method works with breeding. Most corals release their eggs on just one or two nights a year, shortly after a full moon. Teams now collect the eggs in fine nets, raise the young in floating pools, and release millions of them over the reef.

script.speaker: C
script.text: More controversially, some laboratories are breeding coral selected for its tolerance of heat, in the hope that it will survive in warmer seas.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now for the limits. Restoration is extremely expensive, and so far the largest projects have covered only a few hectares, whereas the Great Barrier Reef alone is the size of Italy. Gardening cannot keep pace with losses on that scale. Most scientists therefore see restoration as a way of buying time, and nothing more, unless the warming of the oceans is slowed.

explanations.1: Any music people enjoy improves mood, and mood improves performance for a short time.
explanations.2: Sung words will interfere with the words being learned.
explanations.3: The seminar group all know what is being tested.
explanations.4: With their own list nobody could compare the results with anyone else's.
explanations.5: The unrelated task stops them repeating the words in their heads.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good evening, sir. Baggage services. How can I help?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hi. My suitcase didn't arrive. I waited until the belt stopped, and it just isn't there.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Let's fill in a report, and we'll trace it for you. Which flight were you on?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I came from Toronto, but I changed planes in Dublin. The second flight was E K four one seven.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Four one seven from Dublin. That's helpful, because bags usually go missing at the connection. Could I have your name?

script.speaker: B
script.text: It's Daniel Kessler. K, E, double S, L, E, R.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thank you, Mister Kessler. Now, can you describe the suitcase? What colour is it?

script.speaker: B
script.text: It's dark green. People always expect black or blue, so at least it's easy to spot.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Dark green. Is it a hard case or a soft one?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hard, with four wheels. And there's a yellow ribbon tied to the handle. My wife's idea.

script.speaker: A
script.text: A yellow ribbon. That'll help a lot. Roughly how big is it?

script.speaker: B
script.text: It's a large one. It weighed twenty-one kilos when I checked in.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Twenty-one. And what's inside? I don't need everything, just a few things that would identify it if the label has come off.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Mostly clothes. A pair of walking boots, right on the top. And some books. I'm here for a conference, so my presentation notes are in there too, which is the real worry.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Is there anything valuable? A laptop, a camera?

script.speaker: B
script.text: No, the laptop was in my hand luggage, thank goodness.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. Now, where shall we send the case when it turns up? Are you staying in a hotel?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes, the Carlton Hotel. That's on Park Avenue. I'm there until Friday, and then I move on to Manchester.

script.speaker: A
script.text: If we find it tonight, it'll be delivered tomorrow morning. And a phone number where we can reach you?

script.speaker: B
script.text: My mobile doesn't work over here yet. You'd better call the hotel and ask for room three one two.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Room three one two. Fine. Here's your reference number. You can follow the search on our website.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Thanks. I've got nothing to wear tomorrow, though. Can I claim for that?

script.speaker: A
script.text: You can. Buy what you need for the first day, up to sixty pounds, and keep the receipts. We can't refund anything without them.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Sixty pounds, and keep the receipts. OK. How long does this usually take?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Nine bags out of ten are found within two days. If yours hasn't appeared after five days, you fill in a second form, listing every item, and it becomes a claim for compensation.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Let's hope it doesn't come to that.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And now for our weekly look at what's happening locally. This morning I went down to the farmers' market in Queen's Square, which celebrates its tenth birthday this month.

script.speaker: C
script.text: If you haven't been, the market takes place every Saturday. It used to be held once a month, but it proved so popular that the council agreed to make it weekly two years ago. It opens at eight, and I'd advise you to go early, because by eleven the best bread has gone.

script.speaker: C
script.text: What makes it a farmers' market, as opposed to an ordinary one? The rule here is strict. Everything on sale must be grown, raised or made within thirty miles of the square, and the person behind the stall must be involved in producing it. You won't find anyone simply reselling goods from a wholesaler.

script.speaker: C
script.text: I asked the manager, Carol, whether prices are higher than in the supermarket. She was honest about it. Meat and cheese do cost more. Vegetables, though, are often cheaper, because nothing is spent on packaging or transport.

script.speaker: C
script.text: There are thirty-two stalls at present, and a waiting list of producers hoping for a place. So what did I find? The longest queue was at the cheese stall, run by two sisters whose goat's cheese won a national prize last year. Next to them, a retired teacher sells honey from hives he keeps on the roofs of buildings in the city centre.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Something I didn't expect was the fish. We're sixty miles from the sea, after all. But there's a trout farm in the valley, and they smoke the fish themselves over oak.

script.speaker: C
script.text: It isn't only food. One stall sells wool, dyed with plants, and another sells wooden spoons and bowls. And for children, there's a table where they can plant a seed in a pot and take it home, which costs nothing.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A couple of practical points. Until recently the stalls only took cash, but nearly all of them now accept cards. There's no car park in the square itself, so use the one behind the cinema, where the first hour is free on Saturdays. And please bring your own bags. The market stopped giving out plastic ones last year.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, a date for your diary. On the last Saturday of the month, to mark the anniversary, a local chef will be giving cookery demonstrations on a stage by the fountain, using only ingredients from the stalls. They start at ten o'clock.

explanations.11: It used to be monthly but has been weekly for two years.
explanations.12: The goods must come from within thirty miles and the seller must be involved in producing them.
explanations.13: Meat and cheese cost more; vegetables are often cheaper.
explanations.14: A retired teacher keeps hives on roofs in the city centre.

groups.text:

parts.context: You will hear part of a lecture about how writing was invented.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Sit down, Elena. I've read your report on the footbridge, and there's a lot to like. Before I comment, how do you feel it went?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Honestly, I enjoyed the calculations far more than the writing. I thought the hardest part would be choosing the type of bridge, but that came quickly. It was explaining my decisions that took for ever.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's very common. Well, your calculations are sound. I checked the loading figures, and I couldn't find a single error.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's a relief. I did them three times.

script.speaker: A
script.text: It shows. My main criticism is about the order. You describe your final design on page two, and the reader doesn't discover what the site is like until page nine. I had no way of judging the design.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I see. I put the design first because I thought that was the interesting part.

script.speaker: A
script.text: It is, but the reader needs the problem before the answer. Move the site description to the front.

script.speaker: B
script.text: OK. What about the section comparing the three types of bridge?

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's the strongest part. The table of costs is clear. But you rejected the suspension design in one sentence, saying it was unsuitable. Why?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Because of the ground. The soil on the east bank is too soft to anchor the cables without very deep foundations.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's a perfectly good reason. It simply isn't written down.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll add a paragraph. Should I include my soil test results?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Put the full results in an appendix, and summarise them in two lines in the main text.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fine. And the diagrams? I drew them by hand, because I'm slow with the software.

script.speaker: A
script.text: They're accurate, and I rather like them. What they lack is a scale. Without one, I can't tell whether your bridge is ten metres long or a hundred.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Oh, of course. That's easy to fix.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Now, something you didn't cover at all. How would this bridge be maintained? A steel structure over water needs repainting every few years. Who pays, and how do they reach the underside?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I didn't think about that. I only considered the cost of building it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Clients care about the cost over fifty years, not just the first one. Have a look at the guidance from the Institution of Civil Engineers, and add a short section.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I will. Is the conclusion all right?

script.speaker: A
script.text: It's rather long. You repeat most of the report. A conclusion should fit on half a page.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll cut it. When do you need the new version?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The deadline is the twentieth, but if you send it to me by the fifteenth, I'll read it once more before you submit.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Then I'll aim for the fifteenth. Thank you.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Writing seems so natural to us that it's easy to forget it had to be invented. In fact, as far as we know, it was invented independently only a handful of times, in Mesopotamia, in China, and in Central America. Today I'll concentrate on the earliest of these, in what is now Iraq, a little over five thousand years ago.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The first surprise is what writing was for. We might imagine that people wanted to record stories, or prayers, or the deeds of kings. Not at all. The earliest tablets are lists of goods. Writing began as a tool for accounting.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The story really starts earlier, with small clay tokens. For thousands of years before writing, farmers in the region used these to keep track of what they owned. A token of one shape stood for a sheep, another for a jar of oil. To record a debt of five sheep, you handed over five tokens.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The difficulty was trust. Tokens could be lost or stolen. So people began sealing them inside a hollow ball of clay, a kind of envelope. That created a new problem, because you couldn't see what was inside without breaking it. The answer was to press the tokens into the wet surface of the envelope before sealing it, leaving marks that showed the contents.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And then somebody realised that the tokens themselves were no longer necessary. The marks were enough. The envelope was flattened into a tablet, and the marks were drawn with a cut reed. Because the reed left a shape like a wedge, we call this script cuneiform, from the Latin for wedge.

script.speaker: C
script.text: At this stage, the signs were pictures. The great step forward was to use a sign not for its meaning but for its sound. It's as if we drew a bee and a leaf to write the word belief. Once that happened, names could be written, and then whole sentences of the spoken language.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Learning the system was hard. There were about six hundred signs, and a boy training to be a scribe spent some twelve years at school. We have their exercise tablets, with the teacher's neat version on one side and the pupil's clumsy copy on the other.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Because clay survives fire, when other materials are destroyed, hundreds of thousands of tablets have come down to us. Most are receipts and contracts. But among them are letters, and I'll end with my favourite. It's from a merchant complaining that the copper he was sold was of poor quality, and demanding his money back. It is the oldest known letter of complaint.

explanations.1: Choosing the bridge came quickly; explaining her decisions took for ever.
explanations.2: The design appears on page two and the site not until page nine.
explanations.3: The soil on the east bank is too soft to anchor the cables.
explanations.4: Full results go in an appendix, with a two-line summary in the main text.
explanations.5: Without a scale the tutor cannot tell how long the bridge is.
