script.speaker: A
script.text: Hello, Thornbury Village Hall. Jim speaking.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good morning. I'm organising a party for my parents' wedding anniversary, and I'd like to know whether the hall is free on Saturday the eighteenth of May.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Let me check the diary. The eighteenth. The main hall is booked for a concert, I'm afraid. I could do the Saturday after, the twenty-fifth.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The twenty-fifth would be all right, I think. Most of the family will still be around.

script.speaker: A
script.text: How many guests are you expecting?

script.speaker: B
script.text: About eighty. Is the hall big enough?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The main hall takes a hundred and twenty seated at tables, so you'd have plenty of room. There's also the garden room, but that only holds forty.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The main hall, then. What does it cost?

script.speaker: A
script.text: For an evening, from six until midnight, it's two hundred and ten pounds. If you'd like to get in during the afternoon to decorate, there's an extra charge of thirty pounds.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We'd need the afternoon, definitely. So two hundred and forty altogether. Does that include the kitchen?

script.speaker: A
script.text: It does. There's a large cooker, two fridges and a dishwasher. What we don't supply is tablecloths. You'd need to bring those, or hire them.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll make a note. We're having a caterer, so that's her problem really. What about music? We've booked a band.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's fine, but all music has to stop at half past eleven. We have neighbours, and the licence is very clear.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Half past eleven. And can we serve alcohol?

script.speaker: A
script.text: You can serve it, as long as you're not selling it. If you want to run a paying bar, you'd need a separate licence from the council, and that takes three weeks.

script.speaker: B
script.text: No, it'll all be free. Is there parking?

script.speaker: A
script.text: There are thirty spaces beside the hall. Once those are full, people use the field behind the school. It's only two minutes on foot.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Lovely. Now, my father uses a wheelchair. Is that a problem?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Not at all. There's a ramp at the side entrance, and an accessible toilet.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Perfect. How do I book?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'll need a deposit of fifty pounds to hold the date, and the balance two weeks before the event. You can pay by bank transfer, or drop a cheque in at the post office next door.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll do a transfer today. And the keys?

script.speaker: A
script.text: You collect them from me on the day. I live at number six, Mill Lane, just across the road. Can I take your name?

script.speaker: B
script.text: It's Rachel Oduya. O, D, U, Y, A.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thank you, Rachel. One last thing. We ask everyone to take their rubbish home with them. There's no collection at the weekend.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good afternoon, and welcome to the Greenway Recycling Centre. I'm Tasha, and I'll be taking you round. Before we go in, I'm going to hand out ear protection, because the sorting hall is very noisy, and I'll ask you to stay inside the yellow lines at all times.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let me give you some idea of the scale. Every working day, about four hundred tonnes of material arrive here, from homes across the whole county. When the centre opened, fifteen years ago, we recycled a quarter of what came in. Today the figure is just over sixty per cent.

script.speaker: C
script.text: People often ask what the biggest problem is, and they expect me to say plastic. It isn't. It's food. A single jar that's still half full of sauce can spoil a whole load of paper, and then that paper has to be burned. So if you remember one thing from today, please rinse your containers.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The second problem is newer. Batteries, especially the ones inside old phones and electric toothbrushes, can catch fire when they're crushed. We had three fires last year. Batteries should never go in your household bin. Take them to a collection point in a supermarket.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, here's what you'll see. Lorries tip everything onto the floor of the reception hall. From there, a conveyor belt carries it up to the first stage, where a team of workers remove by hand anything that shouldn't be there. Last month they found a bicycle and a set of golf clubs.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Next, the material passes over a series of rotating discs. Cardboard, being large and flat, rides over the top, while smaller objects fall through.

script.speaker: C
script.text: After that, a powerful magnet lifts out anything made of steel, mainly food tins. Aluminium isn't magnetic, so drinks cans are removed further along by a different machine.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Plastics are the cleverest part. The bottles pass under an infrared light, which identifies the type of plastic, and a jet of air blows each one into the correct container. It happens faster than you can see.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Glass is the last thing left on the belt. It's broken into small pieces and sent to a factory forty miles away, where it becomes new bottles.

script.speaker: C
script.text: At the end, everything is pressed into bales and sold. I'm sometimes asked whether it all ends up abroad. Paper does go overseas, but our plastic and metal are processed in this country.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Right. Ear protection on, please, and follow me.

explanations.11: A quarter was the figure when the centre opened.
explanations.12: Visitors expect her to say plastic, but food spoils whole loads of paper.
explanations.13: They should never go in the household bin; supermarkets have collection points.
explanations.14: Plastic and metal are processed in this country.

- the {{16}} are wide and close to the surface
Tolerating drought
- the resurrection plant looks {{17}} when dry
- it replaces the water in its cells with a kind of {{18}}
Applications
- useful because more {{19}} is becoming dry
- research is mainly being carried out on {{20}}

script.speaker: A
script.text: Leo, we need to settle the plan for the oral history project. Have you had any luck finding people to interview?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Some. I put a notice in the local paper, and four former shipyard workers called me. But the best response came from the retired workers' club. I gave a short talk there, and eleven people signed up.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Fifteen in all. That's more than we can manage. Professor Whitlock suggested eight interviews of about an hour each.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Then we'll have to choose. I'd pick the ones who worked there longest.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'm not sure. If we do that, we'll only get men who were welders and riveters. I'd rather have variety. There were women in the offices and the canteen, and nobody has recorded their memories.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's true. Variety, then. Where should we do the interviews? I'd assumed we'd bring people to the university.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Most of them are over eighty. I think we should go to their homes. People relax and remember more in their own surroundings.

script.speaker: B
script.text: It'll take longer, but you're right. Should we send them the questions beforehand?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I asked Professor Whitlock that. She said no, because people prepare little speeches. Better to send a short list of topics, so they can look out old photographs.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Photographs would be great. Now, recording. My phone has a decent microphone.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The department lends out proper recorders. The sound is much cleaner, and the archive won't accept phone recordings anyway.

script.speaker: B
script.text: OK, I'll borrow two, in case one fails. What about transcribing? Eight hours of speech is a huge job.

script.speaker: A
script.text: There's software that produces a rough version. We'd still have to correct it by hand, especially with the local accent.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Let's split that. Four each.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Agreed. Now, there's one thing we mustn't forget. Every person has to sign a consent form before we start, saying how the recording may be used.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And if somebody says something they regret afterwards?

script.speaker: A
script.text: They can ask us to remove it, at any point up to the day we hand the recordings to the archive. It says so on the form.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good. What do we do for the final presentation? I don't want to just read out quotes.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I thought we could play short clips, so the audience hears the voices themselves.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes. And maybe put a map of the yard on the screen, and mark where each person worked.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I love that. Can you make the map?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll try. The city museum has the original plans. I'll go on Wednesday.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Deserts are defined by a shortage of water, and yet they contain several thousand species of plant. This morning I want to look at the strategies those plants use, and I'll group them under three headings, which are escaping drought, resisting it, and tolerating it.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let's begin with the escapers. These are annual plants that avoid drought altogether by living very short lives. Their seeds lie in the soil, sometimes for decades. When heavy rain finally arrives, they germinate, flower and produce new seeds within a few weeks. What's clever is that the seeds are coated with a chemical that prevents growth, and only a really heavy fall of rain will wash it off. A light shower, which wouldn't keep a plant alive, doesn't trigger them.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Second, the resisters, and the best known are the cacti. A cactus stores water in its stem, and that stem is folded, rather like an accordion, so that it can expand after rain. A large cactus can take up two hundred litres in a single storm.

script.speaker: C
script.text: To avoid losing that water, a cactus has no leaves. What it has are spines. These protect it from thirsty animals, of course, but they also cast a surprising amount of shade on the surface of the plant.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Most plants open the pores in their surface during the day, to take in carbon dioxide. A cactus does the opposite. It opens its pores only at night, when the air is cooler, and stores the gas until the sun comes up.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Roots matter too. People imagine a desert plant sending a root deep underground, and some trees do exactly that. One, the mesquite, has been found with roots fifty metres down. But a cactus spreads its roots wide and very close to the surface, to catch rain before it evaporates.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Third, the tolerators, which I find the most remarkable. These plants can lose almost all their water and survive. One small fern, known as the resurrection plant, curls into a dry brown ball and appears completely dead. Given water, it turns green again within a day. It protects its cells by replacing the water with a kind of sugar.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Why does any of this matter beyond botany? Well, as the climate warms, more farmland is becoming dry. Researchers are trying to transfer some of these abilities to crops. Much of the work is being done on rice, with wheat likely to follow. If they succeed, the humble plants of the desert may turn out to be among the most valuable on earth.

explanations.1: Four people answered the newspaper notice; eleven signed up at the retired workers' club.
explanations.2: Choosing by length of service would give only welders and riveters; she wants variety.
explanations.3: People relax and remember more in their own surroundings.
explanations.4: The professor advised against sending questions; a list of topics lets them look out photographs.
explanations.5: The sound is cleaner and the archive will not accept phone recordings.

script.text: Good morning, everyone. Welcome to Mere Lake. I'm Rob, the safety officer today. If this is your first swim here, please listen carefully. It only takes five minutes.

script.speaker: C
script.text: First, the temperature. The lake is fourteen degrees this morning. That may not sound cold, but an indoor pool is usually twenty-eight. So please don't jump or dive in. Walk in slowly and give your body a minute or two to adjust. The gasp you feel when cold water reaches your chest is normal, and it passes.

script.speaker: C
script.text: How long should you stay in? There's no fixed rule. But if you start to shiver, or your fingers stop working properly, it's time to get out, however good you feel. People get into trouble because they wait too long.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Everyone must wear one of our orange swim caps. They aren't for warmth. They're so that the lifeguards in the kayaks can see you. You'll also be given a numbered wristband when you sign in. Hand it back when you leave. That's how we know nobody is still in the water.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Wetsuits are optional once the water is above twelve degrees, so today it's your choice. If you don't own one, you can hire one from the hut for five pounds.

script.speaker: C

script.speaker: C

script.speaker: C

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, the cafe is open until noon, the car park closes at one, and there's a session for beginners every Sunday if you'd like some coaching. Enjoy your swim.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Joel, have you started the dialect essay yet?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Barely. The title is whether regional dialects in Britain are dying out, and I assumed the answer was obviously yes. Everyone watches the same television and moves around for work.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's what I thought before I did the reading. But it's more complicated. The old rural dialects, with their own vocabulary, have mostly gone. What's happened in the big cities is different. Their accents are actually spreading into the surrounding areas.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So some varieties are getting stronger while others disappear.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Exactly. The article by Kerswill calls it levelling. Small local differences vanish, and you end up with a few large regional varieties.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That gives the essay a shape. First what's been lost, then what's replacing it. Did you find the lecture notes helpful?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Not especially. They're mostly about pronunciation. I got far more from the recordings in the sound archive. You can hear a farmer born in eighteen ninety, and then his great-granddaughter.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I should listen to those. Now, the essay asks for our own data as well. I was planning to send a questionnaire to my family.

script.speaker: A
script.text: A questionnaire tells you what people think they say. It's better to record them talking naturally, and count the features yourself.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Wouldn't they speak more carefully if they know they're being recorded?

script.speaker: A
script.text: At first. That's why you ask them about something emotional, a time they were in danger, for instance. People forget the microphone when they're telling a good story.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Clever. Who would you record?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Three generations of one family, if you can. Then age is the only thing that changes.

script.speaker: B
script.text: My grandmother, my mother and my sister all live in the same town. That would work.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Perfect. What feature will you look at?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I thought vocabulary. My grandmother uses words nobody else knows.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Words are fun, but they're hard to count, because any particular word might not come up. Choose a sound that occurs in every sentence. You'll have hundreds of examples in ten minutes.

script.speaker: B
script.text: All right, a sound. Professor Ince mentioned that the deadline's been moved.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes, from the third of March to the tenth, because of the strike.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That helps. And the length is still two thousand words?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Two thousand five hundred, including the data section.

script.speaker: B
script.text: One last thing. Are we allowed to submit graphs?

script.speaker: A
script.text: She encourages it. A simple bar chart for each generation would make your point at a glance.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Great. I'll record my family this weekend.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Look around this room and you'll see glass everywhere, in the windows, in your phones, in my spectacles. Yet for most of history it was rare and precious. Today I want to trace how that changed.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Glass is made by melting sand with one or two other ingredients, and nature occasionally does this by itself. Volcanoes produce a black glass called obsidian, and Stone Age people valued it for making blades, because it gives an edge sharper than steel.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The first glass made by people comes from the Middle East, about four and a half thousand years ago, and it was used for beads. For many centuries it remained a luxury, as costly as precious stones.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The great change came about two thousand years ago, on the coast of what is now Syria and Lebanon, with the invention of glass blowing. A worker picks up a lump of molten glass on the end of an iron tube and blows air into it. Suddenly a bottle that had taken days could be made in minutes. The Romans spread the method across their empire, and for the first time ordinary families could own a glass cup.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The Romans also made the first window glass, though it was thick and cloudy. It let in light, but you couldn't see through it clearly.

script.speaker: C
script.text: In the Middle Ages, the finest glass came from Venice. In twelve ninety-one, the city ordered all its glass makers to move to the island of Murano. The official reason was the danger of fire in a city built of wood. A happy side effect was that the makers' secrets could be guarded. They were forbidden to leave, on pain of death.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The Venetians produced the first really clear glass, and that made two things possible. One was the mirror. The other was the lens. Spectacles appeared in Italy around thirteen hundred, and they added perhaps fifteen years to the working life of every scholar and craftsman. Later, lenses gave us the telescope and the microscope, so it's fair to say that modern science depended on glass.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Large flat sheets remained difficult to make until the nineteen fifties, when a British firm developed the float process. Molten glass is poured onto a bath of liquid tin, and it spreads out perfectly flat. Almost every window in the world is now made that way.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And the story isn't over. Thin strands of glass, known as optical fibres, now carry nearly all the world's internet traffic under the oceans. A material first used for beads has become the foundation of modern communication.

explanations.1: "That's what I thought before I did the reading."
explanations.2: Small differences vanish, leaving a few large regional varieties.
explanations.3: She got far more from the recordings in the sound archive.
explanations.4: A questionnaire tells you what people think they say.
explanations.5: Any particular word might not come up, but a sound occurs in every sentence.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thank you for calling Skyline Broadband. My name's Oliver. How can I help you today?

script.text: Hi. I've just bought a house, and I need to get the internet connected. I work from home, so it's pretty urgent.

script.text: What's the difference in practice?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Basic is fine for email and browsing. Plus is what we recommend for households with video calls and streaming. Ultra is really for people who send very large files.

script.speaker: A

script.speaker: A
script.text: Friday the twentieth, afternoon only, between one and six.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll take that. How long does the installation take?

script.speaker: A
script.text: About two hours. The engineer needs to drill a small hole through an outside wall, so someone over eighteen has to be at home to agree where it goes.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll be there. Where do people usually put the router?

script.speaker: A
script.text: As near to the middle of the house as you can. Not in a cupboard, and not on the floor. A shelf is ideal.

script.speaker: B
script.text: OK. Does the router cost extra?

script.speaker: A
script.text: No, it's included, and it stays our property. If you leave us, you send it back in the box we provide.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Right. And what if the speed isn't what you promise?

script.speaker: A
script.text: We guarantee a minimum speed in writing. If we don't reach it within thirty days, you can cancel without paying anything.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's reassuring. Can I keep my old phone number, by the way?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The package doesn't include a phone line unless you add one for five pounds a month.

script.speaker: B
script.text: No, I only use my mobile. How do I pay?

script.speaker: A
script.text: By monthly direct debit. The first payment is taken ten days after installation. Could I take your name?

script.speaker: B
script.text: It's Monica Hale. H, A, L, E.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thank you, Miss Hale. I'll email a confirmation within the hour.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good afternoon, and welcome to the Regent Theatre. I'm Lydia, and I've worked here as a stage manager for nineteen years. Over the next hour, I'll show you the parts of the building the audience never sees.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A little history first. The Regent opened in nineteen hundred and eight. In the nineteen sixties it very nearly became a supermarket. The company had already bought the building, and it was only saved because local people collected enough signatures to have it protected by law.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We put on about ten productions a year. People assume the actors are the largest group working here. In fact, for a big musical there may be twenty performers on stage and over fifty people behind it, in lighting, sound, costume and so on.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Before we go through this door, some rules. There's no photography backstage, I'm afraid, because the set designs belong to the designers. And please don't touch any of the ropes. Some of them hold up scenery weighing as much as a small car.

script.speaker: C
script.text: There's also an old theatre tradition, which is that you never whistle backstage. Long ago, scenery was moved by sailors, who signalled to each other by whistling, so a careless whistle could bring a piece of scenery down on your head.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Our first stop will be the wardrobe department. For the current show there are two hundred and thirty costumes, and each one has to be washed or cleaned after every performance. You'll meet Pam, who has been making hats here since before I arrived.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Then we'll visit the props room. A prop is any object an actor handles, from a letter to a sword. One curious fact is that the food eaten on stage is nearly always real, but it's usually something soft, like banana, so that the actor can swallow quickly and say the next line.

script.speaker: C
script.text: After that we go underneath the stage. There's a trapdoor there, which lets a performer appear or vanish in a second. It's still worked by hand, by two members of the crew, exactly as it was a century ago.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Then up to the lighting box at the back of the auditorium. In the old days the operator moved every lamp separately. Now the whole show is stored on a computer, and the operator's real job is to watch for anything going wrong.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We'll end on the stage itself. You'll notice that it isn't level. It slopes down towards the audience, so that people in the front rows can see the actors' feet. You'll feel it as you walk.

parts.context: You will hear part of a lecture about wild animals living in cities.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.
groups.text:
Wildlife in cities
What cities provide
- food all year round, especially from {{11}}
- warmth in winter
- {{12}}: few hunters or large predators
Features of successful species
- a varied diet; not afraid of new things; often active at {{13}}
- the fox arrived when suburbs with large {{14}} were built
How city animals change
- birds sing at a higher {{15}} to be heard above traffic
- city raccoons were quicker to open a difficult {{16}}
- some lizards now have longer {{17}}, for climbing
Dangers
- roads; glass; artificial {{18}}, which confuses insects and birds
Planning
- a park on its own is like an {{19}}
- green spaces should be linked by {{20}}

script.speaker: A
script.text: Ravi, I've been thinking about our research proposal. I'd like to do something on noise at night on the wards.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Because of your placement?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Partly. But what really decided it was a patient survey I read. People were asked what had most affected their recovery, and poor sleep came above pain.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Above pain. That's striking. So what's making the noise? Alarms, I'd guess.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's what I assumed too. But in the studies I've found, the biggest single source is conversation. Staff talking at the desk, and during the handover between shifts.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Really? That's a bit uncomfortable, since it's us.

script.speaker: A
script.text: It is. But it also means it can be changed without spending money.

script.speaker: B
script.text: True. So how do we measure it? I could download a sound meter app on my phone.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The apps aren't accurate enough to publish. The physics department lends out proper meters that record all night. I've already asked, and we can have two.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good. Which wards?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'd like to compare an old ward with open bays and a new one with single rooms.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's two things changing at once, though. The new ward has different staff and different patients. I'd rather take one ward and measure before and after we make a change.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Hmm. You're right, that's cleaner. One ward, before and after. What change would we make?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Some hospitals have a quiet hour. Lights down, no visitors.

script.speaker: A
script.text: At night there are no visitors anyway. What about moving the handover? If nurses changed shifts in the staff room, not at the patients' bedsides, most of the talking would move with them.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Wouldn't we lose something? The bedside handover lets the patient hear what's said about them.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's a fair point, and we should include it in the discussion as a possible cost.

script.speaker: B
script.text: OK. And we need to measure sleep itself, not just decibels. Wrist monitors?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Too expensive for forty patients. A short questionnaire each morning is enough. Five questions.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fine. Who has to approve this?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The ward manager first. Then the hospital ethics committee, which meets on the first Monday of each month.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So we need the forms in by the end of this week.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes. I'll write the background section if you do the method.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Deal. And let's ask Doctor Osei to look at a draft. She ran a noise project in Glasgow.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good idea. I'll email her this afternoon.

script.speaker: C
script.text: When we think about wildlife, we tend to picture forests and mountains. But a growing number of species are making their homes in cities, and some are doing better there than in the countryside. Today I want to ask why.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let's start with what cities offer. The first thing is food. Our rubbish is rich in calories and available all year round. The second is warmth. A city centre can be several degrees warmer than the land around it, which helps small animals through the winter. And the third, which people forget, is safety. In a city there are very few hunters, and large predators are almost entirely absent.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Not every species can take advantage of this. The successful ones tend to share certain features. They eat a wide range of foods. They're not easily frightened by anything new. And, very often, they're active at night, when the streets are empty.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The red fox is the classic example. Foxes began moving into British cities in the nineteen thirties, when suburbs with large gardens were built. A city fox has a much smaller territory than a rural one, because it doesn't need to travel far to eat.

script.speaker: C
script.text: What's particularly interesting is that city life seems to change animals. Studies of birds have found that those in noisy areas sing at a higher pitch, so that their song isn't drowned by the low rumble of traffic. Some also sing at night, when it's quieter.

script.speaker: C
script.text: There's evidence of change in problem solving too. In one experiment, raccoons from a city and from the country were given a box with a difficult lock. The city animals were faster at opening it, and they kept trying for longer.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Evolution can be surprisingly rapid. A species of mosquito in the tunnels of the London Underground can no longer breed with its relatives on the surface. And in several cities, lizards have developed longer legs and stickier feet, which help them to climb walls and windows.

script.speaker: C
script.text: But I don't want to give too rosy a picture. Cities are dangerous in their own ways. Roads kill enormous numbers of animals. Glass kills birds, which can't see it. And artificial light confuses insects and migrating birds, with effects we're only beginning to measure.

script.speaker: C
script.text: So what should planners do? The most effective step turns out to be connecting green spaces. A park that stands alone is like an island. Link it to others by strips of trees along a river or a railway, and animals can move between them. Such strips are known as corridors, and many cities are now building them into their plans.

explanations.1: The placement was only part of it; what decided it was a survey putting poor sleep above pain.
explanations.2: The biggest single source is conversation among staff.
explanations.3: The physics department lends out proper meters; apps are not accurate enough.
explanations.4: A new ward has different staff and patients, so two things change at once.
explanations.5: Moving the handover to the staff room would move most of the talking.

title: Cookery class booking and an allotment association

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

options.C: rent more land from the council

The rent is going up because

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good morning, the Copper Pan Cookery School. Nick speaking.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hello. My sister gave me a voucher for one of your classes, and I'd like to use it before it runs out.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Of course. Which class were you interested in?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I was hoping to do the bread-making day. Is there one coming up?

script.speaker: A
script.text: There's one this Saturday, but it's been full for weeks. The next is on the eleventh of April.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'm away then, unfortunately. What else do you have in March?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Let me see. There's Thai street food on the fourteenth, and fresh pasta on the twenty-first.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I've done a Thai class before, on holiday. I'll take the pasta, please.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Pasta on the twenty-first of March. That's a full day, from ten until four.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Ten until four. Is lunch included, or should I bring something?

script.speaker: A
script.text: You eat what you cook, so there's no need to bring food. You'll make three kinds of pasta and two sauces, and everyone sits down together at about one.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Lovely. My voucher is for seventy-five pounds. Does that cover it?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The full-day classes are ninety-five, so there'd be twenty pounds to pay on the day.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's fine. How many people will be there?

script.speaker: A
script.text: We take a maximum of twelve, and you each have your own work station. You don't have to share.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good. Do I need to bring an apron?

script.speaker: A
script.text: No, we lend you one. The only thing we ask is that you wear flat shoes with closed toes. It's a real kitchen, and things get dropped.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Sensible. I should mention that I can't eat nuts. Is that a problem?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Not for the pasta class. One of the sauces normally contains pine nuts, but the chef can easily make yours without them. I'll put a note on the booking.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Thank you. Who's teaching?

script.speaker: A
script.text: It's Paolo Greco, who used to run a restaurant in Naples. Greco is G, R, E, C, O.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And where are you exactly? I'm coming by train.

script.speaker: A
script.text: We're in the old dairy on Station Road. It's five minutes from the station on foot. Turn left as you come out, and you'll see a large clock on the front of the building.

script.speaker: B
script.text: A clock. That should be easy. Can I take home what I make?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes, we give you boxes for whatever's left, and a booklet with all the recipes.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Wonderful. Could I have the code on my voucher checked? It's W, seven, seven, four, K.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's valid. And your name?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Judith Marsh. M, A, R, S, H.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good evening, everybody, and thank you for coming out on such a wet night. I'll go through the main points of the year, and then we'll have questions.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let me start with numbers. We now have a hundred and forty plots on the site, and every one of them is let. The waiting list has reached sixty-three people, which means that anyone joining today can expect to wait about three years. For that reason, the committee is proposing that when a large plot becomes free, we divide it into two. Most new members tell us a full plot is more than they can manage anyway.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, water. You'll remember that last summer the supply was turned off twice. That wasn't because of the drought, as some people thought. It was a burst pipe near the main gate, and it has now been replaced. We've also installed six large tanks to collect rain from the roof of the shed, and I'd encourage you to use those before the taps.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The rent. I'm afraid it will rise from forty-two pounds to forty-six pounds a year. I know that isn't welcome. But the council has raised what it charges us for the land, and we have no reserves to absorb it.

script.speaker: C
script.text: On a happier note, the new composting toilet is finished. It cost less than we'd budgeted, thanks to members who did the building work themselves.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Some reminders about the rules. Bonfires are only allowed in November, and never on a Sunday. Sheds must not be more than two metres high. And please keep the paths between plots clear. They belong to everybody, and several have been blocked by wheelbarrows and water butts.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We've had a problem with theft, I'm sorry to say. Tools were taken from four sheds in the spring. The police advised us against bigger padlocks. Thieves simply break the door. Their advice was to mark tools with your postcode, and a marking kit is available from the secretary.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, dates. The seed swap is on the first Saturday in February. The plant sale, which raised over eight hundred pounds last year, is on the second Sunday in May. And the autumn show will be in September, as usual, with a new class this year for the heaviest pumpkin.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, we need a new treasurer. Malcolm is stepping down after eleven years, and I'm sure you'll join me in thanking him. If you can add up and have two evenings a month to spare, please speak to me afterwards.

explanations.11: When a large plot becomes free it will be divided into two.
explanations.12: Some thought it was the drought, but it was a burst pipe.
explanations.13: The council has raised its charge and there are no reserves to absorb it.
explanations.14: Bigger padlocks only lead thieves to break the door.

title: Geology field trip and the history of maps

parts.context: You will hear a geology student called Ben asking a tutor about a field trip to the coast.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.prompt: Why is this year's trip shorter than last year's?

options.A: The accommodation has become more expensive.
options.B: The coach is not available for five days.
options.C: There is less work to do.

questions.prompt: The main aim of the trip this year is to

options.C: measure the height of the cliff.

questions.prompt: How are the working pairs decided?

options.C: The tutor matches students of different ability.

questions.prompt: Ben should not bring a hammer because

options.C: using one on the cliff is illegal.

questions.prompt: What does the tutor say about the field notebook?

options.A: It should be handed in as it was written on the beach.
options.B: It should be rewritten neatly before it is handed in.
options.C: It counts for less than the map.

groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
groups.word_limit: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER
groups.text:
Students need a {{6}} to measure the angle of the rock layers.
The notebook should have paper that is {{7}}.
To stay safe on the beach, everyone receives a {{8}}.
A hard hat must be worn within {{9}} of the cliff.
The trip costs £180, which includes the coach, the hostel and {{10}}.

parts.context: You will hear part of a lecture about the history of maps.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Hello, Ben. You wanted to ask about the field trip.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes, Doctor Marsden. I missed the briefing because of a hospital appointment, and I don't want to turn up unprepared.

script.speaker: A
script.text: No problem. We leave on the Monday of week seven, and we're away for four nights.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Someone told me it was five.

script.speaker: A
script.text: It was five last year. We've cut a day because the hostel has put its prices up.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Right. And we're going to the same stretch of coast?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes, but the purpose is different this year. Previous groups spent most of the time collecting fossils. This time, the main task is to make a geological map of a section of cliff. Fossils are a bonus.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I've never made a map in the field.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Very few students have. That's why the first day is spent with me, all together, learning the method. From the second day you work in pairs.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Do we choose our own partner?

script.speaker: A
script.text: No, I put a confident student with a less confident one. People complain, but it works.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fair enough. What should I bring? I've got a hammer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Leave it at home. The whole coast is protected, and hammering the cliff is against the law. What you need is a hand lens, a compass that measures the angle of the rock layers, and a notebook with waterproof paper.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Waterproof paper. I wouldn't have thought of that.

script.speaker: A
script.text: You will after an hour of rain. The department lends out the compasses, but there aren't enough for everyone, so reserve yours this week.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll do it today. Is there anything dangerous I should know about?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The tide. Twice a day, the sea comes right up to the foot of the cliff, and two of the bays have no way out. I give everyone a tide table, and nobody goes onto the beach without checking it.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Understood. What about falling rocks?

script.speaker: A
script.text: You wear a hard hat whenever you're within ten metres of the cliff. No exceptions.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And how is the trip assessed?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Not by an exam. You hand in your field notebook, exactly as you wrote it on the beach, and the finished map. The notebook is worth sixty per cent.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So I shouldn't copy it out neatly afterwards.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Please don't. I want to see what you observed at the time, mistakes included. A tidy notebook written in the hostel is easy to spot.

script.speaker: B
script.text: OK. And the cost?

script.speaker: A
script.text: A hundred and eighty pounds, which covers the coach, the hostel and breakfast. Other meals are your own responsibility. If the cost is a difficulty, there's a hardship fund. The form is on the department website.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Thanks. I'll have a look.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A map is never a neutral picture of the world. Every map is made by someone, for a purpose, and it leaves out far more than it includes. That's the idea I'd like you to keep in mind as we go through a few episodes in the history of map making.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The oldest surviving maps aren't of countries or continents. They're local. A clay tablet from Babylon, about four thousand years old, shows a single estate, with its fields and canals, and it was probably made to settle who owned what.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The Greeks took a huge step. They understood that the earth was a sphere, and one of them, Eratosthenes, calculated its size remarkably accurately. He did it by measuring the length of a shadow in two different cities on the same day.

script.speaker: C
script.text: In medieval Europe, much of that knowledge was set aside. The great maps of the period were not made for travellers at all. They were made for churches, and their purpose was to teach religion. Jerusalem is placed at the centre, and east, not north, is at the top.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Sailors, meanwhile, used something far more practical, the sea chart. These charts, drawn on animal skin, were covered with straight lines radiating from points around the coast. A captain would choose a line and follow it with his compass.

script.speaker: C
script.text: In fifteen sixty-nine, Gerard Mercator solved a problem that had troubled navigators for a century. On his map, a course in a constant direction appears as a straight line. The price is distortion. Areas far from the equator are stretched, so Greenland looks as large as Africa, when in reality Africa is fourteen times bigger.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Maps have also been tools of power. In the eighteenth century, governments began to map their own territory in detail, and the first aim was usually military. The national mapping agency of Britain was set up because the army feared an invasion from France.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Perhaps the most famous map of the twentieth century is the plan of the London Underground, designed in nineteen thirty-three. Its designer, Harry Beck, was not a map maker but an electrical draughtsman, and he drew the system like a circuit diagram. He ignored real distances completely. Passengers, he argued, only needed to know the order of the stations and where to change.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Today, of course, the map is in our pockets, and it puts us at the centre, wherever we go. It's worth asking what that does to our sense of direction. Several studies suggest that people who rely on satellite navigation build a poorer mental picture of their surroundings than those who use a paper map.

explanations.1: A day was cut because the hostel has put its prices up.
explanations.2: Previous groups collected fossils; this time the task is a geological map.
explanations.3: She puts a confident student with a less confident one.
explanations.4: The coast is protected and hammering the cliff is against the law.
explanations.5: She wants to see what was observed at the time; it is worth sixty per cent.

title: Gym consultation and a coach trip

parts.context: You will hear a man talking to a fitness instructor at a gym about a training programme.

groups.instruction: Complete the form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

parts.context: You will hear a tour leader giving information to passengers at the start of a coach trip.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.prompt: Passengers are allowed to

options.A: use the toilet whenever they like.
options.B: have hot drinks at their seats.

questions.prompt: Where does Alan recommend having coffee in Ashbourne?
Where will lunch be served?
What does Alan say about the castle tower?

options.A: It is closed to the public.

questions.prompt: By what time should passengers tell Alan which afternoon activity they want?

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
groups.text:
Coach trip: programme
Day 1
- arrive at the hotel at about {{16}} pm
Day 2
- morning: trip on a steam {{17}}
- afternoon: a walk along the shore, or a museum about the {{18}}
Day 3
- visit some {{19}} on the way home
Reminders
- keep a waterproof {{20}} with you

script.speaker: A
script.text: Hi, you must be my two o'clock. I'm Carla.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hello, Carla. Yes, I joined last week, and reception said I should book a session with you before I use the equipment.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's right. I'll ask a few questions, and then we'll design a programme. Can I take your name?

script.speaker: B
script.text: It's Gareth Finch. F, I, N, C, H.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thanks, Gareth. And how old are you, if you don't mind?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'm fifty-two.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Great. What's brought you to the gym? Is there a particular goal?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Well, my doctor told me to lose some weight, but honestly that's not what motivates me. My daughter has talked me into a charity walk in September. It's twenty-six miles in one day, and I'd like to finish it without collapsing.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's a good target. So we're building stamina. How active are you at the moment?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Not very. I sit at a desk all day. I walk the dog for about twenty minutes each morning, and that's it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: It's a start. Any injuries I should know about?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I hurt my left knee playing football years ago. It's fine for walking, but it aches when I run.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then we'll leave running out for now. I'd put you on the cycling machine and the rowing machine. Both are kind to the knees.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I've never rowed in my life.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'll show you the technique. Most people pull with their arms, and it should come from the legs. How often can you come in?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I was thinking every day.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'd rather you didn't. People who start with seven days a week have usually given up by week three. Three times a week is plenty, with a day of rest in between.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Three times. Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, then.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. Each session will be forty-five minutes. Ten minutes to warm up, half an hour of work, and five minutes of stretching at the end. Please don't skip the stretching.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll try not to. Should I change what I eat?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'm not a dietitian, so I won't give you a diet. One simple thing, though. Drink more water. Most people who feel tired in the afternoon are just thirsty.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's easy enough. How will I know whether I'm improving?

script.speaker: A
script.text: We'll test you today, and again in six weeks. I'll measure how far you can cycle in twelve minutes, and your heart rate afterwards.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And the long walks? Do I need to practise those?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Definitely. Once a fortnight, do a long walk at the weekend, and add two miles each time. And buy your boots now, not in August. They need wearing in.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I hadn't thought of that. I'll go shopping tomorrow.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome aboard. My name's Alan, and I'm your tour leader for the next three days. Our driver is Sunita, who has been driving these roads for twenty years.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Before we set off, some practical points. Seat belts are fitted to every seat, and the law requires you to wear them. There's a toilet at the back of the coach, but we'd ask you to use it only in an emergency, as we'll be stopping every two hours. You're welcome to drink water on board, but please, no hot drinks, because of the risk of spills.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, today's programme. Our first stop is the market town of Ashbourne, where we arrive at about half past ten. You'll have an hour and a quarter there. It happens to be market day, so the square will be lively. If you want coffee, I'd avoid the cafes in the square, which are expensive, and try the bakery behind the church.

script.speaker: C
script.text: From Ashbourne, we drive up into the hills, to Dunmore Castle, arriving at around one. Lunch is included today, and it's served in the old stables, not in the castle itself. After lunch, there's a guided tour of the castle. I should warn you that there are ninety-two steps to the top of the tower. The view is splendid, but nobody will mind if you prefer to stay in the gardens.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We leave the castle at four, and we should reach our hotel in Lakeside by half past five. Your luggage will be taken to your rooms. Dinner is at seven thirty in the hotel restaurant.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Tomorrow is a full day on the lake. In the morning we take the steam boat to the far end, and in the afternoon you have a choice. You can join me for a gentle walk of about three miles along the shore, or you can visit the pencil museum in the village. Yes, a pencil museum. It's better than it sounds. Please tell me at dinner tonight which you'd prefer, so that I can book tickets.

script.speaker: C
script.text: On the third day, we visit the gardens at Holker Hall on the way home, and we expect to be back at the bus station by six in the evening.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Two last things. The weather in the hills changes quickly, so keep a waterproof jacket with you, not in the luggage hold. And if you're delayed at any stop, call the number printed on your ticket. The coach can wait ten minutes, but no longer, because the driver's hours are controlled by law.

explanations.11: The toilet is for emergencies and hot drinks are not allowed.
explanations.12: The cafes in the square are expensive; he suggests the bakery behind the church.
explanations.13: Lunch is in the old stables, not in the castle itself.
explanations.14: There are ninety-two steps, and nobody will mind if people stay in the gardens.
explanations.15: He asks to be told at dinner tonight so that he can book tickets.

title: Classroom observation and how honeybees communicate

parts.context: You will hear two trainee teachers, Amy and Jack, comparing notes on lessons they have observed.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.prompt: Jack would have preferred to

options.A: observe a single class for the whole week.
options.B: observe a wider range of classes.

parts.context: You will hear part of a lecture about how honeybees communicate.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Jack, how was your observation week? Mine was exhausting.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Same here. Twelve lessons in five days. Which school were you at?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Hillside Primary. I watched the same class of nine-year-olds all week, with two different teachers.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I was moved around much more. Six classes. I'd have preferred your arrangement. You only start to notice things once you know the children's names.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's true. By Wednesday I could see which children never put their hands up. On Monday I hadn't noticed them at all.

script.speaker: B
script.text: What was the most useful thing you saw?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The way one teacher asked questions. She'd ask something, and then wait. A full five seconds of silence. It felt very long. But far more children answered, and their answers were longer.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I've read about that. Most teachers wait less than a second.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And the other teacher did exactly that. He answered his own questions half the time.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The thing that struck me was about groups. I'd always assumed children learn best with their friends. One teacher let them choose, and those groups just chatted. Another teacher put the names on the board before the lesson, mixing abilities, and the work was much better.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Did the children complain?

script.speaker: B
script.text: For about thirty seconds. Then they got on with it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What about behaviour? That's what worries me most about teaching.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Me too. What I noticed is that the calm classrooms had routines. In one, the children came in and immediately started a short task that was already on the board. No waiting, no chance for trouble to begin.

script.speaker: A
script.text: My school had something similar for the end of the lesson. The last three minutes were always for tidying, and the teacher never let it slip.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We ought to put routines in our report. Now, the form we had to fill in. Did you find it helpful?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Not really. It asked me to tick boxes every two minutes, and I spent so long ticking that I missed what was happening.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I gave up after the first day and wrote notes in my own words.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I wish I had. Let's recommend that next year's trainees keep a diary.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Agreed. Are you going to mention the teachers by name?

script.speaker: A
script.text: No. We have to keep them anonymous. I'll call them Teacher A and Teacher B.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good. When shall we write this up?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'm free on Thursday afternoon. The library has study rooms we can book.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Thursday at two. I'll reserve one.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A honeybee colony may contain fifty thousand individuals, and no one is in charge. The queen lays eggs, but she gives no orders. And yet the colony behaves as if it had a single mind. This morning I'll look at how information moves through the hive.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The best known method is the waggle dance. When a bee finds a rich source of food, she returns to the hive and dances on the surface of the comb, in the dark, surrounded by other workers. She runs in a straight line, shaking her body from side to side, then circles back and repeats it.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The dance carries two pieces of information. The first is direction. The angle of her straight run, measured from the vertical, matches the angle between the food and the sun. The second is distance, which is shown by how long the waggling lasts. Roughly one second of waggling corresponds to a kilometre of flight.

script.speaker: C
script.text: This was worked out in the nineteen forties by an Austrian scientist, Karl von Frisch. He marked individual bees with dots of paint and watched them for years. Many of his colleagues refused to believe that an insect could use a symbolic language, and he was not awarded the Nobel Prize until nineteen seventy-three.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Because the hive is dark, the other bees can't see the dance. They follow it by touch, using their antennae, and they also pick up the scent of the flowers on the dancer's body.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Dancing isn't the only signal. Chemicals are just as important. The queen produces a substance that is passed from bee to bee as they feed one another. As long as it circulates, the workers know she's alive and well. If she dies, the level drops within hours, and the workers begin raising a new queen.

script.speaker: C
script.text: There's also an alarm chemical. When a bee stings, it releases a scent that marks the target and calls other bees to attack the same spot. Curiously, this scent smells of bananas, which is why beekeepers avoid eating them before opening a hive.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The most remarkable example of communication comes when a colony needs a new home. Scouts fly out and inspect possible sites, hollow trees for instance. Each returns and dances for the site she has found, and the better the site, the longer she dances. Other scouts go to look, and they in turn dance. Over a day or two, support builds for one site, and when enough scouts agree, the whole swarm takes off together. It's a form of voting, and it almost always selects the best site available.

explanations.1: He was moved around six classes and would have preferred Amy's arrangement.
explanations.2: The teacher waited five seconds, and more children gave longer answers.
explanations.3: Friend groups just chatted; mixed groups put on the board worked much better.
explanations.4: Children started a task on the board as soon as they came in.
explanations.5: She spent so long ticking boxes that she missed what was happening.

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: A

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: A

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: A
script.text: I can offer Wednesday or Thursday.

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: A

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: A
script.text: It'll go back onto your card within three days. And the exchange itself will be free, of course. We'll telephone you as soon as the grey sofas arrive, to arrange a date.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Could you email as well? I don't always hear the phone.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Certainly. I have your address here. And if you have any questions, ask for me by name. My surname's Pruett. P, R, U, E, double T.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good morning, and welcome to Saltmarsh Nature Reserve. My name's Erin, and I'm one of the wardens. I'll take a few minutes to tell you about the reserve, and then you're free to explore.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Forty years ago, the land you're standing on was a gravel quarry. When the gravel ran out, the pits filled with water, and the company intended to sell the site for housing. It was a local bird-watching society that raised the money to buy it, and it has been managed for wildlife ever since.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The reserve covers about ninety hectares, and roughly half of that is open water. We've recorded two hundred and thirty species of bird here. What most visitors hope to see is the kingfisher. I have to be honest. They're here all year, but they're small and fast, and plenty of people go home disappointed. Your best chance is early in the morning, from the hide beside the stream.

script.speaker: C
script.text: There are three marked trails. The green trail is the shortest. It takes about half an hour and it's suitable for pushchairs. The blue trail goes all the way round the main lake and takes ninety minutes. And the red trail leads out across the marsh to the sea wall. Please note that part of the red trail is closed at the moment. That isn't because of flooding, as the sign in the car park suggests. A pair of rare birds is nesting right beside the path, and we don't want them disturbed.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We have five hides, which are wooden shelters where you can watch the birds without being seen. Please keep your voices down inside, and close the windows when you leave, or the swallows fly in and can't get out.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Dogs are welcome on the green trail only, and they must be on a lead. I know that disappoints some people, but a single loose dog can empty a lake of birds in seconds.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The visitor centre has a cafe and a small shop. You can also hire binoculars there for three pounds, which I'd recommend if you haven't brought your own.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A few events are coming up. This Saturday there's a walk at dusk to look for bats. Next month we're running a photography workshop. And every Wednesday morning, volunteers meet to cut back the reeds. No experience is needed, and we provide boots and gloves.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Lastly, entry to the reserve is free, but it costs us a thousand pounds a day to run. If you've enjoyed your visit, there's a donation box by the door.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.
groups.text:
The placebo effect
Background
- in wartime, a wounded soldier was injected with {{11}} water
- in a double-blind trial, neither patients nor {{12}} know who gets the drug
What influences the effect
- form: an {{13}} works better than a pill
- colour: {{14}} pills helped people to sleep
- a pill that patients believed was {{15}} relieved more pain
- patients do better when they feel a doctor has {{16}} to them

- placebos affect symptoms, e.g. pain, but do not shrink {{17}}
- asthma patients felt better, but their {{18}} had not improved

- placebos worked even when the bottle carried an honest {{19}}
- nocebo effect: a warning about headaches can produce {{20}}

script.speaker: A
script.text: Marcus, I've finished reading the data on Kerrin Island. Shall we decide what our argument is?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Go ahead. My first impression was that tourism has been a great success there. Visitor numbers have tripled in ten years.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The numbers have, yes. But look at the income of the islanders themselves. It's risen by only eight per cent over the same period.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Eight per cent, against a tripling of visitors? Where's the money going?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Mostly off the island. The three big hotels belong to a company on the mainland, and so do the ferries. The profits leave on the same boat as the tourists.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Economists call that leakage. We should use the term. So what do local people actually get?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Jobs, but mainly cleaning and waiting at tables, and only from May to September. In winter, unemployment is higher now than it was before tourism took off.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Why higher?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Because fishing has declined. Young people left the boats for hotel work, and the skills weren't passed on.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's a strong point. What about housing? I saw something in the council report.

script.speaker: A
script.text: A third of the houses are now holiday homes, empty for most of the year. Prices have doubled, and local families can't afford to buy.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So we argue that growth in tourism hasn't meant development for the islanders. I'm convinced. But we need to offer solutions, not just criticism.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I've found two examples. On one Scottish island, the community bought the land and runs its own hostel and cafe, so the profits stay.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Community ownership. That needs capital, though. Where did they get it?

script.speaker: A
script.text: A national lottery grant, plus small loans from residents.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And the second example?

script.speaker: A
script.text: A visitor tax. An island in Spain charges two euros per person per night and spends it on water and waste services.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'm less keen on that. Kerrin's visitors mostly come for a day, and a tax per night would miss them.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then it could be collected on the ferry ticket.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That would work. OK, structure. I think we open with the figures, the tripling against the eight per cent. That contrast is the whole story.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes. Then leakage, seasonal work, housing, and finally the two solutions.

script.speaker: B
script.text: How do we divide the writing?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'll take leakage and housing. Could you do employment and the solutions?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Sure. And the graphs?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'll make them, since I've got the spreadsheet. We should meet again on Tuesday to put it together.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Tuesday morning suits me. In the library cafe?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Perfect.

script.speaker: C
script.text: This afternoon's topic is one of the strangest in medicine. A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient, a sugar pill, for instance, and yet patients who take one very often improve. I want to look at what we know about this, and at what it does and doesn't mean.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The modern study of the subject is usually traced to the Second World War. An American army doctor, Henry Beecher, ran short of morphine. A nurse, according to the story, injected a wounded soldier with salt water and told him it was a powerful painkiller. To Beecher's amazement, the soldier's pain eased.

script.speaker: C
script.text: After the war, Beecher argued that every new drug should be tested against a placebo, and that's now the standard. In a proper trial, neither the patients nor the doctors know who is receiving the real drug. We call that a double-blind trial.

script.speaker: C
script.text: What have such trials taught us about placebos themselves? First, the form of the treatment matters. Two pills work better than one. An injection works better than a pill. Even the colour has an influence. In several studies, blue pills were better at helping people sleep, while red ones were more effective as stimulants.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Second, the price matters. In one experiment, volunteers were given the same dummy painkiller. Half were told it cost two and a half dollars a pill, and half were told it cost ten cents. The supposedly expensive pill relieved pain much more effectively.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Third, the relationship with the doctor matters. Patients who are given time, and who feel that they've been listened to, improve more than those who are hurried through.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, an important caution. Placebos change how patients feel. They affect symptoms such as pain, nausea and tiredness. They don't shrink tumours or mend broken bones. Asthma patients given a dummy inhaler reported feeling much better, but when their breathing was measured, it hadn't improved at all.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Is a placebo simply imagination? Not entirely. Brain scans show that when people expect relief from pain, the brain releases its own natural painkillers. So the effect is real, in the sense that it has a physical basis.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The most surprising recent finding concerns honesty. Researchers at Harvard gave patients pills in a bottle with a label that clearly said placebo, and explained that they contained no medicine. Those patients still did better than a group who received no treatment.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, there's a darker side, known as the nocebo effect. If patients are warned that a pill may cause headaches, a good number will develop headaches, even when the pill is made of sugar. That raises a real dilemma about how much doctors should say about side effects.

explanations.1: Visitor numbers have tripled in ten years.
explanations.2: The big hotels and the ferries belong to a mainland company.
explanations.3: Young people left the boats for hotel work and the skills were not passed on.
explanations.4: A third of the houses are holiday homes, and prices have doubled.
explanations.5: Most visitors come for a day, so a nightly tax would miss them.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let me start with that pool. It's twenty-five metres long, with eight lanes. The feature I'm most pleased with is the floor at the shallow end, which can be raised and lowered. That means we can make the water suitable for small children in the morning, and deep enough for diving in the evening.

script.speaker: C

script.speaker: C

On parking, we have a hundred and fifty spaces, and residents' streets will become permit-only from next month, so visitors won't be able to park outside your homes.
