title: App usability testing and the history of concrete

parts.context: You will hear two computing students, Zara and Finn, discussing the testing of a mobile app they have designed.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.prompt: Zara is concerned that the first group of testers

options.B: was not typical of future users.
options.C: did not take the test seriously.

questions.prompt: Where will the testers for the second round come from?

options.C: a club at a community centre

questions.prompt: What was the main finding of the first round?

options.A: Booking took much longer than intended.
options.B: Several people failed to make a booking.

questions.prompt: Why did some testers think there were no appointments?

options.B: The dates were shown in the wrong order.
options.C: They did not know how to see the next week.

questions.prompt: Some people booked twice because

options.A: the first booking was not saved.
options.B: the confirmation was not clear enough.
options.C: they pressed the button by mistake.

groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
groups.text:
The feature that every tester praised was the {{6}}.
Testers liked signing in without a {{7}}.
During the sessions, Zara filmed the {{8}}.
Next time, Zara will show testers an example {{9}} first.
The most urgent change is to the {{10}}.

parts.context: You will hear part of an engineering lecture about the history of concrete.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.
groups.text:
Concrete
What it is
- cement is the {{11}} that binds water, sand and stones
Roman concrete
- made with lime and volcanic {{12}}
- could set under {{13}}, so was used for harbours
- the Pantheon's dome: lighter towards the top, where {{14}} was used
Modern concrete
- Portland cement (1824) was named after a kind of {{15}}
- concrete breaks easily when {{16}} or bent
- reinforced concrete was invented by a {{17}}, who put iron wire in pots
Problems
- water gets in and the steel {{18}}
- cement is made by heating {{19}}, which releases carbon dioxide
New ideas
- concrete that can {{20}} its own cracks, like Roman concrete

script.speaker: A
script.text: Finn, I've got the results from the first round of testing. Have you got ten minutes?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Sure. How many people tried the app in the end?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Only six. I'd invited ten, but four cancelled.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Is six enough?

script.speaker: A
script.text: According to the textbook, five users reveal most of the serious problems. What matters more is who they are. And that's my worry. All six were students on our course.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So they're good with technology. Not exactly typical of people who'll use an app for booking doctor's appointments.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Exactly. For the second round, I'd like to recruit older people. My aunt runs a community centre, and she's offered to ask her lunch club.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That would be much more realistic. So what did the first round show?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The good news is that everybody managed to book an appointment. The bad news is how long it took. We'd designed it to take under a minute. The average was nearly three.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Three minutes? Where did they get stuck?

script.speaker: A
script.text: On the calendar. People didn't realise they had to swipe sideways to see the following week. Four of them thought there were no appointments left.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I told you we needed arrows.

script.speaker: A
script.text: You did, and I should have listened. I wanted the screen to look clean.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We'll add arrows. Anything else?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The confirmation. After you book, the app shows a green tick, and that's all. Three people booked twice, because they weren't sure it had worked.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So we need a proper message, with the date and time repeated.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And a text message sent to their phone. People trust a text.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Agreed. What did they like?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The reminder feature. Everyone mentioned it. And the fact that you don't have to create a password. Signing in with a code sent to your phone was popular.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's a relief. It took me two weeks to build. How did you record the sessions?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I filmed the screen, and I asked people to say aloud what they were thinking as they went.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Did that work? I'd feel silly.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Some went quiet. I had to keep prompting them. Next time I'll show a short example video first, so they know what's expected.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good idea. When's the second round?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The lunch club meets on Fridays. If you can make the changes by the twelfth, I'll test on the fourteenth.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The twelfth is tight, but I'll manage the calendar and the confirmation. The text message may have to wait.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's fine. The calendar is the priority.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Concrete is the most widely used man-made material on the planet. We pour enough of it each year to build a wall around the equator. Yet most people know almost nothing about it, so today I'll sketch its history and then look at the problem it now poses.

script.speaker: C
script.text: First, a definition, because people confuse concrete with cement. Cement is a grey powder, and it's only one ingredient. Mix it with water, sand and small stones, and you get concrete. The cement is the glue that binds the rest.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The Romans were the first great builders in concrete. Their recipe used lime and a volcanic ash found near Naples. This produced a material that would even set under water, which let them build harbours. Their most famous concrete structure is the Pantheon in Rome. Its dome, almost two thousand years old, is still the largest in the world made of concrete without steel inside it.

script.speaker: C
script.text: How did they keep such a dome from collapsing under its own weight? By varying the mix. At the base, the concrete contains heavy stone. Near the top, they used pumice, a volcanic rock so light that it floats.

script.speaker: C
script.text: When the Roman empire fell, the recipe was lost for over a thousand years. Modern concrete dates from eighteen twenty-four, when an English bricklayer, Joseph Aspdin, patented what he called Portland cement, because its colour reminded him of a stone quarried at Portland on the south coast.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Concrete has one great weakness. It's enormously strong when you squeeze it, but it cracks easily when it's stretched or bent. The solution, discovered in France, came from an unlikely source. A gardener named Joseph Monier was tired of his clay flowerpots breaking, and in the eighteen sixties he made pots of concrete with a mesh of iron wire inside. The idea of reinforced concrete was born, and it made tall buildings and long bridges possible.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Ironically, the steel is also the reason modern concrete doesn't last as long as Roman concrete. Water slowly gets in, the steel rusts, and as it rusts it expands and breaks the concrete from within.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And there's a larger problem. Making cement means heating limestone to about fourteen hundred degrees, and the process releases carbon dioxide. Cement production is responsible for roughly eight per cent of the world's emissions, more than aviation.

script.speaker: C
script.text: So researchers are looking for alternatives. Some replace part of the cement with ash, a waste product from power stations. Others are developing concrete that absorbs carbon dioxide as it hardens. And one team has gone back to the Romans, whose concrete, we've learned, could heal its own cracks.

explanations.1: Six is enough, but all were computing students, good with technology.
explanations.2: Her aunt will ask the lunch club at the community centre she runs.
explanations.3: Everybody managed to book, but it took nearly three minutes, not under one.
explanations.4: They did not realise they had to swipe sideways.
explanations.5: The app only showed a green tick, so they were not sure it had worked.

title: Travel insurance claim and a conference venue

parts.context: You will hear a woman phoning an insurance company to make a claim after a holiday.

groups.instruction: Complete the form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

parts.context: You will hear an organiser giving information to people attending a conference.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.prompt: Apart from showing a name, what is the purpose of the badge?

options.A: It gives access to the wireless network.
options.C: It must be shown at lunch.

questions.prompt: Why is the opening lecture being given by a different speaker?

options.A: The original speaker has been delayed by a travel problem.
options.C: The original speaker asked to speak later.

questions.prompt: Where will lunch be served?

options.C: in a restaurant in the other building

questions.prompt: People asking questions must use a microphone because
What does Paula say about the conference dinner?

options.B: It will be held at the museum.
options.C: Tickets are on sale at the help desk.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
groups.text:
Conference arrangements
- posters: in the west building, reached by a glass {{16}}
- special diets: table with a {{17}} flag
- network password: on the {{18}} of the badge
- evening reception: at the city {{19}}, at 7 pm
- fire: meet in the car {{20}} by the river

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good afternoon, Beacon Travel Insurance, claims department. My name is Rashid.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hello. I need to make a claim. My camera was stolen while I was on holiday last week.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Could I have your policy number, please?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes. It's B T, six six, zero four, one nine.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Six six, zero four, one nine. Thank you. And your surname?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Abbott. A, double B, O, double T.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thank you, Mrs Abbott. Where were you when it happened?

script.speaker: B
script.text: In Lisbon. We were there for five days.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And can you tell me what happened?

script.speaker: B
script.text: We were having lunch outside a cafe. I'd put my bag on the chair next to me, and when we got up to leave, it had gone. I didn't see anyone take it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So the bag was taken, with the camera inside. What else was in it?

script.speaker: B
script.text: My sunglasses, and a guidebook. My purse and my passport were in my coat pocket, luckily.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That is lucky. On what date did this happen?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The ninth of June. It was our last full day.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And did you report it to the police?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I did, the same afternoon. They gave me a report with a number on it. It's all in Portuguese, I'm afraid.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's no problem. We need a copy, and we arrange a translation ourselves. Now, the camera. What make was it?

script.speaker: B
script.text: A Lumina. L, U, M, I, N, A. It was about two years old.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Do you remember what you paid for it?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Six hundred and forty pounds. I still have the receipt at home.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's very useful. I should explain that we don't pay the full price of a two-year-old item. We take off a percentage for age, so you'd receive roughly four hundred and fifty. There's also an excess of fifty pounds, which you pay towards any claim.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So about four hundred. I suppose that's fair. What about the bag and the sunglasses?

script.speaker: A
script.text: You can claim for those too, but for anything worth over a hundred pounds, we need proof that you owned it.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The sunglasses were cheap. The bag was leather, a present. I've got photographs of me carrying it, if that helps.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Photographs are accepted. Now, I'll email you a claim form today. Please send it back with the police report, the receipt and the photographs.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Do they have to be posted? I'm not keen on sending originals.

script.speaker: A
script.text: No, you can upload scans on our website. It's quicker, too. The deadline is thirty days from the date of the theft.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Thirty days. And how long before I hear?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Usually within ten working days. Payment goes directly into your bank account.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Thank you. You've been very helpful.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Riverside Conference Centre. I'm Paula, from the organising team. Before the first talk, I'd like to explain a few arrangements.

script.speaker: C
script.text: You should each have collected a badge at the door. Please wear it at all times. It isn't simply so that we know your names. The badge also opens the doors between the two buildings, and without it you won't get through.

script.speaker: C
script.text: There's been one change to the printed programme. The opening lecture was due to be given by Professor Lang, but her flight from Chicago was cancelled last night. She'll now speak tomorrow at nine. In her place this morning, Doctor Mensah has kindly agreed to bring his talk forward.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let me describe the layout. We're in the main hall, on the ground floor of the east building. The smaller sessions take place upstairs, in rooms one to six. The exhibition of posters is in the west building, which you reach by the glass bridge on the first floor.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Coffee will be served at half past ten, in the foyer outside this hall. Lunch is at one o'clock. Lunch is not served in the foyer, please note, but in the restaurant on the ground floor of the west building. If you told us about a special diet when you registered, your meal will be at the table marked with a green flag.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The wireless network is called Riverside Guest, and the password is printed on the back of your badge. It's rather slow when everyone connects at once, so please don't download large files during the talks.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A word about questions. After each talk there'll be ten minutes for discussion. Please wait for the microphone before you speak. The sessions are being recorded, and without the microphone, your question won't be heard on the recording.

script.speaker: C
script.text: This evening, there's a reception at the city museum, starting at seven. It's fifteen minutes away on foot. For anyone who'd prefer not to walk, a bus will leave from the front entrance at a quarter to seven. The conference dinner, tomorrow night, is for those who booked in advance, and I'm sorry to say that there are no tickets left.

script.speaker: C
script.text: If you have a problem at any point, come to the help desk. It's beside the cloakroom, and it's staffed until six. We can print documents and look after luggage, and we hold a small supply of phone chargers.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, in the unlikely event of a fire alarm, leave by the nearest exit and gather in the car park by the river. Thank you, and enjoy the day.

explanations.11: The badge opens the doors between the two buildings.
explanations.12: Professor Lang's flight was cancelled.
explanations.13: In the restaurant on the ground floor of the west building.
explanations.14: Without it the question will not be heard on the recording.
explanations.15: It is for those who booked in advance, and there are no tickets left.

title: Commuting survey and the science of taste

parts.context: You will hear two sociology students, Imogen and Dev, discussing a survey they carried out on how people travel to work.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.prompt: Why did the survey receive more replies than expected?

options.A: It stayed open longer than planned.
options.B: It was shared on a council web page.

questions.prompt: What is the weakness of the sample?

options.A: Too many of those who replied work in city-centre offices.
options.B: Too few of those who replied have jobs.
options.C: Most of those who replied are cyclists.

questions.prompt: Compared with five years ago, the proportion of people driving to work
What was the most important factor in people's choice of transport?
What would be most likely to persuade drivers to use buses?

options.A: routes that avoid the city centre

groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
groups.text:
The use of one form of transport, {{6}}, has doubled.
Cyclists are most concerned about safety at {{7}}.
Bus users complain that there are too few {{8}}.
Comments from the survey will be quoted {{9}}.
Dev will produce a {{10}} of where people travel from.

parts.context: You will hear part of a lecture about the science of taste.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Dev, the survey closed last night. We got three hundred and twelve replies.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's more than I expected. I thought we'd be lucky to reach two hundred.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The link was shared on the city council's page, which helped enormously. But there's a catch. Nearly two thirds of the people who replied work in offices in the centre.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So people in factories and shops on the edge of town are missing.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Largely. We'll have to say clearly that the sample isn't representative.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fine. So what are the headline results?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The car is still the most common way to get to work, at forty-one per cent. But five years ago, in the council's own survey, it was fifty-eight.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's a big drop. Where have the drivers gone? To the buses?

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's what I assumed. Bus use has barely changed, though. The growth is in cycling, which has doubled, and in people who don't commute at all on some days because they work from home.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Interesting. Did we ask why people chose the way they travel?

script.speaker: A
script.text: We did. I expected cost to come first. It came third. The top reason, by a long way, was the time the journey takes. Second was reliability, knowing when you'll arrive.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That makes sense. A cheap bus is no use if it doesn't turn up. What did drivers say would persuade them to switch?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Most said nothing would. But among those who'd consider it, the most popular answer was a direct bus route that doesn't go through the centre.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Not lower fares?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Lower fares came well down the list.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The council should hear that. Now, the open question at the end. Did anyone write anything useful?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Over a hundred people did. I've started sorting the comments into themes. The biggest theme among cyclists is safety at junctions. And among bus users, it's the lack of shelters. People hate waiting in the rain.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We could quote a few of those. They'd bring the numbers to life.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes, but anonymously. We promised that nobody would be identified.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Of course. Now, how do we present the figures? A table for each question would be dull.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'd use bar charts for the main comparisons. And a map, to show where people travel from. We collected the first half of everyone's postcode.

script.speaker: B
script.text: A map would be great. I can make that. I've used the mapping software before.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then I'll do the charts and write up the method. Shall we aim to have a draft by the end of next week?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Friday. Send me the postcode data tonight, and I'll start.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Most of us learned at school that the tongue has a map, with sweetness tasted at the tip and bitterness at the back. It's a neat picture, and it's wrong. It came from the mistranslation of a German paper published in nineteen hundred and one. In reality, every part of the tongue can detect every taste. Today I'll go through what science now says.

script.speaker: C
script.text: There are five basic tastes that everyone accepts. Sweet, sour, salty and bitter you know. The fifth is umami, a Japanese word meaning roughly a pleasant savoury taste. It was identified in nineteen hundred and eight by a chemist in Tokyo, who wondered why a soup made from seaweed was so satisfying.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Each taste seems to have a purpose. Sweetness signals energy. Saltiness signals minerals the body needs. Umami indicates protein. Sourness can warn that fruit isn't ripe, or that food has gone off. And bitterness is above all a warning of poison, since many toxic plants are bitter. That's why young children refuse bitter vegetables. It's an instinct, and they generally grow out of it.

script.speaker: C
script.text: People differ a great deal. About a quarter of the population are what researchers call supertasters. They have far more taste buds than average, and they experience bitterness, in particular, much more intensely. They often dislike coffee and strong cheese.

script.speaker: C
script.text: But here's the essential point. Most of what we call taste isn't taste at all. It's smell. When you chew, air carries the scent of the food up the back of the throat to the nose. Try holding your nose while you eat a piece of apple and a piece of raw onion. You'll find them surprisingly hard to tell apart.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The other senses join in too. In a well-known experiment, wine experts were given a white wine that had been coloured red. They described it in the language normally used for red wine. Sound matters as well. People judge crisps to be fresher when the crunch they hear is made louder.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Even the plate has an effect. A dessert served on a white plate is rated sweeter than the same dessert on a black one. And heavy cutlery makes people think a meal is of higher quality and worth paying more for.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Airlines have learned a practical lesson from all this. In a cabin, the dry air and the constant noise of the engines dull our sense of sweetness and saltiness by up to thirty per cent, which is why airline food is so heavily seasoned. Umami, curiously, isn't affected, and that may explain why tomato juice is so popular on planes.

explanations.1: The link on the city council's page helped enormously.
explanations.2: Nearly two thirds work in offices in the centre.
explanations.3: Forty-one per cent now, against fifty-eight.
explanations.4: Time came first, reliability second, and cost third.
explanations.5: A direct route that does not go through the centre; lower fares came well down the list.

title: Removal company booking and a zoo education programme

parts.context: You will hear a man phoning a removal company to arrange a house move.

groups.instruction: Complete the form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

parts.context: You will hear an education officer at a zoo talking to a group of teachers about school visits.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.prompt: How does Luis answer teachers who doubt the value of zoos?

options.A: He says the zoo's main work is conservation.
options.B: He says children enjoy seeing the animals.
options.C: He says the animals are well treated.

questions.prompt: The zoo's research showed that pupils remembered most when they

options.C: had taken part in a workshop.

questions.prompt: Why does Luis recommend visiting in the autumn?
What does Luis say about the gift shop?

options.A: It should not be left until the end of the visit.
options.B: It is too small for school groups.
options.C: It gives a discount to schools.

groups.instruction: Which workshop is described in each of the following ways? Choose the correct letter, A-D, for questions 15-17.

questions.prompt: It involves collecting information by watching animals.
It allows children to touch things.
It is held in a heated building.

groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
groups.text:
A workshop costs £{{18}} for each class.
Lunch can be eaten in the picnic {{19}}.
The zoo's website provides {{20}} for all ages.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good morning, Swift Removals. This is Angela. How can I help?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Morning. I'm moving house next month, and I'd like a quotation.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Certainly. Where are you moving from?

script.speaker: B
script.text: From a flat in Bristol to a house in Exeter.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Bristol to Exeter. That's about eighty miles, so one day's work. What size is the flat?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Two bedrooms. It's on the third floor, I should warn you.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Is there a lift?

script.speaker: B
script.text: There is, but it's small. I doubt the wardrobe would fit in it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Our team can carry large items down the stairs. It just means sending a crew of three, not two. And the new house?

script.speaker: B
script.text: It's a normal two-storey house, with a drive, so the van can park right outside.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That makes things easier. Do you have any very heavy or delicate items? A piano, for example.

script.speaker: B
script.text: No piano. There's a large fish tank, though. It's about a metre and a half long.

script.speaker: A
script.text: A fish tank. We can move the tank itself, but it has to be empty. I'm afraid we can't transport the fish.

script.speaker: B
script.text: My brother's going to take the fish in his car, so that's fine.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. Now, would you like us to do the packing, or will you pack yourselves?

script.speaker: B
script.text: What's the difference in price?

script.speaker: A
script.text: If you pack, the move would cost six hundred and eighty pounds. With our packing service, where we come the day before and pack everything, it's nine hundred and fifty.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's quite a jump. I think we'll pack ourselves. Can you supply boxes?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes. We deliver thirty boxes free of charge a fortnight before the move. Extra ones are two pounds each.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Thirty should be enough. What about insurance?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Everything is covered up to a total of twenty thousand pounds. But there's one condition. We're only responsible for breakages in boxes we've packed ourselves. So wrap your glasses and plates carefully.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll remember that. Now, the date. We were hoping for Friday the twenty-eighth.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Fridays are our busiest day, and the twenty-eighth is already full. I could do Thursday the twenty-seventh, or the following Monday.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We have to be out by the weekend. It'll have to be the Thursday.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thursday the twenty-seventh, then. The crew will arrive at eight in the morning. You should be unloaded by about five.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And how do I confirm?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'll email the quotation now. To secure the date, we ask for a deposit of twenty per cent. The balance is paid on the day, when the job is finished.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Great. My email is under my surname, which is Trevelyan. T, R, E, V, E, L, Y, A, N.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thank you, Mister Trevelyan. One last question. Is there anything in a garage or a loft?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Only a bicycle and some garden chairs.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good afternoon, and thank you for coming to our teachers' evening at Fenwick Zoo. I'm Luis, and I run the education department. I'd like to explain what we can offer your pupils, and how to get the most out of a visit.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let me deal with a common question first. Some teachers ask whether a zoo is the right place to learn about animals at all. It's a fair question. Our answer is that the zoo today is a conservation organisation. Eleven of the species here are extinct in the wild or close to it, and money from every ticket supports projects in the countries those animals come from.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Last year, forty thousand schoolchildren visited us. Our research shows something interesting. Pupils who simply walked round remembered very little a month later. Those who took part in a workshop remembered a great deal. So I'd urge you to book one.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We offer four workshops. For the youngest children, there's Animal Coverings, where they handle real feathers, fur and snake skin. For ages seven to eleven, we have Rainforest Detectives, which takes place inside the tropical house. For secondary pupils, there's a session on animal behaviour, in which they observe the monkeys and record data. And finally there's Careers at the Zoo, for older students, with a vet and a keeper.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Each workshop lasts fifty minutes and costs forty pounds per class, on top of the entrance fee. They get booked up early, particularly in June and July. If you can come in the autumn term, you'll have far more choice, and the animals are often more active in cooler weather.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Some practical advice. Please make sure you have one adult for every six children under eight. Those adults come in free. Lunch can be eaten in the picnic barn, which is under cover, but you need to reserve a time when you book. And we'd ask you not to schedule the gift shop for the end of the day. Thirty children in the shop at half past two means a missed coach.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Before your trip, do come for a free planning visit. Any teacher who has made a booking can come in without charge, to walk the route and check the facilities.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And on our website you'll find worksheets for every age group. Please don't give out too many. A child who spends the whole day filling in a sheet hardly looks at the animals. One good question is worth twenty boxes to tick.

explanations.11: The zoo is a conservation organisation and ticket money supports projects abroad.
explanations.12: Those who simply walked round remembered very little a month later.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.
groups.text:
Monitoring volcanoes
Signs of a coming eruption
- earthquakes: the key factor is their {{11}}, not their strength
- swelling of the volcano, measured from satellites by {{12}}
- gas: a rise in sulphur dioxide; samples now often collected by {{13}}
- heat: cameras detect the ground {{14}} up

- had been quiet for 500 years
- scientists examined {{16}} from ancient eruptions

- most deaths were caused by {{17}} collapsing under wet {{18}}

- {{19}}, not science

script.speaker: A
script.text: So, the exhibition. You have the small gallery for two weeks in May. What's your theme?

script.speaker: B
script.text: We've called it The Working Hand. It's about how artists have shown manual labour, from the eighteen fifties to today.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We started with a much wider idea, work in general, but there was far too much material.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Narrowing it was wise. How many pieces?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Twenty-two. Mostly prints and photographs from the university collection, plus four paintings.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And how will you arrange them? By date?

script.speaker: C
script.text: That was my first thought. But Clara persuaded me that by date, you just get a history lesson.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We're grouping them by the kind of work instead. Farming, factories, the home. Then visitors can compare how a Victorian painter and a modern photographer treat the same subject.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I think that's the right choice. Now, the room has one very large wall, opposite the door. What goes there?

script.speaker: C
script.text: I wanted the biggest painting, the harvest scene.

script.speaker: B
script.text: But it's quite dark, and from the door it looks like a brown rectangle. We've decided to put the series of six photographs of hands there. They're striking even from a distance.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. First impressions matter. What about the labels?

script.speaker: B
script.text: We disagree a little. I'd like long labels, explaining the context.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And I think people don't read more than fifty words standing up.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Theo's right about that, I'm afraid. Keep the labels short, and put the longer texts in a printed guide that people can carry round.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's a good compromise. I'll write the guide.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Lighting. The prints are sensitive, remember.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The conservator told us the light on works on paper must be kept low. So that side of the room will be dim, and we'll explain why on a sign, or visitors will think a bulb has failed.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Sensible. Have you thought about who'll come?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Students, obviously. But we'd like to bring in people from the town. We've invited a retired steelworkers' group to the opening.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Excellent. Could they contribute something?

script.speaker: C
script.text: We're recording interviews with three of them, talking about one picture each. Visitors can listen through headphones.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That will make the show. Now, money. You have three hundred pounds.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Most of it is going on frames. The printing of the guide is being done free by the department.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And the opening?

script.speaker: C
script.text: The art society has offered to pay for drinks.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then you're in good shape. Send me the label texts by the end of April.

script.speaker: D
script.text: About eight hundred million people live within a hundred kilometres of an active volcano. We can't prevent eruptions, but we're increasingly able to see them coming. Today I'll describe the main techniques, and I'll finish with a case where they saved many lives.

script.speaker: D
script.text: The oldest and still the most important tool is the seismometer, which records vibrations in the ground. Before an eruption, molten rock, or magma, forces its way upward, cracking the rock around it, and this produces swarms of small earthquakes. What scientists watch for is not their strength but their depth. If the earthquakes become shallower day by day, the magma is rising.

script.speaker: D
script.text: The second sign is a change in shape. As magma collects beneath it, a volcano swells, rather like a balloon. The movement may be only a few centimetres, far too small to see, but it can be measured from satellites using radar.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Third, gas. Magma contains dissolved gases, and they escape as it nears the surface. A sudden rise in sulphur dioxide is one of the most reliable warnings. Collecting samples by hand at the crater is dangerous, so nowadays the job is often done by drones.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Fourth, temperature. Cameras that detect heat can show ground warming up weeks before anything is visible. Lakes inside craters are monitored too. If the water changes colour or becomes more acidic, something is happening below.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Now, none of these signs is enough alone. Many volcanoes swell and shake and then go quiet again. The skill lies in combining the evidence, and in knowing the history of the particular mountain.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Let me turn to my example. In nineteen ninety-one, Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines had been silent for five hundred years. In April, small explosions began. A team installed instruments within days. Crucially, they also studied the deposits left by ancient eruptions, and realised that when this volcano erupted, it erupted on an enormous scale.

script.speaker: D
script.text: As the earthquakes multiplied, the alert level was raised step by step, and some sixty thousand people were moved. The eruption, on the fifteenth of June, was the second largest of the century. Several hundred people died, mostly when roofs collapsed under wet ash. Without the evacuation, the figure would have been in the tens of thousands.

script.speaker: D
script.text: The hardest part of the job, though, isn't the science. It's communication. A warning that proves to be a false alarm costs money and destroys trust, so that people may refuse to leave the next time. Volcanologists must give clear advice while being honest about uncertainty, and that's a skill no instrument can provide.

explanations.1: Work in general produced far too much material.
explanations.2: Arranging by date would just give a history lesson.
explanations.3: The harvest painting looks dark from the door; the six photographs of hands are striking.
explanations.4: People do not read more than fifty words standing up; longer texts go in a guide.
explanations.5: The conservator said the light on works on paper must be kept low.

options.C: switch off the heat if it is safe to do so

script.speaker: A
script.text: Hello, Greenfields Festival office. Liam speaking.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hi. I saw online that you need volunteers this summer, and I'd love to help if there are still places.

script.speaker: A
script.text: There are a few. Have you volunteered at a festival before?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Never. I've been to plenty, though, as a paying customer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's fine. Most of our team are first-timers. Let me explain how it works. The festival runs from Thursday to Sunday, the last weekend in July. Volunteers work three shifts of six hours each, and the rest of the time is your own.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So eighteen hours altogether. And in return, I get in free?

script.speaker: A
script.text: You do. You also get a place in the staff campsite, which is quieter than the public one and has hot showers, and one meal for each shift you work.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hot showers. I'm convinced already. What kind of work is it?

script.speaker: A
script.text: There are four teams. Gates, where you check tickets. Recycling. Information. And stewarding at the stages. Do you have a preference?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Not the stages. I'd like to hear the music, not stand with my back to it. I speak Spanish and French, so maybe information?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Languages are really useful there. I'll put you down for information. Now, I should say that we ask for a deposit. It's the price of a ticket, a hundred and ninety pounds, and you get it all back once you've completed your shifts.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Why a deposit?

script.speaker: A
script.text: A few years ago, a number of people signed up, walked in free, and never turned up for work. The deposit put a stop to that.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fair enough. Is there any training?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes, on the Wednesday evening, the day before the gates open. It starts at six and lasts about two hours. It's compulsory, so you'll need to arrive on Wednesday.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's OK. I'll take the day off. What should I bring, apart from a tent?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Strong boots, waterproofs, and a torch. The fields are very dark at night. We give you a T-shirt and a staff wristband.

script.speaker: B
script.text: How old do you have to be? My younger brother might want to come.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Eighteen or over on the first day of the festival.

script.speaker: B
script.text: He's seventeen, so that's a no. How do I apply?

script.speaker: A
script.text: There's a form on the website, under the heading Crew. You'll need to upload a photograph for your pass. The closing date is the thirtieth of April.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll do it tonight. Who do I contact if I have questions?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Email me. My surname's Hadfield. H, A, D, F, I, E, L, D. And your name is?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Camila Torres.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thanks, Camila. One tip. Choose your shifts quickly once the list opens. The morning ones go first.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good evening. I'm Station Officer Kate Rowe, and I've been asked to talk for a few minutes about keeping your home safe from fire.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let me start with a question. Where do most house fires begin? People usually say the living room, because of candles and open fires. In fact, more than half start in the kitchen, and the most common cause is simply leaving a pan on the heat and walking away. So my first piece of advice costs nothing. If you're called away, to the door or the phone, turn the cooker off first.

script.speaker: C
script.text: If a pan of oil does catch fire, never throw water on it. The water turns to steam in an instant and throws burning oil across the room. Turn off the heat if you can reach the control safely, leave the kitchen, close the door, and call us.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The second great cause is electrical. I'm often asked about old wiring. It can be a problem, but far more fires are started by overloaded sockets, where four or five appliances run from a single point. Heaters and kettles should always have a wall socket to themselves.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A newer risk is the charger. Batteries for phones, and especially for electric bikes and scooters, can overheat. Please don't charge them overnight, and never in the hallway, because if they catch fire, they block your way out.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, smoke alarms. You need at least one on every floor. The best place is the ceiling of the hall or landing, not the kitchen, where steam and toast will set it off and tempt you to remove the battery. Test each alarm once a month by pressing the button, and replace the whole unit after ten years.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Every household should also have an escape plan. Decide on your route, and make sure everyone knows where the door keys are kept. At night, close the doors of the rooms downstairs. A closed door can hold back a fire for twenty minutes.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And if the worst happens, get out, stay out, and call the fire service. Don't go back for pets or possessions. More people are killed by smoke than by flames, and most of them are trying to rescue something.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, my service offers a free home safety visit. An officer will come to your house, check your alarms, and fit new ones if needed, at no charge. Priority goes to people over sixty-five and families with young children. You can book through the number on the leaflet.

explanations.11: People usually say the living room, but more than half start in the kitchen.
explanations.12: Never use water; turn off the heat if the control can be reached safely, then leave.
explanations.13: Old wiring can be a problem, but far more fires are started by overloaded sockets.
explanations.14: If they catch fire they block the way out.
explanations.15: Steam and toast set off an alarm in the kitchen.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Luke, we've got to hand in the campaign plan next week. Shall we go over where we are?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes. So the hospital wants more visitors to clean their hands when they enter a ward. At the moment, it's about one in five.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Which is low. I was surprised, because there's a gel dispenser at every door.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I went and watched for an hour on Tuesday. The dispensers are there, but they're on the wall behind the door. Once the door's open, you can't see them.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So it's partly a question of position, not attitude. Did you tell the ward manager?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I did, and she's agreed to move two of them onto stands in the middle of the corridor, as a trial.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Brilliant. That may do more than any poster. But we still need to design the poster. I've been reading about what works.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Go on.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The existing one says that infections kill five thousand patients a year. It's meant to frighten people.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And it doesn't work?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Fear makes people look away, apparently. A study in an American hospital compared two signs. One said hand hygiene protects you. The other said hand hygiene protects patients. The second increased the use of gel by a third. The first did nothing.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So we appeal to people's concern for others. Whoever they're visiting.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Exactly. Something like, the person you've come to see is counting on you.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I like that. What about a picture?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'd assumed a photo of hands under a tap. But there's research showing that a pair of eyes on a sign makes people behave better, because they feel they're being watched.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's a bit sinister for a hospital.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Maybe. A friendly face, then. A nurse, smiling.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Better. And where do the posters go? If we put them everywhere, nobody will notice them after a week.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Just one, at eye level, immediately above each dispenser. And we change the design every month, so it stays fresh.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good. Now, how do we know whether it's worked?

script.speaker: A
script.text: We could count how many people use the gel, like you did on Tuesday.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That takes hours, and people behave differently if they notice someone watching. A simpler way is to weigh the gel bags each week. If more gel's being used, more hands are being cleaned.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's clever, and nobody's being observed. Who does the weighing?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The cleaning staff change the bags anyway. I'll ask their supervisor.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then I'll draft three versions of the poster and test them on the students in our seminar.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'd test them on actual visitors, in the hospital cafe.

script.speaker: A
script.text: You're right. I'll go on Saturday.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We tend to imagine memory as a kind of recording, a film that we can play back. Almost everything psychologists have learned in the last century suggests that this picture is false. Memory isn't a recording. It's a reconstruction, built afresh each time we remember.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let me begin with the basic structure. Information first enters short-term memory, which is very limited. It holds about seven items, and for only about twenty seconds unless we keep repeating them. To last, a memory must be transferred to long-term storage, and that process depends heavily on sleep. Students who stay up all night before an exam are working against their own brains.

script.speaker: C
script.text: What decides whether something is transferred? Above all, meaning. In a classic experiment, chess masters were shown a board for five seconds and could reproduce it almost perfectly. But when the pieces were placed at random, in positions that could never occur in a game, the masters did no better than beginners. They weren't remembering pieces. They were remembering patterns that meant something to them.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Emotion matters too. Events that frighten or delight us are remembered vividly. But vivid doesn't mean accurate. The day after the space shuttle Challenger exploded, a psychologist asked his students to write down how they'd heard the news. Three years later, he asked them again. A quarter gave a completely different account, and they were astonished when they were shown their own handwriting.

script.speaker: C
script.text: This brings me to the work of Elizabeth Loftus. She showed people a film of a car accident, and then asked how fast the cars were going when they hit each other. With other viewers, she changed one word, and asked how fast they were going when they smashed into each other. The second group gave higher speeds, and a week later, many of them remembered seeing broken glass, although there was none in the film.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The implications for courts of law are serious. Juries find a confident witness very convincing. Yet research shows that confidence and accuracy are only weakly related.

script.speaker: C
script.text: So is forgetting simply a failure? Not at all. A brain that kept everything would be overwhelmed by detail. Forgetting lets us keep the general lesson and discard the rest.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, some practical advice, since you all have exams. Rereading your notes feels productive, but it's one of the least effective methods. Far better is to close the book and test yourself. And spread your study over several days. An hour on each of three days beats three hours in one evening.

explanations.2: Two will be moved onto stands in the middle of the corridor as a trial.
explanations.3: The sign saying hand hygiene protects patients increased gel use by a third.
explanations.4: Eyes seemed too sinister for a hospital.
explanations.5: One poster above each dispenser, with a new design every month.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Thank you. Yes, the exhibition is called Made in Dunmore, and it opens on Saturday. It tells the story of the things this town used to make, and of the people who made them.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The idea came about by chance. Two years ago, a building firm was clearing out the old Crown Works before turning it into flats, and they found a room that had been locked since the factory closed in nineteen seventy-eight. Inside were order books, tools, and hundreds of photographs of the staff. The firm rang us, and we realised we had the makings of a show.

script.speaker: C
script.text: For anyone who doesn't know, Dunmore was once famous for three things. Clocks, which were exported all over the world. Bicycles. And, less well known, buttons, which were made from shells brought from the Pacific.

script.speaker: C
script.text: I think what will surprise visitors most is the scale. In nineteen twenty, one in three adults in the town worked in one of those three trades. Whole streets were built by the factory owners for their workers, and many of those houses are still lived in.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We didn't want simply to fill cases with objects. So in the first room, you can sit at a real workbench and try to put together the mechanism of a clock, with a retired clockmaker to guide you. It's harder than it looks.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The second room is devoted to the bicycle. The centrepiece is a racing machine on which a local woman, Edith Shaw, broke the national record over a hundred miles in nineteen thirty-six. Her granddaughter has lent us her medals.

script.speaker: C
script.text: In the third room, we've recreated part of the button workshop. We've added the sound, from recordings, because former workers all told us the same thing, that what they remembered most was the noise.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Throughout the exhibition, you'll hear the voices of people who worked in the factories. We recorded thirty interviews, and the oldest speaker is a hundred and one.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Some practical details. The exhibition runs until the end of September. The museum is free, as always, but we're asking for a contribution of four pounds for this show, to cover the cost of putting it on. Children don't pay.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We're open every day except Monday, from ten until five, and on Thursdays we stay open until eight.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And one request. If you have anything at home that was made in Dunmore, a clock, a bicycle badge, a card of buttons, please bring it in on the first Sunday of the month. We'll photograph it and add it to our online collection.

explanations.11: Builders found a locked room full of order books, tools and photographs.
explanations.12: Shells brought from the Pacific.
explanations.13: In 1920, one in three adults worked in the three trades.
explanations.14: They sit at a workbench and put together a clock mechanism with a clockmaker's help.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Kofi, have you finished reading the case study on Brightline?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Last night. The camera company. It's a sad story, really. They invented the product that destroyed them.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The digital camera. Their own engineer built one in the seventies, and the management told him to keep quiet about it.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Because all their profit came from film. Selling the cameras was never the point. They made their money on the rolls of film and on developing the pictures.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Right. So the first question asks why the company failed. The easy answer is that they didn't see digital coming.

script.speaker: B
script.text: But that's not true, is it? They saw it earlier than anyone. They even commissioned a report in nineteen eighty-one that predicted, quite accurately, how long film had left.

script.speaker: A
script.text: About ten years before digital became a real threat. So they had the knowledge and the time.

script.speaker: B
script.text: What they didn't have was the will. Every digital camera sold would mean one less customer for film. They'd have been competing with themselves.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I think that's our main argument. It wasn't a failure of technology. It was a failure to give up a profitable business before someone else took it away.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Agreed. Now the second question. Could they have survived?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The case mentions a Japanese rival that was in the same position.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes, and that company is still thriving. It used its knowledge of chemicals to move into cosmetics and medical products.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So the rival asked, what are we good at, and not, what do we sell.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's a nice way to put it. Let's use that line.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What about the managers? The report seems to blame the chief executive.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I think that's unfair. Four chief executives came and went, and nothing changed. The problem was in the culture of the whole firm. Middle managers who'd spent thirty years in film had no reason to support a change.

script.speaker: A
script.text: OK. And for the last section, we need a lesson for companies today.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The obvious one is car makers and electric vehicles.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Everyone will choose that. What about newspapers? They knew the internet was coming, and most held on to print advertising far too long.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's a closer match, actually. Advertising was their film.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then newspapers it is. How shall we split the presentation?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll take the history and the reasons for failure. You do the rival and the lesson.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Fine. Ten slides at most. Professor Adler takes marks off for more.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And no reading from notes. She hates that.

script.speaker: A
script.text: We'd better rehearse, then. Thursday evening?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Thursday at six, in the seminar room.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We walk on it, we build on it, and we rarely give it a thought. Yet soil is one of the most complex materials on the planet, and almost all of our food depends on it. This morning I'd like to introduce what soil is and why scientists are worried about it.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Soil has four ingredients. There are particles of rock, broken down over thousands of years. There's organic matter, which is the remains of dead plants and animals. And there's air and water, held in the spaces between. A healthy soil is roughly half solid and half space.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The rock particles come in three sizes. The largest is sand, the smallest is clay, and in between is silt. The proportions decide how a soil behaves. A sandy soil drains quickly and warms up early in spring, but it holds few nutrients. Clay is rich, but heavy and slow to drain. The ideal for most crops is a mixture that gardeners call loam.

script.speaker: C
script.text: What really distinguishes soil from crushed rock, though, is life. A teaspoon of healthy soil contains more living organisms than there are people on earth. The majority are bacteria and fungi. Fungi form fine threads that connect to the roots of plants. The plant supplies the fungus with sugar, and in return the fungus brings water and minerals from much further away than the roots could reach.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Then there are the larger creatures, and the earthworm is the most important. Its tunnels let air and water into the ground. Charles Darwin spent forty years studying earthworms. In his last book, he suggested that no other animal had played so important a part in the history of the world.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Soil forms extremely slowly. It can take five hundred years to produce two centimetres. And that's why erosion is so serious. When land is ploughed and left bare, wind and rain can remove in one season what took centuries to form. The classic example is the Dust Bowl of the nineteen thirties in the United States, when drought struck land that had been ploughed too deeply, and storms carried the soil as far as the Atlantic.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Farmers have responded. Many now leave the remains of the previous crop on the surface, and sow the next one without ploughing. Others plant what's called a cover crop in the winter, purely to protect the ground.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, soil matters for the climate. It holds about three times as much carbon as the atmosphere. Manage it badly and that carbon escapes. Manage it well and soil could absorb a significant share of our emissions.

explanations.1: The money came from rolls of film and from developing pictures.
explanations.2: It saw digital earlier than anyone, and a 1981 report predicted how long film had left.
explanations.3: Each digital camera sold would mean one less customer for film.
explanations.4: It used its knowledge of chemicals to move into cosmetics and medical products.
explanations.5: Four chief executives came and went and nothing changed.

script.text: Oh, hello. My boiler's stopped working, and I've got no heating or hot water. Could somebody come and look at it?

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: A
script.text: No problem. I'll take a few details. What's your name, please?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Margaret Yates. Y, A, T, E, S.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And the address?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fourteen Orchard Close, in Benfield.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Benfield. That's fine, it's within our area. Now, can you tell me what make the boiler is?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thank you. And roughly how old is it?

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: A
script.text: Nine years. Not ancient, then. What exactly is it doing? Is there a light flashing, or a message on the display?

script.speaker: B
script.text: There's a red light flashing, and the display shows the letter F and the number twenty-eight.

script.speaker: A
script.text: F twenty-eight. That's helpful. On that model it usually means the boiler has tried to light and failed. Have you checked the pressure? There's a small dial with a needle underneath.

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's normal, so it isn't the pressure. Is your gas cooker working?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes, I made tea on it this morning.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then the gas supply is fine. It's most likely a part inside the boiler. I'll send an engineer. The call-out charge is sixty-five pounds, which covers the first hour. Any parts are extra, and he'll give you a price before he fits anything.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Sixty-five. All right. How soon can he come? It's freezing in here.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Is there anyone elderly or very young in the house? We give priority in those cases.

script.speaker: B
script.text: My mother lives with us. She's eighty-four.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then I'll mark it as urgent. I can get someone to you this afternoon, between two and four.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Oh, that's wonderful. I'd expected to wait until tomorrow.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The engineer's name is Derek. He'll phone when he's on his way. What's the best number?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll give you my mobile. I'll be in the garden, and I won't hear the house phone.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Fine. I have the mobile number on my screen from this call. Is there somewhere he can park?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Not in the close, it's too narrow for a van. He should use the lay-by on the main road and walk round. It's less than a minute.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'll tell him. One more thing. Could you clear the cupboard around the boiler before he arrives? It saves time, and time is what you're paying for.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll do it now. It's full of towels.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good morning, everyone. Welcome to Northgate Distribution. I'm Denise, the day-shift supervisor. Today is mostly training, and you'll start real work tomorrow.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let me tell you about the building. It covers the area of six football pitches. Around forty thousand parcels pass through every day, and in the weeks before New Year that figure more than doubles. You'll walk a long way on each shift, about ten kilometres on average, so I hope you've brought comfortable footwear.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The first rule here is safety. More accidents in warehouses are caused by forklift trucks than by anything else. The floor is painted with green walkways. Pedestrians stay on the green, and the trucks stay off it. If you have to cross a truck lane, make eye contact with the driver first. Don't assume you've been seen.

script.speaker: C
script.text: You've each been given a yellow jacket and a pair of safety boots. Both must be worn everywhere apart from the canteen and the offices. Gloves are in the boxes by each work station, and you can take a fresh pair whenever you need one.

script.speaker: C
script.text: When you lift, bend your knees and keep your back straight. Anything marked with a red label weighs more than twenty kilos, and must be lifted by two people or with a trolley. Nobody will think you're weak for asking for help. They'll think you're sensible.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, shifts. The day shift runs from six in the morning until two in the afternoon. You get a thirty-minute meal break, which is unpaid, and two paid breaks of ten minutes. Please clock in with your card as you arrive. If you forget, tell me the same day, because I can't correct the record after the week has closed, and you could lose pay.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The canteen serves hot food until one thirty, and staff get it at half price. There are lockers for your belongings. Bring your own padlock. And phones stay in the lockers. That isn't because we don't trust you. A person looking at a screen isn't looking out for trucks.

script.speaker: C
script.text: For your first two weeks, you'll each work beside a trained colleague, whom we call a buddy. Ask them anything. After a fortnight, I'll sit down with each of you to review how things are going.

script.speaker: C
script.text: If you're ill, ring the absence line at least one hour before your shift starts. Don't send a message to a friend and ask them to tell me. It has to come from you.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Right. Let's begin with a tour.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Daniel, have you finished the novel? The seminar's on Monday.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I finished it on the train. I have to admit I struggled with the first hundred pages. Nothing seemed to happen.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I had the opposite problem. I loved the slow opening, all those descriptions of the village, and then I felt the ending was rushed.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Interesting. Well, our topic isn't the plot anyway. It's the translation. Professor Okafor wants us to compare the two English versions.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes, the one from nineteen fifty-four and the new one from last year. I've got them side by side. The differences are remarkable.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I noticed the old one is shorter.

script.speaker: A
script.text: By about forty pages. The first translator cut passages he thought English readers would find dull, mostly the long conversations about politics.

script.speaker: B
script.text: He just removed them? Could he do that?

script.speaker: A
script.text: It wasn't unusual then. The publisher wanted a book that would sell. The new translator has put everything back.

script.speaker: B
script.text: What about the style? The old version reads very smoothly to me. Almost like an English novel.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's exactly the point. He made it sound English. He even changed the food. Where the original has a dish of fermented cabbage, he wrote stew.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And the new one?

script.speaker: A
script.text: She keeps the original word and trusts the reader to work it out. There are no footnotes, and no glossary either.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I found that hard going at first. But after a while, the strangeness became part of the pleasure. You feel you're somewhere else.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So which do we argue is better?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I don't think we should say better. They had different aims. One brings the book to the reader. The other takes the reader to the book.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I like that. Can we use it as our title?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Sure. Now, we need examples. Three short passages, with both versions on the screen.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'd choose the opening paragraph, the wedding scene, and the grandmother's letter. In the letter, she writes in dialect, and the two translators handle it completely differently.

script.speaker: B
script.text: How?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The old one puts it into standard English. The new one invents a kind of rural English, with odd spelling.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That will get a discussion going. Some people will hate it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. Professor Okafor says the best seminars are arguments.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Shall we give the group a handout with the three passages?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes, and send it round the day before, so that people can read them in advance.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll make the handout. You do the slides?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Deal. Let's keep our talking to fifteen minutes and leave the rest for questions.

script.speaker: C
script.text: If you want to know what the earth's climate was like before anyone kept records, one of the best places to look is deep inside the ice of Antarctica. Today I'll explain how ice cores are collected and what we've learned from them.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The principle is simple. Snow falls on the ice sheet every year and never melts. It is buried and pressed down by later layers, and over centuries the snow is squeezed into solid ice. So the deeper you go, the older the ice. In the centre of Antarctica, the sheet is more than three kilometres thick.

script.speaker: C
script.text: To sample it, scientists use a hollow drill, which brings up cylinders of ice about ten centimetres across. The work can only be done in summer, and even then the temperature may be minus thirty. Drilling to the bottom takes several seasons.

script.speaker: C
script.text: What makes the ice so valuable is that it contains tiny bubbles. As the snow is compressed, air is trapped inside it. Those bubbles are samples of the atmosphere from the time the snow fell. By crushing the ice in a vacuum and analysing the air released, we can measure directly how much carbon dioxide the atmosphere held hundreds of thousands of years ago.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The ice itself tells us about temperature. Water molecules come in slightly lighter and heavier forms, and the proportion in snow depends on how cold it was when the snow formed. So one core gives two records, temperature and carbon dioxide, side by side.

script.speaker: C
script.text: There are other clues. Layers of ash mark volcanic eruptions, and since many eruptions have known dates, they help us to check the age of the ice. Dust shows how windy and dry the world was. During ice ages, the ice contains far more dust.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The longest continuous record so far comes from a site called Dome C, and it reaches back eight hundred thousand years. It shows eight ice ages, each lasting about a hundred thousand years, separated by shorter warm periods.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And here's the central finding. Through all those cycles, temperature and carbon dioxide rose and fell together. In that entire record, carbon dioxide never rose above three hundred parts per million. Today it's over four hundred and twenty, and the speed of the increase is at least a hundred times faster than anything in the ice.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A new project is now searching for ice one and a half million years old. The reason is a puzzle. Before about a million years ago, ice ages came every forty thousand years, not every hundred thousand, and nobody knows why the rhythm changed.

explanations.1: He struggled with the first hundred pages; Elise felt the ending was rushed.
explanations.2: He cut passages he thought English readers would find dull.
explanations.3: She keeps the original word; there are no footnotes or glossary.
explanations.4: They had different aims, so the students will not say one is better.
explanations.5: One uses standard English; the other invents a rural English.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Two adults, Thursday at ten. That's forty-eight pounds. Can I take a name?

script.speaker: B
script.text: It's Brennan. B, R, E, double N, A, N.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thank you. Now, the boat leaves from pier three, which is the one beside the lifeboat station, not the main pier. Please be there fifteen minutes early.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Pier three. What should we bring?

script.speaker: A
script.text: A warm jacket, even if it's sunny on land. It's always colder on the water. And binoculars, if you have them.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We do. Is there shelter on board if it rains?

script.speaker: A
script.text: There's a small covered cabin, but it only seats twelve, so I wouldn't rely on it.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And if the weather's really bad?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The skipper decides at eight in the morning. If he cancels, you can have your money back or move to another day. We'd text you. Could I take a mobile number?

script.speaker: C
script.text: Thanks, Mike. Yes, today I'm talking about food waste. The average household in this country throws away around seventy kilos of edible food a year. That's roughly sixty pounds a month for a family of four, straight into the bin.

script.speaker: C
script.text: When I ask people what they waste most, they say meat or dairy. But the surveys are clear. The food we throw away in the largest quantity is bread, followed by potatoes and then salad.

script.speaker: C
script.text: So what can you do? My first tip is the most boring and the most effective. Before you go shopping, look in the fridge and write a list. People who shop with a list waste about a quarter less than people who don't.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Second, understand the dates on the packet. A use-by date is about safety. You shouldn't eat the food after it. A best-before date is only about quality. Biscuits a month past their best-before date may be a little soft, but they won't hurt you. Half of us, according to one study, treat the two as the same, and throw away perfectly good food.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Third, check the temperature of your fridge. It should be below five degrees. Most domestic fridges are set too warm, at around seven, and at that temperature milk lasts two days less.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Where you keep things matters as well. Tomatoes and bananas don't belong in the fridge. The cold spoils the flavour. Potatoes should be stored somewhere dark, and kept apart from onions, because each makes the other go off faster.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Fourth, love your freezer. Nearly everything can be frozen. Bread, of course. Slice it first, and you can toast it straight from frozen. But also grated cheese, milk, and even eggs, as long as you crack them out of their shells and beat them first.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And fifth, use what's left over. My rule is that Thursday is use-it-up night in our house. Whatever vegetables remain go into a soup or an omelette. My children complain, and then they eat it.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A word about technology. There are now apps that let cafes and supermarkets sell unsold food cheaply at the end of the day. You pay about a third of the normal price and collect a bag in the evening. You don't know what's in it until you open it, which is half the fun.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, whatever can't be eaten, peelings and tea bags and so on, should go in a compost bin, not the general rubbish. Buried in landfill, food rots and produces methane, which is a far more powerful greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.

explanations.11: People guess meat or dairy, but it is bread, then potatoes and salad.
explanations.12: People who shop with a list waste about a quarter less.
explanations.13: Use-by is about safety; best-before is only about quality.
explanations.14: They should be below five degrees but are set at around seven.
explanations.15: You do not know what is in the bag until you open it.

title: Vertical farming project and the economics of happiness

parts.context: You will hear two agriculture students, Mei and Jonas, talking to their tutor about a project on vertical farming.

options.C: The crops are harvested very quickly.

How will the students obtain detailed figures on costs?

options.A: They will eventually replace farming in fields.
options.B: They are unlikely to survive as businesses.
options.C: They are a useful addition to traditional farming.

groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.
