parts.context: You will hear part of a lecture about what economists have learned about happiness.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.
groups.text:
The economics of happiness
The Easterlin paradox
- within a country, richer people are happier
- over time, a nation's average {{11}} hardly changes as it grows richer
Explanations
- {{12}}: people judge their income against others'
- {{13}}: people get used to improvements, e.g. a larger {{14}}
- lottery {{15}} return to their earlier level
Things people do not get used to
- a long {{16}} to work; noise; time with {{17}}
What predicts happiness
- a long study found the key factor was a person's {{18}}
- unemployment is harmful because work gives {{19}} and status
Criticism
- answers to surveys may be affected even by the {{20}}

script.speaker: A
script.text: So, you've chosen vertical farming for your project. Tell me why.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We visited one last month, in an old warehouse near the docks. Salad leaves growing on shelves, twelve layers high, under pink lights. It was extraordinary.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And there's a lot of excitement about it in the press. We'd like to find out whether it deserves it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: A healthy attitude. What are the claimed advantages?

script.speaker: C
script.text: Water, mainly. The farm we saw uses ninety-five per cent less water than a field, because whatever the plants don't take up is collected and used again.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And there are no pesticides, because the building is sealed and insects can't get in.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Those are real benefits. What about the yield?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Per square metre of ground, it's enormous. They harvest every three weeks, all year round, whatever the weather.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So why isn't all our food grown this way?

script.speaker: C
script.text: Energy. In a field, the sunlight is free. Indoors, every bit of light has to be paid for. The manager told us electricity is his largest cost, bigger than wages.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Did he give you figures?

script.speaker: C
script.text: He wouldn't. He said they were confidential.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's a difficulty. You can't evaluate a business without the costs.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We've found two published studies with detailed figures, one from the Netherlands and one from Japan. We'll use those.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. And what crops can be grown?

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's the other limit. Leafy things, salad and herbs, do well, because nearly the whole plant is sold. Wheat or rice would never pay. Most of the plant is stalk, and you'd be buying light to grow something you throw away.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So vertical farms won't feed the world.

script.speaker: C
script.text: No. That's going to be our conclusion. They're useful for fresh salad in cities, especially in places with little water or a harsh climate. But they add to field farming. They don't replace it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I think that's a defensible position. Now, how will you structure the report?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Advantages, then limits, then a case study of the farm we visited.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'd put the case study first. Start with something concrete, and the reader will care about the analysis that follows.

script.speaker: C
script.text: That makes sense. We've got good photographs.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Use them. And I'd like to see a simple calculation. Take one tray of lettuce and work out the energy used to grow it, in a form the reader can picture.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Such as the number of hours a kettle would run?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Exactly that kind of thing. When can you send me a draft?

script.speaker: C
script.text: In two weeks?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Fine. And do mention who paid for the studies you rely on. Some research in this field is funded by the companies that make the lights.

script.speaker: D
script.text: For most of its history, economics assumed that people want more income, and that more income makes them better off. That seems obvious. But about fifty years ago, an economist named Richard Easterlin looked at the data and found something odd.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Within any one country, at any one time, richer people do report being happier than poorer people. No surprise there. But when Easterlin followed countries over decades, he found that as a nation grew richer, the average level of happiness hardly moved. The United States tripled its income per head after the war, and Americans were no more satisfied than before. This became known as the Easterlin paradox.

script.speaker: D
script.text: How can both things be true? There are two main explanations. The first is comparison. We judge our income not in absolute terms but against the people around us. In one survey, students were asked to choose between two worlds. In the first, they earn fifty thousand dollars and others earn twenty-five. In the second, they earn a hundred thousand, and others earn two hundred. A majority preferred the first.

script.speaker: D
script.text: The second explanation is adaptation. We get used to things. A larger house is a delight for about a year, and then it's simply the house. Studies of lottery winners find that after the first excitement, most return to roughly their earlier level of happiness.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Interestingly, there are things we don't adapt to. One is a long journey to work. People consistently underestimate how much it will cost them in well-being. Another is noise. And another, on the positive side, is time with friends, which goes on giving pleasure however often it's repeated.

script.speaker: D
script.text: So what does predict happiness, if not ever more income? The largest long-term study, which has followed a group of men from Harvard since nineteen thirty-eight, gives a clear answer. The best predictor of a happy and healthy old age was not wealth, or fame, or even cholesterol. It was the quality of a person's relationships.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Unemployment, by contrast, is devastating, and far more so than the loss of income alone would explain. People value work for the purpose and status it provides.

script.speaker: D
script.text: What follows for policy? Some governments now measure well-being directly, alongside national income. And some economists argue that spending on mental health would raise national happiness more cheaply than almost anything else.

script.speaker: D
script.text: A final caution. Critics point out that asking people to rate their lives from one to ten is a crude measure, and that the answers are influenced by small things, even by the weather on the day of the survey.

explanations.1: There is a lot of excitement in the press and they want to find out whether it is deserved.
explanations.2: The building is sealed.
explanations.3: Every bit of light has to be paid for; electricity costs more than wages.
explanations.4: The manager said the figures were confidential; they found two published studies.
explanations.5: They suit fresh salad in cities but add to field farming and do not replace it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Hello, Peter Lowe speaking.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good evening. I'm phoning about the Millbrook Community Choir. A friend said you're the person to ask about joining.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I am. I'm the membership secretary. Do you sing already?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I sang at school, but that was thirty years ago. I can't read music, I'm afraid.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That doesn't matter at all. About half of us can't. Our conductor teaches every part by ear, and we send out recordings so that people can practise at home.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's a relief. Do I have to do an audition?

script.speaker: A
script.text: No audition. The only thing the conductor does is listen to you for a minute to decide which section you belong in. Do you know whether you're a soprano or an alto?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I've got quite a low voice. Alto, I'd guess.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good, we're short of altos. We've got too many sopranos, to be honest, and hardly any tenors.

script.speaker: B
script.text: When do you rehearse?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Every Monday evening during school terms, from seven fifteen until nine fifteen, with a break for tea in the middle.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And where?

script.speaker: A
script.text: At Saint Luke's School, in the main hall. We were at the Methodist chapel for years, but the heating failed last winter, and we never went back.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Saint Luke's. That's close to me. How much does it cost?

script.speaker: A
script.text: It's fifty-five pounds a term, and there are three terms a year. The first rehearsal is free, so you can see whether you like us.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's reasonable. What kind of music do you sing?

script.speaker: A
script.text: A mixture. Folk songs, some gospel, songs from musicals. This term we're preparing for a concert with a film theme.

script.speaker: B
script.text: A concert? I'm not sure I'm ready for that.

script.speaker: A
script.text: It isn't until the sixth of December, so you'd have ten weeks. And nobody has to sing alone. We perform as a group.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Where's the concert?

script.speaker: A
script.text: In the town hall. It raises money for the local hospice. Last year we collected over two thousand pounds.

script.speaker: B
script.text: How lovely. Do I need to wear anything special?

script.speaker: A
script.text: For concerts, black, with a scarf in a bright colour, which we lend you. For rehearsals, wear whatever you like.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And should I bring anything on Monday?

script.speaker: A
script.text: A bottle of water, and a folder for your song sheets. We hand out the words. And a pencil, to mark where to breathe.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I can manage that. How many are in the choir?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Sixty-two at the last count. Don't let that put you off. New people always say it's easier to hide in a big choir.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That suits me. Shall I just turn up?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Please do. Come ten minutes early and ask for me. And your name is?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fiona Castle.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good morning. Yes, after four years of building work, I'm pleased to say that the new tram line between the city centre and Eastfield opens to passengers on Monday.

script.speaker: C
script.text: I know the construction has tested everybody's patience, and I'd like to thank people for putting up with it. The delay of eight months wasn't caused by the weather, or by money, as some reports said. When we dug up Bridge Street, we found gas pipes that weren't on any map, and they had to be moved before the track could be laid.

script.speaker: C
script.text: So what are you getting? The line is nine kilometres long, with fourteen stops. Trams will run every eight minutes during the day and every fifteen in the evening. The whole journey takes twenty-two minutes. By bus, at busy times, the same trip can take fifty.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Fares are the same as on the buses. A single journey costs two pounds, and a day ticket covering both trams and buses is five pounds. You can't pay the driver. Buy a ticket from the machine at the stop, or simply touch your bank card on the reader as you board.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Something I'd like to stress is access. The floor of every tram is level with the platform, so wheelchairs and pushchairs can roll straight on. Each tram also has space for four bicycles, though not between seven and nine in the morning, when it's simply too crowded.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let me mention a few of the stops. At Eastfield, the end of the line, there's a new car park with six hundred spaces. Parking is free if you show a tram ticket, so we hope drivers from the villages will leave their cars there.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The stop at the university has the longest platform on the line, because we expect the largest crowds there.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The hospital stop is right at the main entrance, and the shelter there is heated in winter, with patients in mind.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Market Square is the stop for the shops, and it's the one place where you can change to every bus route in the city.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And at the stadium, extra trams will run on match days, starting two hours before kick-off.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A word on safety. Trams are quiet, much quieter than buses, and they can't swerve. Please look both ways when you cross the tracks, and take your headphones off. And cyclists, do cross the rails at a right angle, or your wheel may slip into the groove.

script.speaker: C
script.text: To celebrate, travel on the tram is free all day this Saturday, before the full service begins on Monday. Come and try it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Callum, have you looked at our results from Tuesday's lab? Something's gone wrong.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I plotted them last night. The concentration we calculated for the acid is nearly twenty per cent higher than it should be.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Twenty per cent. That's far too much to be a rounding error. Did we make a mistake in the arithmetic?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I checked it twice, and I asked Jen to check it as well. The calculation's right. The problem has to be in what we did at the bench.

script.speaker: A
script.text: OK, let's go through it. We weighed out the solid, dissolved it, and made it up to two hundred and fifty millilitres in the flask.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Could the balance have been wrong?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I doubt it. The technician calibrates the balances every morning. And the other groups used the same one and got sensible answers.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Then the flask. Did we fill it exactly to the line?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I did that part, and I was careful. I got my eye level with the mark.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So it's the titration itself. We ran it three times, and the three readings agreed closely with each other.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Which means that whatever we did wrong, we did it the same way every time.

script.speaker: B
script.text: A consistent error. What about the burette? Did we rinse it properly?

script.speaker: A
script.text: We rinsed it with distilled water.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Only water? Not with the solution we were about to put in it?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Just water. Oh. So there'd have been drops of water left inside, and they'd have diluted the first part of the solution.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That would make us use more of it to reach the end point. And that pushes the calculated concentration up.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Would it be enough to explain twenty per cent?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Not twenty. A few per cent, maybe. There must be something else as well.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The indicator. Which one did we use?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The bottle on our bench. I assumed it was the one in the instructions.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The instructions said methyl orange. I'm fairly sure the bottle was the pink one.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Then we used the wrong indicator, and it changes colour at a different point. That's the main cause.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So, two errors. One small, one large. What do we do? Repeat the whole thing?

script.speaker: B
script.text: There's no lab slot until after the deadline. I think we report what happened honestly.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Will we lose marks?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Doctor Fenn said in the first lecture that she gives more credit for a wrong result properly explained than for a right one with no discussion.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then let's explain it properly. We could estimate how big each error is.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes. And recommend labelling the indicator bottles more clearly.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'll write the error analysis if you redo the graphs.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fine. Let's swap drafts on Friday.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Smallpox killed perhaps three hundred million people in the twentieth century alone, and today it no longer exists outside two laboratories. That is the greatest achievement in the history of medicine, and this afternoon I'd like to trace how it began.

script.speaker: C
script.text: People had noticed long ago that anyone who survived smallpox never caught it again. From that observation came a practice known as inoculation. Material from the sore of a patient with a mild case was scratched into the skin of a healthy person. The person usually developed a mild illness and was protected for life. The method was used in China and India, and in parts of Africa, centuries before it reached Europe.

script.speaker: C
script.text: It arrived in England in seventeen twenty-one, thanks to Lady Mary Wortley Montagu. She was the wife of the British ambassador to Turkey, she had been scarred by smallpox herself, and she'd seen the procedure carried out in Constantinople. She had her own children inoculated, and persuaded the royal family to do the same.

script.speaker: C
script.text: But inoculation was risky. Roughly one person in fifty died of it, and those who'd been treated could pass on the real disease to others.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The safer alternative came from the countryside. It was common knowledge among farmers that milkmaids rarely caught smallpox. They did catch cowpox, a mild disease of cattle that produced a few sores on the hands.

script.speaker: C
script.text: In seventeen ninety-six, a country doctor named Edward Jenner put this to the test. He took material from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid and scratched it into the arm of an eight-year-old boy, the son of his gardener. Six weeks later, he deliberately tried to infect the boy with smallpox. Nothing happened. By modern standards, the experiment was deeply unethical, but it worked.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Jenner called his method vaccination, from the Latin word for cow. It spread with astonishing speed. Within five years, it was in use from Russia to the United States.

script.speaker: C
script.text: There was opposition too. Cartoons showed patients growing horns. And when the British government made vaccination compulsory for babies in eighteen fifty-three, there were riots, and an organised movement against it.

script.speaker: C
script.text: One difficulty was transport. The material didn't keep, and there was no refrigeration. So when Spain sent vaccine to its colonies in eighteen hundred and three, it did so in the arms of twenty-two orphan boys. Two were vaccinated before sailing, and the infection was passed from one pair to the next throughout the voyage.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The final chapter came in nineteen eighty, when the World Health Organization declared that smallpox had been wiped out.

explanations.1: Callum checked it twice and another student checked it too.
explanations.2: It is calibrated daily and other groups got sensible answers.
explanations.3: Whatever they did wrong, they did it the same way every time.
explanations.4: The water explains only a few per cent; the wrong indicator is the main cause.
explanations.5: There is no lab slot until after the deadline.

script.text: For that number, I'd suggest our private room upstairs, the Granary. It seats up to thirty.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Is there a charge for the room?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Not if you're all having dinner. We only charge when the room is hired for a meeting. Which evening were you thinking of?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Friday the seventh of March. She finishes work that day.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Let me look. Friday the seventh. I'm afraid the Granary is taken that night by a wedding party. I could offer you the Thursday, the sixth.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hmm. Thursday would mean people coming to work the next morning. But it can't be helped. Thursday it is.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thursday the sixth. What time?

script.speaker: B
script.text: We finish at half past five, so seven o'clock.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Seven is fine. Now, for groups over twelve, we ask you to choose from a set menu, to help the kitchen. There's a two-course menu at twenty-eight pounds and a three-course menu at thirty-four pounds.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Three courses, I think. It's a celebration.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Each guest chooses a starter, a main course and a dessert, and we need everyone's choices a week in advance.

script.speaker: B
script.text: A week ahead. I can collect those. A few of the team are vegetarian.

script.speaker: A
script.text: There's a vegetarian option for every course. Is anybody allergic to anything?

script.speaker: B
script.text: One person can't eat fish. I'll check with the others.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Please do, and write it beside their name. Would you like wine included, or will people buy their own drinks?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The company's paying for the meal but not for alcohol. So people will pay for their own.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's simple enough. We'll run a separate bill for the bar.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Could we bring a cake? Someone's wife is baking one.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Of course. We'll keep it in the kitchen and bring it out with candles, if you'd like. There's no charge.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Wonderful. And we'd like to show some photographs. Is there a screen in the room?

script.speaker: A
script.text: There's a projector and a screen. Just bring a laptop. I'd come a quarter of an hour early to set it up.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I will. Is a deposit needed?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes, ten pounds per person, so that would be two hundred and sixty pounds. The rest is paid on the night.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll get our accounts department to transfer it. Who should the invoice go to?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Send me the company name by email. And whose name shall I put on the booking?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Mine. Gordon Ashby. A, S, H, B, Y.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Wetherby Botanical Garden. I'm Simon. I'll give you a short introduction here at the gate, and then you can wander wherever you like.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The garden was founded in eighteen forty-two, and its original purpose was strictly practical. It belonged to the medical school, and it was where students learned to recognise the plants used in medicines. Pleasure had nothing to do with it. The public weren't admitted until fifty years later.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Today we grow about eight thousand species. Our most important work is one that visitors never see. Under the building behind me is a seed bank, where seeds of rare plants are dried and frozen. Some will stay alive for two hundred years.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let me suggest a route. Turn left from here and you come to the rock garden, which is at its best in spring. I'm afraid that in this hot weather, there's not much in flower there now.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Beyond it is the glasshouse, the oldest building in the garden. It contains our tropical collection, including a giant water lily with leaves strong enough to hold the weight of a small child. Please don't try it.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Behind the glasshouse is the herb garden. Unlike the rest of the garden, where we ask you not to touch, here you're invited to rub the leaves and smell them. It was designed with blind and partially sighted visitors in mind, and the labels are in Braille.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Carry on, and you reach the lake. The path round it is being relaid this month, so it's closed. You can still enjoy the view from the wooden bridge.

script.speaker: C
script.text: On the far side of the lake is the woodland, which is the best place to be on a day like today, since it's shaded and several degrees cooler than the lawns.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, the path brings you back past the vegetable garden. Everything grown there is used in our cafe, and whatever's left is sold at a stall by the exit on Friday afternoons.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A few rules. Please keep to the paths and don't pick anything. Picnics are welcome on the main lawn but nowhere else. Ball games aren't allowed, I'm afraid.

script.speaker: C
script.text: If you'd like to know more, there's a free guided walk at two o'clock every day, starting from the sundial. It lasts an hour. And children can collect a trail sheet from the ticket office. If they find all ten plants on it, there's a small prize.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The garden closes at six, and the gates are locked promptly, so please start making your way back by a quarter to. Enjoy your afternoon.

title: Planning a student podcast and how animals navigate

parts.context: You will hear two journalism students, Bella and Omar, planning a podcast episode for their course.

options.A: it has been covered by other groups.

options.A: It will be simple to research.

options.C: It has been reported in the newspapers.

questions.prompt: If the council refuses an interview, the students will

options.B: the nurse has little free time.
options.C: it is quieter than the bus stop.

options.B: They made their programmes too long.

parts.context: You will hear part of a lecture about how animals find their way over long distances.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Omar, we need to choose a subject for the podcast by Friday. Any thoughts?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'd been thinking about student debt. It affects everyone we know.

script.speaker: A
script.text: It does, but two groups did it last year, and I'm not sure we'd find anything new to say. What about the night bus? The council's planning to cut it.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The N seven? I take that home from my job at the restaurant.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Exactly. It's used by cleaners, nurses, bar staff. People who don't usually get asked what they think.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I like it. It's local, and it has a deadline, because the council votes next month. How long does the episode have to be?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Between twelve and fifteen minutes. The brief is strict about that.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's shorter than I'd assumed. We won't have room for many voices.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Three, I'd say. A passenger, a driver, and someone from the council.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Will the council speak to students?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Their press office has to answer questions from anybody. Whether a councillor will be interviewed on tape is another matter. I'll email them today.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And if they refuse?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then we say so in the programme. Listeners can draw their own conclusions.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fine. I can find a passenger easily. There's a nurse I chat to most nights.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Don't just interview her at the bus stop, though. Record on the bus itself. The engine, the doors, the announcements. Sound puts the listener there.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Do we need permission to record on a bus?

script.speaker: A
script.text: From the bus company, yes. Miss Greene said that was the mistake most groups made last year. They recorded first and asked afterwards, and couldn't use the material.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll write to the company. What about the script? I'd planned to write everything out in full.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Write the links between the interviews, but let the interviews tell the story. If we talk for more than a third of the time, we'll lose marks.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Understood. Who edits?

script.speaker: A
script.text: You're faster with the software than I am. I'll do the research and write the script, if you record and edit.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Deal. What about music?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Only at the very beginning and the end, and it has to be free of copyright. The department has a library of tracks we're allowed to use.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good. When do we record?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The vote is on the nineteenth, so I'd like everything recorded by the tenth. That leaves a week to edit.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'm working Friday and Saturday night. I could ride the bus home with the recorder on both.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Perfect. Take spare batteries. It gets cold, and they run down fast.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Each autumn, a small bird called the Arctic tern leaves Greenland and flies to Antarctica, and each spring it flies back. Over a lifetime of thirty years, that's equal to three return trips to the moon. How does it know the way? Today I'll outline what we understand about animal navigation, and what remains a mystery.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Navigation requires two things. You need a compass, to tell you which direction is which. And you need a map, to tell you where you are in relation to your goal. A compass by itself isn't enough. If I blindfolded you, drove you a hundred kilometres and gave you a compass, you'd know where north was, but not which way was home.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let's take compasses first, since they're better understood. Many birds use the sun. That's harder than it sounds, because the sun moves across the sky, so the bird must allow for the time of day. Experiments in which birds' internal clocks were shifted by six hours showed that they then flew off at ninety degrees to the correct course.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Birds that migrate at night use the stars. Young birds raised in a planetarium learned to identify north from the point around which the stars rotate. They weren't born knowing a star map. They learned it by watching the sky turn.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The third compass is the earth's magnetic field. This was proved in the nineteen sixties with robins kept in a cage. When researchers used electric coils to turn the magnetic field around the cage, the birds changed direction to match. We still aren't certain how they detect it. The leading theory involves a chemical reaction in the eye, which would mean that birds, in some sense, see the field.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now the map, which is far more puzzling. Sea turtles hatch on a beach, spend twenty years wandering the ocean, and return to lay eggs on the very beach where they were born. The evidence suggests that each stretch of coast has its own magnetic signature, and that the young turtle memorises it.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Salmon do something similar at sea, but for the last stage, finding the right river, they rely on smell. Each stream has a particular chemical character, and the fish follow it home.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And insects shouldn't be overlooked. Desert ants find their way back to the nest in a straight line after a winding search for food. They do it by counting their steps. When researchers attached tiny stilts to their legs, the ants walked straight past the nest.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A final thought. Artificial light at night and electrical noise from our cities both interfere with these senses, and we're only beginning to measure the damage.

explanations.2: The council votes next month, so it has a deadline.
explanations.3: They will say so in the programme.
explanations.4: The engine, doors and announcements put the listener there.
explanations.5: They recorded first and asked afterwards, and could not use the material.

script.text: Good morning, Ravenscar Outdoor Centre. Hugh speaking.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hi. I teach at Dalton High School, and I'd like to bring a group of students for a few days of activities.

script.speaker: A
script.text: We'd be glad to have you. How many students, and how old?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Twenty-four, all aged fourteen and fifteen. And three teachers.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Twenty-four is a good number. We split groups into teams of eight for most activities. When were you hoping to come?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The week beginning the twelfth of May, if you have room. We'd planned on five days.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Let me look. That week, we have another school in from Monday to Wednesday, and we can't take both. I could offer you Wednesday afternoon to Friday.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So three days and two nights. That might actually suit our budget better. What would that cost?

script.speaker: A
script.text: For two nights, with all meals and activities, it's a hundred and thirty-five pounds per student. Staff come free.

script.speaker: B
script.text: A hundred and thirty-five. I'd budgeted for a hundred and sixty, so that's good news. What activities would they do?

script.speaker: A
script.text: In three days, we'd normally fit in four. Kayaking on the lake, rock climbing, a navigation exercise on the moor, and on the last morning, a raft-building challenge, which is always the favourite.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Not all of them can swim. Is that a problem for the kayaking?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Not at all. Everyone wears a buoyancy aid, and the lake is shallow at the edge where beginners stay. We just need to know who the non-swimmers are.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll put it on the forms. Where do they sleep?

script.speaker: A
script.text: In dormitories of six, with separate buildings for boys and girls. Staff have single rooms.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And do they need to bring sleeping bags?

script.speaker: A
script.text: No, bedding is supplied. What they must bring is a towel, and two pairs of shoes, one of which will get soaked. We lend waterproof jackets and trousers, and all the safety equipment.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Great. Some parents will ask about phones.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Our policy is that phones are collected on arrival and returned at the end. Parents are given an emergency number. Schools tell us it's what the students remember most fondly, oddly enough.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I can imagine. What do you need from us in advance?

script.speaker: A
script.text: A medical form for each student, signed by a parent, at least two weeks beforehand. And a list of any special diets.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Two weeks. And the deposit?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Twenty per cent when you book, and the rest a month before you arrive.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fine. I'll need to confirm with the head teacher. Can you hold the dates?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I can hold them for seven days. Who shall I say?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Laura Pennick. P, E, double N, I, C, K.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Stanton University. I'm Hilary, from the accommodation office. I know you've had a long day, so I'll be brief.

script.speaker: C
script.text: There are nine halls of residence, and eighty per cent of first-year students live in one. People often believe the newest halls are the most popular. In our surveys, the highest satisfaction is in the two oldest, Carver and Wells, even though the rooms are smaller. The reason seems to be the shared dining rooms, where everyone eats together and gets to know each other.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Your room key is the card you were given at reception. It also opens the main door and the laundry. If you lose it, the first replacement is free. After that, there's a charge of fifteen pounds.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Each of you shares a kitchen with seven other people. In my experience, more arguments start over washing up than over anything else. So please agree a rota in the first week, and stick to it. The cleaners come on Tuesdays and Fridays, but they clean floors and surfaces only. They won't wash your dishes.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Every hall has a team of senior students, called wardens, who live in the building. They're your first contact if you're locked out, if something's broken, or if you simply feel homesick. One of them is on duty all night, and the number is on the back of your door.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, noise. Quiet hours run from eleven at night until seven in the morning. During exam periods, they start at nine.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Guests are welcome. A friend can stay for up to three nights in a row. Please sign them in on the website. That isn't to check up on you. If there's a fire, we must know who's in the building.

script.speaker: C
script.text: On that subject, the fire alarm is tested every Wednesday at ten in the morning. It lasts ten seconds. If it sounds at any other time, or for longer, leave at once. And please don't cover the smoke detector in your room. Every year, someone does, and the fine is two hundred pounds.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Your rent includes heating, electricity and internet. It doesn't include insurance for your possessions, so I'd advise you to arrange that, particularly for laptops and bicycles.

script.speaker: C
script.text: If you'd like to change rooms, you can apply from week four. We don't allow it earlier, because most problems settle down once people have got to know one another.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, the accommodation office is in the Hartley Building, and we're open from nine to five. Come and see us.

options.C: It is cheaper than buying a real one.

groups.word_limit: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER
groups.text:
The reviews trusted most are those that give a specific {{6}}.
The invented product will be a pair of {{7}}.

Volunteers can be contacted through the {{9}}.

parts.context: You will hear part of a lecture about the history of paper.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Ines, come in. I've read your draft chapter on online reviews. How do you think it's going?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The reading has gone well. It's the survey I'm nervous about. I've never designed one.

script.speaker: A
script.text: We'll come to that. First, your research question. You ask whether customer reviews influence what people buy. I think we know the answer to that already.

script.speaker: B
script.text: It's too obvious?

script.speaker: A
script.text: A little. Every study says yes. What's less clear is which reviews people trust. That would be a sharper question.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Actually, that's where my reading was heading. There's a finding I found fascinating. Products with a perfect score of five stars sell less well than products with around four and a half.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Why do you think that is?

script.speaker: B
script.text: People seem to feel that a perfect score is too good to be true. A few complaints make the rest believable.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So a small number of negative reviews can help a seller. That's worth building on. What else did you find?

script.speaker: B
script.text: That the number of reviews matters, up to a point. Shoppers trust a product with fifty reviews much more than one with five. But beyond a few hundred, more makes no difference.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And the content?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Long reviews are trusted more than short ones. And reviews that mention a specific detail, how the buyer used the product, for instance, are trusted most.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. Now, your method. You propose sending a questionnaire asking people how they use reviews.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes. Is that a problem?

script.speaker: A
script.text: People are poor at describing their own behaviour. They'll tell you they read reviews carefully, and in practice they glance at the stars. I'd suggest an experiment in place of the questionnaire.

script.speaker: B
script.text: What kind?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Create two versions of a web page for the same product. Identical in every way, but one has only glowing reviews, and the other includes a couple of mild complaints. Show each to a different group, and ask how likely they are to buy.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's much better. Could I do it with a product that doesn't exist? Then nobody would have an opinion already.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's exactly what I'd do. An invented brand of headphones, say.

script.speaker: B
script.text: How many people would I need?

script.speaker: A
script.text: At least eighty in each group. Don't just use your friends. The university has a panel of volunteers who take part in research, and they're a wider range of ages.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I didn't know that. How do I reach them?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Through the research office. You'll need ethics approval first, which takes about three weeks.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Then I should apply this week.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Do. And rewrite your first chapter around the new question. I'd like to see it by the end of the month.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We're often told that we live in a paperless age, and yet the world uses more paper today than at any time in history. This morning I'd like to follow the story of this very ordinary, very remarkable material.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Before paper, people wrote on whatever was available. In Egypt, it was papyrus, made from a reed that grew along the Nile. In Europe, it was parchment, made from the skins of sheep and calves. A single large Bible might require the skins of two hundred animals, which tells you why books were so rare.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Paper was invented in China. The traditional date is the year one hundred and five, and the credit goes to an official at the imperial court named Cai Lun, although examples have been found that are two centuries older. Early Chinese paper was made from old rags, fishing nets and the bark of the mulberry tree, all beaten to a pulp in water. A fine screen was dipped into the pulp, and the thin layer of fibres left on it dried into a sheet.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Its first uses weren't for writing at all. It was used for wrapping and for padding, to protect delicate objects such as bronze mirrors.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The secret stayed in East Asia for six hundred years. According to tradition, it travelled west after a battle in seven fifty-one, in central Asia, when Chinese paper makers were taken prisoner. Within decades, there was a paper mill in Baghdad. And paper transformed the Islamic world. It was far cheaper than parchment, and there was a further advantage that rulers appreciated. Ink soaks into paper, so a document couldn't be altered without leaving a trace. That made paper ideal for official records.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Paper reached Spain in the eleventh century and spread slowly north. Europeans improved the process by using water wheels to drive the hammers that beat the rags.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Then, around fourteen fifty, came the printing press, and demand exploded. For three hundred years, the limit on paper making was the supply of rags. There are accounts of rags being so scarce in England that a law required the dead to be buried in wool, in order to save linen for the mills.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The answer came from watching insects. A French scientist noticed that wasps build their nests by chewing wood into a kind of paper. It took another century to turn that idea into an industrial process, but by the eighteen fifties, paper was being made from wood pulp. It became cheap, and with cheap paper came the mass newspaper and the paperback book.

script.speaker: C
script.text: There was a cost. Wood-pulp paper is acidic, and it slowly destroys itself. Libraries are full of books from that period that are crumbling to dust.

explanations.1: Every study already says that reviews influence buying.
explanations.2: A perfect score seems too good to be true.
explanations.3: Fifty are trusted far more than five, but beyond a few hundred it makes no difference.
explanations.4: They say they read carefully but in practice glance at the stars.
explanations.5: Nobody would have an opinion already.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good morning, Parkside Vets. Emma speaking.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hello. We've just got a puppy, and I'd like to register her with you and find out what she needs.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Congratulations. I'll take some details. What's your surname, please?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Holloway. H, O, double L, O, W, A, Y.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And the puppy's name?

script.speaker: B
script.text: She's called Pepper.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Lovely. What breed is she?

script.speaker: B
script.text: She's a border terrier.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And how old?

script.speaker: B
script.text: She was born on the third of January, so she's ten weeks now. We collected her on Saturday.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Ten weeks. Has she had any vaccinations yet?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The breeder gave us a card. It says she had her first injection at eight weeks.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. Then she's due for the second in two weeks' time. Until a week after that, she shouldn't walk in parks or on pavements where other dogs have been. Your own garden is fine.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's a long time to keep her in.

script.speaker: A
script.text: You can carry her around, so she gets used to traffic and people. She just mustn't be on the ground. Has she been microchipped?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes, the breeder did that. But the chip is still registered in his name.

script.speaker: A
script.text: You'll need to change that. It's done online, and there's a small fee. The law requires the details to be up to date.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll do it tonight. What about worms and fleas?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Puppies should be treated for worms every month until they're six months old. We'll weigh her at each visit and give you the right dose. How's she eating?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Very well. The breeder gave us a bag of the food she's used to.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Keep her on that for now. If you'd like to change it, do it gradually, over about a week, or she'll have an upset stomach. How many meals does she have?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Four a day at the moment.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's right for her age. You can drop to three at around twelve weeks.

script.speaker: B
script.text: OK. When can we bring her in?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The vet likes to see every new puppy for a health check, and it's free. I've got Thursday at ten past four, or Friday at nine.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Thursday's better. My wife would like to come, and she works on Friday mornings.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thursday at ten past four, with Mister Baines. Please bring the vaccination card.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Will do. One other thing. A neighbour mentioned puppy classes.

script.speaker: A
script.text: We run them here on Wednesday evenings, at seven. They can join after the second vaccination. It's four sessions for thirty pounds, and it's mostly about getting used to other dogs.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Put us down for that as well.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'll add you to the list for the course starting in April.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good afternoon, and welcome to the Hadley Chocolate Works. I'm Marco, and I've been making chocolate here for eleven years. The tour lasts about an hour, and yes, there is tasting at the end.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Before we go in, I must ask you to put on a hairnet and a white coat. You'll also need to remove any jewellery from your hands and wrists. That isn't about safety around the machines. It's about hygiene. A lost ring in a batch means throwing away half a tonne of chocolate.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A little history. The company was started in nineteen twenty-three by two brothers who'd been selling cocoa as a drink. During the war, when sugar was rationed, the factory almost closed, and it survived by making soap. We don't mention that on the wrappers.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, where does chocolate come from? It begins as the seed of a tree that only grows within twenty degrees of the equator. Ours come from Ghana and Ecuador. Inside each fruit, or pod, there are about forty beans, and it takes the beans from a whole pod to make one of our small bars.

script.speaker: C
script.text: At the farm, the beans are fermented for six days under banana leaves. It's this stage that creates the flavour. A raw bean tastes bitter and nothing like chocolate. They're then dried in the sun and shipped to us in sacks.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Here's what you'll see inside. First, the beans are roasted, for about half an hour. You'll notice the smell before you see anything.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Next, a machine cracks the beans and blows away the shells. What's left are small pieces called nibs. The shells don't go to waste. We sell them to garden centres, where they're used on flower beds.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The nibs are ground between heavy rollers until they turn into a thick liquid. At this point, we add sugar, and milk powder for milk chocolate.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Then comes a stage called conching, and it's the one that separates good chocolate from ordinary. The mixture is stirred continuously for up to three days. That makes it smooth and removes any sour taste.

script.speaker: C
script.text: After that, the chocolate is cooled and warmed again very precisely. Without that step, the bar would be dull and crumbly. Done properly, it's shiny, and it breaks with a clean snap.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, it's poured into moulds, shaken to remove bubbles, cooled, and wrapped.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Two requests. Please stay behind the blue line on the floor. And photographs are fine everywhere apart from the moulding room, where the shapes for next season are still secret.

explanations.11: A lost ring means throwing away half a tonne of chocolate.
explanations.12: It made soap when sugar was rationed.
explanations.13: The six days of fermentation create the flavour; a raw bean tastes bitter.
explanations.14: They are sold to garden centres for flower beds.
explanations.15: The shapes for next season are still secret.

parts.context: You will hear part of a lecture about plastic in the oceans.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Harry, I've been looking at the council's proposal to close Castle Street to cars. Have you decided what line our report should take?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I started out against it, to be honest. My uncle has a shop there, and he's convinced it would ruin him.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's what shopkeepers nearly always say. I've been reading the evidence from other towns. In almost every case, takings went up after traffic was removed, not down.

script.speaker: B
script.text: By how much?

script.speaker: A
script.text: It varies. A study of a hundred streets in Europe found an average rise of around a quarter. But there's usually a difficult first year, while people change their habits.

script.speaker: B
script.text: My uncle's argument is that his customers come by car.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's the interesting part. Shopkeepers consistently overestimate that. In one survey in Bristol, owners guessed that forty per cent of their customers arrived by car. When the customers were actually counted, it was twenty-two.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's a big gap. Has anyone counted on Castle Street?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Not yet. I think we should. An afternoon each, asking people how they got there.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'm happy to do that. It would give us something original. What about deliveries? Lorries need to reach the shops.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Most schemes allow them in before ten in the morning. Then the street is closed until evening.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And disabled drivers?

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's a real weakness in the council's plan. The nearest parking would be three hundred metres away, which is too far for many people. We should recommend some reserved spaces at each end.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Agreed. What about the buses? Three routes use that street.

script.speaker: A
script.text: They'd be moved to Queen's Road, one block north. The stops would be about two minutes further away on foot.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's acceptable. I'm coming round to the idea, I admit. But the proposal's vague about what replaces the traffic. An empty street isn't attractive.

script.speaker: A
script.text: No. The successful schemes add things. Trees, benches, a place for a market.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And somebody has to pay for all that.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The council's budgeted for new paving, but nothing else. We could propose that the shops contribute through a small annual fee, as they do in Norwich.

script.speaker: B
script.text: My uncle won't like that either.

script.speaker: A
script.text: If his takings rise by a quarter, he might. So, shall we support the scheme, with conditions?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes. Support, with three conditions. The parking for disabled drivers, proper seating and trees, and a review after twelve months.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. I'll write up the evidence from other towns.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And I'll organise the count. Saturday is the busiest day, so let's do it then.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Each year, somewhere between eight and twelve million tonnes of plastic enter the sea. That's roughly a lorry load every minute. In today's lecture, I'd like to look at where it comes from, where it goes, and what might be done.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let's begin with sources. You might suppose that most of it is thrown from ships. That was true fifty years ago. Today, about four fifths comes from the land, and it reaches the sea mainly by way of rivers. A small number of rivers, most of them in Asia, carry a very large share of the total, and that isn't because people there use more plastic. It's because the systems for collecting waste haven't kept up with the growth of cities.

script.speaker: C
script.text: What happens to it once it's in the sea? Some sinks. Some washes up on beaches. And some is carried by currents into enormous slowly rotating systems called gyres. The best known is in the North Pacific, and it's often described as an island of rubbish twice the size of France. That description is misleading. You couldn't walk on it. For the most part, you can't even see it. It's more like a thin soup of small fragments.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Those fragments are the real concern. Plastic doesn't rot. Sunlight and waves simply break it into smaller and smaller pieces, known as microplastics. And there's a second source, which surprises people. Every time we wash clothes made of synthetic fabric, thousands of tiny fibres go down the drain. Another is the dust worn from car tyres.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The effects on wildlife are well documented. Turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish. Seabirds feed bottle tops to their chicks, which then starve with full stomachs. Microplastics are eaten by the smallest animals in the sea and pass up the food chain. They've been found in fish on sale in markets, in sea salt, and in drinking water. What that means for human health, we simply don't know yet.

script.speaker: C
script.text: So what can be done? There's a great deal of publicity for machines that would sweep the oceans clean. I'm sceptical. The quantity collected so far is tiny, and the nets catch living creatures as well. Most researchers agree that the priority is to stop plastic reaching the sea in the first place.

script.speaker: C
script.text: That means better waste collection in the countries where the rivers are. It means designing packaging that can actually be recycled. Only about nine per cent of all the plastic ever made has been. And it means using less. Bans on plastic bags have cut the number found on beaches in several countries by more than half.

explanations.1: He started out against it because of his uncle's shop.
explanations.2: In almost every case they went up, by around a quarter on average.
explanations.3: They guessed forty per cent; the true figure was twenty-two.
explanations.4: The nearest parking would be three hundred metres away.
explanations.5: The shops could contribute a small annual fee, as in Norwich.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good morning, Weaver's Yard Arts Centre. Tom speaking.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hello. I've seen that you run art workshops in the school holidays. I've got two children who'd love that sort of thing.

script.speaker: A
script.text: We do. How old are they?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Lucy's eleven and Sam's seven.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then they'd be in different groups. We have one for ages six to nine and another for ten to fourteen.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Oh. I'd hoped they could be together.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'm afraid the older group uses tools that aren't suitable for little ones. But both groups run at the same times, so you'd only make one journey.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's something. What do they do?

script.speaker: A
script.text: This summer, the younger group is doing puppet making. They make a puppet each, and on the last afternoon they put on a show for the parents. The older group is doing printing. They design a pattern, cut it into a block, and print it onto a bag they can take home.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Lucy would enjoy that. How long is the course?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Each workshop runs for four days, Monday to Thursday, from ten until three.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And which weeks?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The first starts on the twenty-first of July, and it's repeated the following week.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We're away for the last week of July. The first week, then. What's the cost?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Eighty-five pounds per child. That includes all the materials. If you book two children, the second is seventy pounds.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So a hundred and fifty-five altogether. Is lunch provided?

script.speaker: A
script.text: No, they need to bring a packed lunch. We give them a drink and fruit in the middle of the morning. We do ask parents not to send anything containing nuts.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fine. What should they wear?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Old clothes. The printing ink doesn't wash out. We have aprons, but accidents happen.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll remember. Who runs the workshops?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The puppets are with Rosie, who used to work in children's theatre. The printing is taught by a local artist, Ben Okoro. All our tutors have had the police checks required for working with children.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good. Where exactly are you? I know the area, but I've never been in.

script.speaker: A
script.text: We're on Tanner's Lane, in the old textile mill. There's nowhere to park outside. Most parents use the supermarket car park opposite. It's free for two hours.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And what happens at three o'clock? I may be a few minutes late on the Tuesday.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Children stay with the tutor in the cafe until they're collected. Each child can only be handed over to an adult named on the booking form, so if a grandparent or a neighbour is coming, do add them.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll put my mother down as well. Can I book now?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Certainly. Could I take your surname?

script.speaker: B
script.text: It's Fairley. F, A, I, R, L, E, Y.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good morning, and welcome to Glen Carran National Park. My name's Jess, and I'm one of the rangers. A lot of you are setting off on walks today, so I'd like to say a few words about staying safe.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Our mountain rescue team was called out a hundred and twelve times last year. You might imagine most of those were climbers on steep rock. In fact, the largest group were ordinary walkers on marked paths, who slipped on the way down. People are tired on the descent, and that's when ankles get broken.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The second most common problem is getting lost when the cloud comes down. It can happen in minutes. So please carry a paper map and a compass, and know how to use them. A phone is useful, but batteries die quickly in the cold, and in most of the valleys there's no signal at all.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let me talk about the weather. The forecast in the visitor centre is updated at seven every morning. Read the mountain forecast, not the general one. It can be mild and sunny in the car park, and close to freezing with a strong wind on the summit. As a rough guide, the temperature drops one degree for every hundred and fifty metres you climb.

script.speaker: C
script.text: What should you take? Waterproofs, always, even on a fine day. An extra warm layer. A hat and gloves. Plenty of food, and at least a litre of water each. And a torch, because walks take longer than people expect, and it's dark by five at this time of year.

script.speaker: C
script.text: On your feet, boots with a good grip. I see people every day in trainers, and it's the thing that worries me most.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Before you leave, tell someone your route and when you expect to be back. You can fill in a card at the desk here. If you haven't returned, that's how we know where to start looking.

script.speaker: C
script.text: If something does go wrong, stay where you are. Call the emergency number and ask for police, then mountain rescue. If you have no signal, the recognised distress call is six blasts on a whistle, repeated every minute. Keep the injured person warm, and don't give them anything to eat.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A word about turning back. There's no shame in it. The mountain will still be here next week. The experienced walkers are the ones who turn round when conditions change.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, please take all your litter home, keep dogs on a lead while there are lambs in the fields, and close every gate behind you. Have a wonderful day.

explanations.11: The largest group were ordinary walkers who slipped on the way down.
explanations.12: Batteries die in the cold and most valleys have no signal.
explanations.13: It can be mild in the car park and near freezing on the summit.
explanations.14: She sees people in trainers every day.
explanations.15: Stay where you are and call for help.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Emily, I've finished entering the data from the two schools. Shall we look at what we've got?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Please. Remind me how many days we observed.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Ten at each school. A hundred children at Northfield, and a hundred and ten at Saint Anne's.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And at both schools, the meals meet the national standards.

script.speaker: A
script.text: On paper, yes. Each lunch is supposed to include a portion of vegetables, a portion of fruit, and so on. The menus are almost identical.

script.speaker: B
script.text: But the standards describe what's put on the tray, not what's eaten.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Exactly, and that's where it gets interesting. At Northfield, the children ate about a third of their vegetables. At Saint Anne's, nearly two thirds.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Twice as much. Is the food better at Saint Anne's?

script.speaker: A
script.text: That was my first thought. But it's the same catering company, and the same recipes.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So what's different?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Two things, I think. First, the timetable. At Northfield, lunch comes before playtime. The children rush their food to get outside. At Saint Anne's, they play first and eat afterwards.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So they arrive hungry, and they're in no hurry to leave. That's so simple.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And it costs nothing. The second difference is the length of the lunch period. Northfield allows twenty-five minutes, including queuing. Saint Anne's gives forty.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I timed the queue at Northfield. Some children had only nine minutes sitting down.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Nine minutes. No wonder the vegetables are left.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Is there anything about the dining rooms themselves?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Saint Anne's has small round tables, and a teacher sits at each one. Northfield has long benches, and the staff stand at the side.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Do we have any way of knowing which of these factors matters most?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Not from two schools. That's the weakness. We can describe the differences, but we can't prove what causes what.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We should say that clearly. And suggest a proper experiment. Take one school, change only the timetable, and measure before and after.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Northfield's head teacher seemed open to that. I'll ask her.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good. How did we measure what was left? I joined the project late.

script.speaker: A
script.text: We photographed every tray before and after the meal, and estimated the amounts from the pictures. It's quicker than weighing, and nearly as accurate.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Did the children change their behaviour because of the camera?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Possibly, on the first day. So we left the first day's data out of the analysis.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Sensible. Now, the report. I'd lead with the wasted vegetables. It's the figure people will remember.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Agreed. And a recommendation for schools. Play first, eat second.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll draft the introduction and the method.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'll do the results. Let's meet on Monday at eleven.

script.speaker: C
script.text: There are roughly seven thousand languages spoken in the world today. By the end of this century, on current trends, at least half will have fallen silent. In this lecture, I'll consider why languages die, why it matters, and whether anything can be done.

script.speaker: C
script.text: First, the distribution is extremely uneven. A handful of languages, Mandarin, Spanish, English and a few others, are spoken by half of humanity. At the other extreme, about a third of all languages have fewer than a thousand speakers. The island of New Guinea alone has more than eight hundred, in a population smaller than that of London.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Languages rarely die because their speakers die. They die because parents stop passing them on. And parents generally make that choice for a practical reason. They believe that a major language will give their children a better chance of finding work. In many countries, the process was pushed along by schools, where children were punished for using their mother tongue.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A language is usually considered endangered when children no longer learn it at home. After that, it can vanish within two generations.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Why should we care? One reason is knowledge. Small languages often contain detailed information about local plants and animals that science hasn't recorded. A second is that each language shows a different way in which the human mind can organise experience. Some have no words for left and right, and their speakers use compass directions all the time. They always know which way north is. A third reason, and for communities the most important, is identity.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Can a language be brought back? There are encouraging examples. Hebrew had not been used in daily conversation for nearly two thousand years. It survived in religion, and was revived as a spoken language in the late nineteenth century. Today it has nine million speakers.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Welsh is a different kind of success. By the nineteen sixties, it was in steep decline. What turned it round was a campaign that won schools teaching in Welsh, and a television channel. The number of young speakers is now rising.

script.speaker: C
script.text: In New Zealand, the Maori community set up what they called language nests. These were nurseries where very small children spent the day with grandparents who spoke only Maori. The idea has since been copied in Hawaii and elsewhere.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Technology helps as well. Linguists now record the last speakers on video, and communities build dictionaries on their phones. But a recording isn't a living language. In the end, a language survives only if children use it with one another when no adult is listening.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Before you set off, a brief history. The first castle on this hill was built of wood, soon after ten sixty-six. Nothing of that remains. script.text: The castle was attacked only once in its history, in twelve sixteen, and it held out for three months. It was never taken by force. Its decline was gradual. script.speaker: A
script.text: Rahul, we've got the roof booked for Thursday. Are the cookers ready?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Two of the three. The box cooker and the panel cooker are finished. The dish one is giving me trouble.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The parabolic dish? What's the matter with it?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I covered an old satellite dish with kitchen foil, and the foil keeps wrinkling. Every wrinkle scatters the light.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The technician has some mirror film left over from another project. It's sticky on the back, and it goes on smoothly.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That would be much better. I'll ask him tomorrow.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So, to recap the aim. We're comparing how quickly each design heats a litre of water.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Right. And how hot it gets in the end. I'd expect the dish to win easily. It focuses all the light on one small spot.

script.speaker: A
script.text: It should reach the highest temperature. But it has to be turned every ten minutes or so to follow the sun, or the hot spot moves off the pot. The box cooker can be left alone for an hour.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So for someone cooking a meal, the box might be more practical.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's what the reports from aid organisations say. Dish cookers get abandoned, because nobody has time to stand beside them.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We should mention that. It isn't just about peak temperature.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Now, to make it a fair test, what do we need to keep the same?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The amount of water, obviously. The starting temperature. And the pots.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The pots are a problem. We've got two black ones and a shiny steel one.

script.speaker: B
script.text: A shiny pot reflects the light. It would put whichever cooker gets it at a disadvantage.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'll paint it black tonight. There's some heat-resistant paint in the workshop.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good. What about wind? It was gusty up there last time.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Wind cools the pots. We can't control it, but we can measure it, and run all three cookers at the same time, so they're affected equally.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And cloud?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Same answer. I've borrowed a light meter, so we can record how strong the sun is every five minutes.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Who takes the temperatures?

script.speaker: A
script.text: We don't need to. I've got three probes that record automatically, once a minute, onto a laptop.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Excellent. That leaves us free to turn the dish. How long shall we run it?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Two hours, from eleven until one, when the sun's at its highest.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And if it's cloudy on Thursday?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then we move to Friday. I've booked the roof for both days, just in case.

script.speaker: B
script.text: You think of everything. I'll bring sun cream, and a kettle, so we know what we're competing with.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Few names in history are as evocative as the Silk Road. It suggests a single highway, with caravans of camels plodding from China to Rome. The reality was rather different, and today I'd like to correct a few misunderstandings.

script.speaker: C
script.text: To begin with, the name itself is modern. Nobody who travelled the routes ever used it. It was invented in eighteen seventy-seven by a German geographer. And there was never one road. There was a shifting network of tracks across deserts and mountain passes, together with sea routes through the Indian Ocean, which eventually carried far more goods than the land.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Second, almost nobody travelled the whole distance. Goods moved in stages, passing from one merchant to another at the great market towns, such as Samarkand. A roll of silk might change hands a dozen times, and its price rose at each exchange.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The people who dominated this business for centuries were not Chinese or Roman but a people called the Sogdians, from the region of modern Uzbekistan. Their language became the common language of the caravans.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And silk was far from the only cargo. Travelling west went paper, porcelain and tea. Travelling east went glass, silver, wine and, above all, horses, which the Chinese valued enormously for their army.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The animal that made it possible was the camel, and specifically the two-humped camel of central Asia. It can carry two hundred kilos, go for a week without water, and, according to Chinese writers, sense a sandstorm before it arrives.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Far more important than any goods, however, were the ideas that travelled with them. Buddhism spread from India to China along these routes. So did techniques, the making of paper going west, and of glass going east. Crops moved too. The peach and the orange came to Europe from China, and grapes travelled the other way.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Not everything that travelled was welcome. Most historians believe that the plague which killed perhaps a third of Europe's population in the fourteenth century was carried along the same routes.

script.speaker: C
script.text: What ended the overland trade? There was no single moment. But after fourteen ninety-eight, when Portuguese ships reached India by sailing round Africa, the sea became cheaper and safer, and the cities of central Asia slowly declined.

script.speaker: C
script.text: I'll end with a thought. We speak of globalisation as though it were new. The Silk Road is a reminder that people, goods and beliefs have been crossing continents for two thousand years.

script.speaker: C
