script.speaker: A
script.text: Carlos, how's the reading going for the homework paper?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I've got through most of it. I have to say, I started with a strong opinion. I assumed homework was simply a good thing. More practice, better results.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And now?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Now I think it depends almost entirely on age. For secondary pupils, the studies show a clear benefit. For children under eleven, the link between homework and achievement is close to zero.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That matches what I found. Although there's one exception for the little ones, which is reading at home with a parent. That does seem to help.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes. So it's the worksheets that make no difference, not the reading.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What surprised me was the research on amount. I'd imagined that the more time pupils spent, the better.

script.speaker: B
script.text: It doesn't work like that?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Only up to a point. For teenagers, the benefit increases up to about an hour and a half a night. Beyond two hours, results actually start to fall.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Because they're tired?

script.speaker: A
script.text: That, and they give up sleep. One study in California found that pupils with more than three hours a night reported more stress and more health problems, with no gain in their marks.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So we could argue for a limit. What about the kind of homework?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The strongest finding is about feedback. Homework the teacher marks and discusses has roughly twice the effect of homework that's simply collected and ticked.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Which means that setting less, and marking it properly, might achieve more.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's going to be my main recommendation.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'd add something about fairness. Homework assumes that every child has a quiet place to work, and an adult who can help. Plenty don't.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's an important point. Some schools have responded by opening a homework club after lessons, with a teacher present.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I visited one for my placement. The pupils who went were mostly those who'd have done the work anyway.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So it didn't reach the ones who needed it.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Not unless teachers invited particular pupils personally. Then it did.

script.speaker: A
script.text: We should include that. Now, how do we organise the paper?

script.speaker: B
script.text: By age group first, then amount, then type, then fairness.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And we need to be careful with the word proves. Most of these studies show a connection, not a cause. Pupils who do more homework may simply be more motivated to begin with.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good point. I'll put that in the introduction as a warning.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The limit is three thousand words. Shall we take two sections each?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll take age and fairness. You do amount and type.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Fine. First drafts by the twentieth?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The twentieth. I'll send mine by email.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The skyscraper is so much a part of the modern city that it's easy to forget how recently it became possible. Until the eighteen eighties, the tallest ordinary buildings had five or six storeys. Today I'll explain the three inventions that changed that, and what limits remain.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The first obstacle was the wall. In a traditional building, the walls carry the weight of everything above them. The higher you build, the thicker the walls at the bottom must be. The Monadnock Building in Chicago, sixteen storeys of brick, has walls nearly two metres thick at the base, and they take up a great deal of the ground floor.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The solution was the steel frame. In a framed building, a skeleton of steel columns and beams carries the load, and the walls simply hang on it, like a curtain. The first building of this kind went up in Chicago in eighteen eighty-five. It had only ten storeys, but the principle was established.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The second obstacle was human. Nobody will climb twenty flights of stairs. Lifts existed, but people didn't trust them, because the ropes sometimes broke. The breakthrough came from Elisha Otis. At an exhibition in New York in eighteen fifty-four, he stood on a platform high above the crowd and ordered the rope to be cut. His safety brake held. Interestingly, the lift reversed the pattern of rents. Before it, the cheapest rooms were at the top. Afterwards, the top floors became the most expensive.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The third requirement is less obvious. A tall building full of people needs fresh air, and above a certain height you can't simply open a window, because of the wind. So the skyscraper depended on mechanical ventilation, and later on air conditioning.

script.speaker: C
script.text: With those three things in place, buildings rose quickly. But a new enemy appeared, and that was the wind. A very tall tower sways, and although it's perfectly safe, the people on the upper floors feel sick. Engineers now fit a huge weight near the top, which swings in the opposite direction and cancels the movement. The one in Taipei weighs six hundred and sixty tonnes, and it's become a tourist attraction.

script.speaker: C
script.text: So what limits height today? Not structure. Engineers could build far higher. The real limit is the lift. The taller the tower, the more lift shafts it needs, and eventually they occupy so much of each floor that there's too little space left to rent.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A final point. Tall buildings are sometimes defended as green, because they use little land. But they need a great deal of energy to build and run, and several studies suggest that buildings of six to ten storeys are more efficient.

explanations.1: He assumed more practice meant better results.
explanations.2: The link is otherwise close to zero; reading at home is the exception.
explanations.3: The benefit rises up to about an hour and a half, and results fall beyond two hours.
explanations.4: Marked and discussed homework has roughly twice the effect.
explanations.5: Those who went would have done the work anyway.

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: A
script.text: We stopped charging fines two years ago. If a book is more than four weeks late, your card is blocked until you bring it back, and that's all.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's generous. I work from home, and I was hoping to use the library as an office now and then.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Lots of people do. The wireless network is free, and you don't need a password. The study area is on the second floor. If you'd like one of the private study rooms, you can book it for up to two hours a day.

script.speaker: B

script.speaker: A

script.speaker: B
script.text: Wonderful. Is there a printer?

script.text: Yes, on the first floor. Printing costs ten pence a page in black and white, and you pay with your library card. You put credit on it at the machine by the stairs.

script.text: Nine until seven, Monday to Friday, and nine until five on Saturdays. We're closed on Sundays, though there's a box at the door for returning books.

script.speaker: A

script.speaker: C
script.text: Thanks, Julie. Yes, this week's letter comes from a listener who lives in a flat on the fourth floor and wants to know whether it's worth trying to grow food on a balcony. My answer is a definite yes, as long as you avoid a few common mistakes.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The first thing to check is weight. Wet soil is heavy. A large pot full of compost can weigh as much as an adult, and a balcony has its limits. So before you buy anything, ask the owner of the building how much load the balcony can take. Use plastic or fabric pots, not stone ones, and place the heaviest containers close to the wall, where the structure is strongest.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Second, light. Most vegetables need at least six hours of direct sun. If your balcony faces north, don't despair. You can still grow salad leaves, spinach and herbs such as mint and parsley, which are happy in shade.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The third factor, and it's the one people forget, is wind. On a high balcony, wind dries out plants far faster than sun does, and it can snap tall stems. I'd put up a screen of netting, which filters the wind without blocking the light.

script.speaker: C

script.speaker: C

script.speaker: C

script.speaker: C
script.text: Feed the plants once a week from midsummer. There's very little goodness in a pot of compost, and it's used up within six weeks.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Finally, think about your neighbours. Water running off your balcony onto the one below is the fastest way to lose friends. Saucers under every pot, please.

questions.prompt: How does the documentary present itself?

options.A: as a personal journey by the director

options.A: The music begins before the storm does.
options.B: It was filmed in a different place.

parts.context: You will hear part of a lecture about mangrove forests.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Ravi, did you watch the documentary about the fishing village?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Twice. Once for pleasure, and once with a notebook. It's beautifully made.

script.speaker: A
script.text: It is. But I came away feeling slightly manipulated, and I've been trying to work out why.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Go on.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Well, the film presents itself as simply observing. There's no narrator, and no interviews. We just watch the villagers go about their lives.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The fly-on-the-wall style. And you don't believe it?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I believe the footage is real. But think about the storm sequence. It's the emotional centre of the film. And the music starts thirty seconds before the first cloud appears.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So we're told how to feel before anything has happened.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Exactly. Without the music, it's a rather ordinary storm.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I noticed something about the editing. The director was there for eleven months. That must be hundreds of hours of material, cut down to ninety minutes.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And what's left out?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Anything modern. You never see a phone, or a television, or a car. But in one shot, there's a satellite dish on a roof in the background, for about two seconds.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I missed that. So the village isn't as cut off from the world as the film suggests.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The director wanted a timeless place, and he chose his shots to make one.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's our argument, then. Observation is never neutral. Every decision about where to point the camera and when to cut is a kind of comment.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Should we say the film is dishonest?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I wouldn't go that far. All documentaries select. I'd say it hides its own choices, which a film with a narrator doesn't.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's fair. We could compare it with the other film on the list, the one about the oil workers, where the director appears on screen and admits what she doesn't know.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good idea. A contrast would sharpen the point. Which scenes should we analyse closely?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The storm, for the music. And the opening, because it sets up the idea of a place outside time.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And the final shot. The old man looks straight at the camera for the first time. It's as if the film finally admits that someone's been watching.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I hadn't thought of it like that. Brilliant.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Can we get stills for the essay?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The library has the film on disc. I'll take screenshots tomorrow.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Then I'll draft the section on sound tonight.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And I'll do the editing. Two thousand words each?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Fifteen hundred each, and five hundred for a joint conclusion.

script.speaker: C
script.text: If you stand on a tropical coast where a river meets the sea, you may find yourself facing a wall of tangled roots rising out of the mud. This is a mangrove forest, and although it isn't beautiful in the usual sense, it's among the most valuable ecosystems on earth.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Mangroves are trees that have solved a problem that kills almost every other plant, which is salt water. Different species manage this in different ways. Some filter out the salt at the roots. Others take it in and get rid of it through their leaves, and if you lick a leaf, you can taste it.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The second problem is the mud itself, which contains almost no oxygen. So many mangroves send up roots that stick out of the mud like pencils and take in air directly. Others stand on arching roots that look like stilts.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Their seeds are unusual as well. In most species, the seed begins to grow while it's still attached to the parent tree. When it drops, it's already a young plant, shaped like a spear. If the tide is out, it sticks in the mud. If the tide is in, it floats, sometimes for months, until it reaches a shore.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, why do these forests matter? First, as a nursery. The roots give shelter to young fish and shrimps. It's estimated that three quarters of the fish caught commercially in the tropics spend part of their lives among mangroves.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Second, as protection. The roots break the force of the waves. After the tsunami of two thousand and four, studies in India and Sri Lanka found that villages behind intact mangroves suffered far fewer deaths than those where the trees had been cleared.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Third, and this has only been appreciated recently, mangroves store carbon. The mud beneath them holds up to four times as much per hectare as a tropical rainforest, because dead material doesn't rot in mud without oxygen.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Despite all this, we've lost about a third of the world's mangroves in the last fifty years. The greatest single cause has been the farming of shrimps. The trees are cut down to make ponds, and the ponds are often abandoned after five years, when disease sets in.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Can the forests be restored? Early attempts frequently failed. People planted thousands of young trees in neat rows, often of a single species, in places that were flooded too deeply. Most of them died. The more successful approach is to repair the natural flow of water, by opening up blocked channels, and then to let the seeds arrive by themselves on the tide.

explanations.1: There is no narrator and no interviews; viewers simply watch.
explanations.2: The music starts thirty seconds before the first cloud appears.
explanations.3: Anything modern was left out, but the dish shows the village is not cut off.
explanations.4: All documentaries select; this one hides its own choices.
explanations.5: Its director appears on screen and admits what she does not know.

script.text: Hello, Greenlight Driving School. Sandra speaking.

script.text: Hi. I'd like to start learning to drive. I've never had a lesson.

script.speaker: B
script.text: What's the difference, in terms of the test?

script.speaker: A
script.text: If you pass in a manual, you can drive both. If you pass in an automatic, you can only drive automatics. Automatic is easier to learn, and people usually need fewer lessons.

script.speaker: B
script.text: My parents' car is a manual, and I'll want to borrow it. So manual.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Manual, then. Lessons are thirty-four pounds an hour. Most people take two hours at a time, because one hour disappears very quickly at the beginning.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Is there a discount if I pay for several?

script.speaker: A
script.text: If you pay for ten hours in advance, it's three hundred and ten pounds. So you'd save thirty.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll do that. How many lessons will I need altogether?

script.speaker: A
script.text: It varies a lot. The national average is around forty-five hours with an instructor, plus practice with family. Some people need thirty. I've had pupils who needed seventy.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Forty-five. That's more than I'd thought. Can I practise with my dad in between?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'd encourage it, once you've had about ten hours with me and can control the car. He must be over twenty-one and have held a licence for three years, and the car needs L plates and the right insurance.

script.speaker: B
script.text: He's fifty, so that's fine. When could I start?

script.speaker: A
script.text: I've got space on Saturday mornings, or Wednesdays after four.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I play football on Saturdays. Wednesday would be better.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Wednesday at four thirty. I'll pick you up from home. What's the address?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Twenty-two Linton Avenue. L, I, N, T, O, N.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Linton Avenue. And your name?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Jake Mallory.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thank you, Jake. One thing you can do before we start is study for the theory test. You must pass that before you can book the practical one.

script.speaker: B
script.text: What's in it?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Fifty multiple-choice questions, and a video section where you spot hazards as they develop. There's an official app with practice questions.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll download it tonight. Anything else I should bring on Wednesday?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Wear flat shoes with thin soles, so that you can feel the pedals. And if you need glasses, bring them. I'll ask you to read a number plate from twenty metres before we set off.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Evening, everybody. It's great to see so many of you. I count twenty-three, which is the biggest group we've ever started with. My name's Pete, and I'll be your coach for the next nine weeks.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Let me explain the idea. The programme takes people who do no running at all and gets them to the point where they can run for thirty minutes without stopping. We don't talk about distance at this stage, only time. For most people, half an hour works out at something between four and five kilometres.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We do it gradually. Tonight, you'll run for one minute and walk for a minute and a half, and repeat that eight times. That's all. I promise you'll go home thinking it was too easy. That's deliberate. The people who get injured are nearly always the ones who do too much in the first fortnight.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We meet here at the park gates every Tuesday at half past six. But one session a week isn't enough. You need to do two more by yourselves, with at least a day's rest in between. I'll send the plan for each week by email.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A word about speed. Please forget about it. The right pace is one at which you could hold a conversation. If you can't speak a full sentence, you're going too fast. I'd honestly prefer to see you jog slower than you walk than see you sprint and stop.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, what do you need? Not much. Comfortable clothes, and a proper pair of running shoes. They don't have to be expensive. What matters is that they fit, with a thumb's width of space in front of your toes, and that they aren't worn out. The shop on Mill Street will watch you run and advise you, and they give members of this group ten per cent off.

script.speaker: C
script.text: As the evenings get darker, wear something bright, or a reflective band.

script.speaker: C
script.text: You will ache. Some stiffness in the legs the day after is normal, and it fades. Sharp pain in a joint is different. If that happens, stop, rest for a few days, and tell me.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Eat something light about two hours before you run, not immediately before. And drink water during the day, so that you don't need to carry a bottle for a session as short as these.

script.speaker: C
script.text: In week nine, we all run together in the Saturday morning event here in the park. It's free, it's five kilometres, and nobody comes last, because a volunteer always walks at the back.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Right. Let's warm up with five minutes of brisk walking.

explanations.12: Those who get injured usually do too much in the first fortnight.
explanations.13: The group session plus two more runs alone.

script.text: That makes sense. And each person does it twice?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes, once with caffeine and once without, a week apart, at the same time of day. Half of them get the caffeine first, and half get it second.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So that any effect of practice cancels out.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Right. How many volunteers have we got?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Sixteen have signed up. I'd expect two or three to drop out.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Sixteen should be enough. Now, the dose. We said three hundred milligrams for everyone.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Shouldn't it depend on body weight?

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's what the literature does. Three milligrams per kilo. I'll change it.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And we need to screen people. Anyone with a heart condition must be excluded.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I'll write a health questionnaire. Can you book the lab?

script.speaker: B
script.text: For which dates?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The first two Wednesdays in March.

script.speaker: C
script.text: It would be hard to find a more ordinary food than the potato. Yet its arrival in Europe changed the continent's history, and this afternoon I'll explain how.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The potato was first grown about eight thousand years ago, high in the Andes, in what is now Peru and Bolivia. The farmers there developed thousands of varieties, and they invented a way of preserving them. They left the potatoes out to freeze at night, and trampled them by day to squeeze out the water. The result could be stored for ten years.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Spanish sailors brought the plant to Europe in about fifteen seventy. They carried it not as a treasure but simply as cheap food for the voyage home. And for nearly two centuries, most Europeans refused to eat it. There were several reasons. It wasn't mentioned in the Bible. It grew underground, which seemed unnatural. And it belongs to the same family as some poisonous plants, so people believed it caused disease.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Governments, however, saw its value. An acre of potatoes fed three or four times as many people as an acre of wheat. And potatoes had a military advantage. An army marching through could seize or burn a field of grain, but potatoes stayed hidden in the ground.

script.speaker: C
script.text: So rulers tried persuasion. In Prussia, the king ordered peasants to plant them. In France, a scientist named Parmentier used a cleverer method. He planted a field near Paris and had it guarded by soldiers during the day. At night, the guards were withdrawn. Local people, assuming that anything guarded must be valuable, crept in and stole the plants.

script.speaker: C
script.text: By eighteen hundred, the potato had been accepted, and its effect was dramatic. The population of Europe roughly doubled in a century, and many historians give the potato much of the credit. It fed the workers who moved to the new industrial cities.

script.speaker: C
script.text: But there was a hidden danger. Unlike the farmers of the Andes, Europeans grew only a few varieties. In Ireland, a third of the population depended on a single type. When a disease called blight arrived from America in eighteen forty-five, it destroyed the crop three years out of four. About a million people died, and a million more left the country.

script.speaker: C
script.text: The lesson has not been forgotten. Scientists now keep collections of wild and traditional potatoes, so that their genes can be used to breed resistance. The largest is in Peru, where the story began. It holds more than four thousand varieties.

explanations.1: The effect may differ in ordinary people; they will state this as a limitation.
explanations.2: With coffee and water, any improvement could be due to expectation.
explanations.3: The technician will label them with codes.
explanations.4: Forty-eight hours without tea, cola, chocolate or coffee.
explanations.5: It is closer to a real race and the results are more consistent.

title: Holiday cottage booking and flood preparation

parts.context: You will hear a woman phoning an agency to book a holiday cottage.

groups.instruction: Complete the form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

parts.context: You will hear a council officer talking to residents about preparing for floods.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.prompt: What caused most of the flooding last winter?
What will happen to the playing field?

options.A: It will store water during storms.
options.B: It will be replaced by a reservoir.
options.C: It will be raised above the flood level.

questions.prompt: Where should the emergency bag be kept?
Why should plugs be put in sinks and baths?

options.B: to stop dirty water coming up

questions.prompt: What does the officer say about sandbags?

options.A: The council no longer supplies them.
options.B: They are available from the sports centre.
options.C: They work better than door barriers.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good afternoon, Coast and Country Cottages. David speaking.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hello. I'm looking for a cottage for a week in August, somewhere near the sea. There'll be six of us.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Six. August is our busiest month, but let me see what's left. Which week?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The week beginning Saturday the ninth.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I've got two that sleep six. The first is Rose Cottage, in the village of Trennick. It's five minutes' walk from the beach.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That sounds ideal. What's it like?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Three bedrooms, one bathroom, and a small garden. It's an old fisherman's house, so the rooms are cosy. I should mention that the stairs are steep.

script.speaker: B
script.text: My father's eighty, and stairs are difficult for him. What's the other one?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Harbour View. It's a mile from the sea, on a hill, so you'd need the car to reach the beach. But it has a bedroom and a shower room on the ground floor.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That would suit Dad much better. How many bedrooms altogether?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Three. One downstairs and two up. There are two bathrooms.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And outside?

script.speaker: A
script.text: A large garden with a barbecue, and parking for two cars.

script.speaker: B
script.text: We'll have two cars, so that's good. Does it have a washing machine?

script.speaker: A
script.text: It does, and a dishwasher. There's no tumble dryer, but there's a washing line in the garden.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fine. What about the internet? The teenagers will ask.

script.speaker: A
script.text: There is wireless internet. The owner warns that it's slow, because the house is quite remote. Fine for messages, not for films.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That might be a good thing. How much is it?

script.speaker: A
script.text: For that week, nine hundred and eighty pounds. Rose Cottage would have been eleven hundred and fifty, as it's nearer the beach.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Nine eighty. Does that include everything?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Electricity and bed linen are included. You'd need to bring your own towels.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Towels. I'll make a note. We have a small dog. Is that allowed?

script.speaker: A
script.text: One dog is permitted at Harbour View, for an extra twenty-five pounds, to cover cleaning.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's fair. What time can we arrive?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Any time after four on the Saturday. You must leave by ten on the following Saturday.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And how do we get in?

script.speaker: A
script.text: There's a key safe by the front door. I'll send you the code a week before.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Lovely. I'd like to book it. What do you need from me?

script.speaker: A
script.text: A deposit of a quarter of the cost now, and the balance eight weeks before your stay. Can I take your surname?

script.speaker: B
script.text: It's Wetherall. W, E, T, H, E, R, A, double L.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thank you. And I'd suggest taking out cancellation insurance. We can't give refunds within eight weeks of the holiday.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good evening, and thank you for coming. I'm Renee Alvarez, from the council's emergency planning team. After last winter, I don't need to persuade anyone in this room that flooding is a real risk. What I'd like to do is explain what's being done, and what you can do yourselves.

script.speaker: C
script.text: First, the cause. Many of you blamed the river, and it did overflow. But our investigation found that two thirds of the homes affected were flooded from another source, which was the drains. The rain fell faster than the drains could carry it away, and water came up through the covers in the road.

script.speaker: C
script.text: So the council is spending four million pounds over three years. The largest share goes on bigger drains under Mill Lane and Station Road. We're also turning the playing field into a storage area. In a storm, it'll be allowed to fill with water, which will then be released slowly. It'll remain a playing field for the rest of the year.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Now, what you can do. Sign up for the free flood warning service. You'll get a text or a phone call when a warning is issued, usually several hours ahead.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Second, make a plan. Know how to turn off your gas, electricity and water. You'd be surprised how many people don't know where the switches are.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Third, prepare a bag. It should contain your insurance documents, any medicines, a torch, a phone charger, and warm clothes. Keep it upstairs, not under the stairs, which is the first place to flood.

script.speaker: C
script.text: When a warning comes, move your car to higher ground straight away. The car park at the sports centre will be open free of charge. Take valuables and electrical items upstairs. And put the plugs in your sinks and bath, and weigh them down, because dirty water can come up through the pipes.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A word about sandbags. The council no longer hands them out. They're slow to fill and they don't seal well. Barriers that clip across a doorway are far more effective, and there's a grant of up to five hundred pounds per household towards the cost. The form is at the back of the hall.

script.speaker: C
script.text: If your home does flood, don't walk through the water if you can avoid it. Fifteen centimetres of fast-flowing water will knock an adult over, and it's usually contaminated.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Afterwards, take photographs of everything before you clean up, for the insurance claim. And please check on your neighbours, particularly anyone elderly or living alone.

explanations.11: Two thirds of the affected homes were flooded from the drains.
explanations.12: It will fill with water in a storm and remain a playing field the rest of the year.
explanations.13: Under the stairs is the first place to flood.
explanations.14: Dirty water can come up through the pipes.
explanations.15: They are slow to fill and do not seal well.

title: Wind farm survey and the human microbiome

parts.context: You will hear two environmental studies students, Kate and Liam, discussing a survey of opinions about a proposed wind farm.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.prompt: What did the survey show about opinions on the wind farm?
Why does opposition appear greater than it is?

options.A: Opponents are more likely to attend meetings.
options.B: The newspaper is owned by an opponent.
options.C: Supporters did not answer the survey.

questions.prompt: What is the main objection to the wind farm?
What is the most common reason for supporting it?

options.C: the money offered to the villages

questions.prompt: Which factor was most closely linked to people's opinions?

options.A: how long they had lived in the area
options.C: how close they lived to the site

groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
groups.word_limit: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER
groups.text:
The survey received {{6}} replies.
Most people would like the fund to pay for a {{7}}.
One question will be left out because it was badly {{8}}.
The students will present their findings to the {{9}}.
Kate will write a summary that is {{10}} long.

parts.context: You will hear part of a biology lecture about the microbes that live in the human body.

groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Liam, I've been through the responses to our wind farm survey. There are some surprises.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good ones, I hope. How many replies?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Two hundred and six, from the three villages nearest the site.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And the headline? I'm guessing most people are against it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's what the local paper suggests. But in our survey, fifty-eight per cent are in favour, and only twenty-four per cent are opposed. The rest are undecided.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So the opposition is louder than it is large.

script.speaker: A
script.text: It seems so. The public meeting last month was packed with objectors, but those who approve tend not to go to meetings.

script.speaker: B
script.text: What reasons do the opponents give? Noise?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Noise is mentioned, but it's well down the list. The main objection, by far, is the effect on the view.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And the supporters?

script.speaker: A
script.text: This is interesting. I expected them to talk about the climate. Some do. But the most common reason is the community fund. The developer has promised to pay eighty thousand pounds a year to the villages.

script.speaker: B
script.text: So people support it because of a local benefit, not a global one.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes. And when we asked what the fund should be spent on, the top answer was a bus service, which the villages lost three years ago.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Did age make a difference?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Less than I'd assumed. Young and old were about equally in favour. What did matter was how long people had lived there. Those who'd moved in during the last ten years were much more likely to object.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Perhaps because they chose the area for its scenery.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That's my guess, but we didn't ask, so we can't claim it.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fair. Is there anything we got wrong in the design?

script.speaker: A
script.text: One question was badly worded. We asked, do you agree that wind farms are ugly and noisy? That's two questions in one.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Someone might think they're ugly but quiet.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Exactly. I think we have to leave that question out of the analysis.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Agreed. And for the report, should we name the villages?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Yes, but not individuals. Some of the written comments are quite personal.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Could we present the findings to the parish council? They'd be interested.

script.speaker: A
script.text: I've already been asked. They meet on the second Thursday of the month.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Then let's aim for that. I'll make the charts.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And I'll write a one-page summary for people who won't read the full report.

script.speaker: C
script.text: You probably think of yourself as an individual. A biologist might describe you differently, as a community. The human body contains about as many bacterial cells as human ones, most of them in the gut, and together they weigh about as much as the brain. This collection is known as the microbiome, and it's the subject of today's lecture.

script.speaker: C
script.text: For most of the twentieth century, medicine regarded bacteria almost entirely as enemies. That view has changed. The vast majority of our microbes are harmless, and many are essential.

script.speaker: C
script.text: What do they do for us? First, digestion. We can't break down many of the fibres in plants. Our gut bacteria can, and in the process they release substances that feed the cells lining the gut. Second, they manufacture certain vitamins. Third, simply by occupying the space, they prevent harmful species from settling.

script.speaker: C
script.text: And fourth, they train the immune system. A baby's immune system has to learn the difference between a threat and a friend, and it learns by meeting microbes. This may explain a striking pattern. Allergies and asthma have become far more common in wealthy countries. Children who grow up on farms, around animals, have much lower rates than children raised in cities.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Where do our microbes come from? The first arrive at birth, from the mother. More come from milk, from food, from pets and from soil. By the age of about three, a child's microbiome resembles an adult's.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Diet has a powerful influence. In a famous comparison, researchers studied children in a village in West Africa, who ate mainly grains and vegetables, and children in an Italian city. The African children had a far wider variety of gut bacteria. Variety seems to be a sign of health, and it's reduced by a diet that's low in fibre.

script.speaker: C
script.text: It's also reduced by antibiotics. These drugs save lives, and I'm not suggesting anyone refuse them. But they kill useful bacteria along with harmful ones, and after a course of treatment, the gut can take months to recover.

script.speaker: C
script.text: One of the most remarkable treatments to emerge from this research is the transplant of gut bacteria from a healthy donor. For one serious infection of the bowel, which kills thousands of patients in hospital every year, it cures about nine cases in ten, far more than any drug.

script.speaker: C
script.text: A caution to finish. You'll see claims that the microbiome explains everything from depression to obesity. Most of that evidence comes from experiments on mice, and it shows a link, not a cause. It's an exciting field, but a young one.

explanations.1: Fifty-eight per cent in favour and twenty-four per cent opposed.
explanations.2: The public meeting was packed with objectors; those who approve tend not to go.
explanations.3: Noise is well down the list; the main objection is the effect on the view.
explanations.4: The developer has promised a community fund of eighty thousand pounds a year.
explanations.5: People who had moved in during the last ten years were more likely to object.
